abstract: The major problem that has prevented practical application of analog neuro-LSIs has been poor accuracy due to fluctuating analog device characteristics inherent in each device as a result of manufacturing. This paper proposes a dynamic control architecture that allows analog silicon neural networks to compensate for the fluctuating device characteristics and adapt to a change in input DC level. We have applied this architecture to compensate for input offset voltages of an analog CMOS WTA (Winner-Take-AlI) chip that we have fabricated. Experimental data show the effectiveness of the architecture.
originalAbstract: The major problem that has prevented practical application of analog neuro-LSIs has been poor accuracy due to fluctuating analog device characteristics inherent in each device as a result of manufacturing. This paper proposes a dynamic control architecture that allows analog silicon neural networks to compensate for the fluctuating device characteristics and adapt to a change in input DC level. We have applied this architecture to compensate for input offset voltages of an analog CMOS WTA (Winner-Take-AlI) chip that we have fabricated. Experimental data show the effectiveness of the architecture.

paragraphs: Analog neural circuits can lose accuracy because manufacturing leaves individual electronic devices with differing characteristics. This paper addresses that practical obstacle through dynamic control. Its goal is to let a silicon neural network compensate for device variation while also adapting when the steady input level changes.

The authors apply their architecture to a fabricated CMOS winner-take-all chip. Such a circuit compares competing inputs and selects a winner, so unintended input offsets can distort the comparison. Compensating for these offset voltages addresses a concrete way in which the physical circuit can depart from its intended computation.

Experimental data show that the proposed control architecture is effective in this implementation. The significance lies in making adaptation part of the hardware's operation, allowing the circuit to respond to device characteristics and input conditions. The paper therefore connects a broad obstacle for analog neural systems with a demonstrated corrective mechanism on a specific chip. Its reported evidence concerns compensation in that fabricated winner-take-all implementation.
summary.tldr: Dynamic control compensates for device offsets and changing input levels in a fabricated analog winner-take-all chip.

title: Dynamically Adaptable CMOS Winner-Take-All Neural Network

abstract: The kernel-parameter is one of the few tunable parameters in Sup(cid:173) port Vector machines, controlling the complexity of the resulting hypothesis. Its choice amounts to model selection and its value is usually found by means of a validation set. We present an algo(cid:173) rithm which can automatically perform model selection with little additional computational cost and with no need of a validation set . In this procedure model selection and learning are not separate, but kernels are dynamically adjusted during the learning process to find the kernel parameter which provides the best possible upper bound on the generalisation error. Theoretical results motivating the approach and experimental results confirming its validity are presented.

paragraphs: The paper addresses model selection in support vector machines through the kernel parameter. This parameter controls the complexity of the learned hypothesis, so choosing it is part of deciding what kind of model to fit. The usual approach described by the authors uses a validation set to make that choice separately from training.

Their algorithm brings parameter selection into the learning process. It adjusts the kernel dynamically, seeking the parameter that gives the best possible upper bound on generalization error. The optimization target is therefore a bound on performance for unseen data. Improving this bound provides a principled selection criterion, although the bound and the actual generalization error are distinct quantities.

The authors report that the method needs no validation set and adds little computational cost. They provide theoretical motivation and experiments supporting the approach's validity. Its significance is the integration of two tasks normally handled separately: learning the classifier and selecting its kernel parameter. The claimed efficiency concerns this integrated procedure, while the theoretical objective explains how it chooses among parameter values.
summary.tldr: The method adapts SVM kernels during training to optimize a generalization-error bound without a validation set and with little added computation.

title: Dynamically Adapting Kernels in Support Vector Machines

abstract: We introduce a method of feature selection for Support Vector Machines. The method is based upon finding those features which minimize bounds on the leave-one-out error. This search can be efficiently performed via gradient descent. The resulting algorithms are shown to be superior to some standard feature selection algorithms on both toy data and real-life problems of face recognition, pedestrian detection and analyzing DNA micro array data.
originalAbstract: We introduce a method of feature selection for Support Vector Machines. The method is based upon finding those features which minimize bounds on the leave-one-out error. This search can be efficiently performed via gradient descent. The resulting algorithms are shown to be superior to some standard feature selection algorithms on both toy data and real-life problems of face recognition, pedestrian detection and analyzing DNA micro array data.

paragraphs: This paper introduces feature selection for support vector machines by tying the choice of inputs to a measure of predictive error. The goal is to find features that minimize bounds on leave-one-out error. That criterion connects feature choice to how the classifier would perform when individual training examples are withheld from fitting.

The method optimizes a bound on that error rather than treating feature selection as an unrelated preprocessing rule. The authors show that the search can be carried out efficiently with gradient descent. This creates a direct optimization route from a proposed set of features to a criterion intended to reflect the classifier's predictive behavior.

The resulting algorithms outperform some standard feature-selection methods in the reported tests. Those tests include toy data and real applications involving face recognition, pedestrian detection, and DNA microarray analysis. The evidence spans several kinds of input data, supporting the method's usefulness across the evaluated problems. The comparative claim concerns the methods and tasks studied, rather than all possible feature-selection approaches.
summary.tldr: The paper selects SVM features by minimizing leave-one-out error bounds with gradient descent and reports improvements over some standard methods.

title: Feature Selection for SVMs

abstract: An active set strategy is applied to the dual of a simple reformula(cid:173) tion of the standard quadratic program of a linear support vector machine. This application generates a fast new dual algorithm that consists of solving a finite number of linear equations, with a typically large dimensionality equal to the number of points to be classified. However, by making novel use of the Sherman-Morrison(cid:173) Woodbury formula, a much smaller matrix of the order of the orig(cid:173) inal input space is inverted at each step. Thus, a problem with a 32-dimensional input space and 7 million points required inverting positive definite symmetric matrices of size 33 x 33 with a total run(cid:173) ning time of 96 minutes on a 400 MHz Pentium II. The algorithm requires no specialized quadratic or linear programming code, but merely a linear equation solver which is publicly available.

paragraphs: Training a linear support vector machine involves an optimization problem whose size can become substantial when there are many examples. This paper develops a new algorithm by applying an active set strategy to the dual of a reformulated version of that problem. The resulting procedure solves a finite sequence of systems of linear equations.

Those systems would ordinarily have a dimension tied to the number of training points. The key computational step uses the Sherman–Morrison–Woodbury formula to replace the large matrix inversion with an inversion whose size is tied to the input dimension. This changes which aspect of the dataset determines the matrix size at each step.

The reported example contains seven million points with 32 input dimensions. Training requires inversions of symmetric positive definite matrices measuring 33 by 33 and takes 96 minutes on a 400 MHz Pentium II. The implementation needs an available linear equation solver rather than specialized quadratic or linear programming software. This demonstrates the approach's practicality for the reported large, low-dimensional problem.
summary.tldr: A reformulated linear SVM algorithm handles millions of examples by solving systems whose matrix size follows the input dimension.

title: Active Support Vector Machine Classification

abstract: Since the discovery that the best error-correcting decoding algo(cid:173) rithm can be viewed as belief propagation in a cycle-bound graph, researchers have been trying to determine under what circum(cid:173) stances "loopy belief propagation" is effective for probabilistic infer(cid:173) ence. Despite several theoretical advances in our understanding of loopy belief propagation, to our knowledge, the only problem that has been solved using loopy belief propagation is error-correcting decoding on Gaussian channels. We propose a new representation for the two-dimensional phase unwrapping problem, and we show that loopy belief propagation produces results that are superior to existing techniques. This is an important result, since many imag(cid:173) ing techniques, including magnetic resonance imaging and interfer(cid:173) ometric synthetic aperture radar, produce phase-wrapped images. Interestingly, the graph that we use has a very large number of very short cycles, supporting evidence that a large minimum cycle length is not needed for excellent results using belief propagation.

paragraphs: The paper investigates belief propagation on graphs containing cycles through the problem of two-dimensional phase unwrapping. Phase-wrapped images arise in imaging methods including magnetic resonance imaging and interferometric synthetic aperture radar. The authors propose a new representation of the unwrapping problem and use loopy belief propagation to perform inference within it.

They report results superior to existing techniques. This supplies an application beyond the error-correcting decoding setting that motivates their discussion of loopy inference. The representation is central to the contribution because it makes phase unwrapping a problem on which this inference procedure can be applied successfully.

The graph contains many very short cycles, yet the method still achieves excellent results. That observation supports the conclusion that a large minimum cycle length is not necessary for strong belief-propagation performance. It is evidence from the proposed application, rather than a claim that short cycles are harmless in every graph or that loopy belief propagation always produces accurate inference.
summary.tldr: A new phase-unwrapping representation lets loopy belief propagation outperform existing techniques despite having many very short graph cycles.

title: Very loopy belief propagation for unwrapping phase images

abstract: In this paper we introduce a new sparseness inducing prior which does not involve any (hy- per)parameters that need to be adjusted or estimated. Although other applications are possi- ble, we focus here on supervised learning problems: regression and classiﬁcation. Experi- ments with several publicly available benchmark data sets show that the proposed approach yields state-of-the-art performance. In particular, our method outperforms support vector machines and performs competitively with the best alternative techniques, both in terms of error rates and sparseness, although it involves no tuning or adjusting of sparseness- controlling hyper-parameters.
originalAbstract: In this paper we introduce a new sparseness inducing prior which does not involve any (hy- per)parameters that need to be adjusted or estimated. Although other applications are possi- ble, we focus here on supervised learning problems: regression and classiﬁcation. Experi- ments with several publicly available benchmark data sets show that the proposed approach yields state-of-the-art performance. In particular, our method outperforms support vector machines and performs competitively with the best alternative techniques, both in terms of error rates and sparseness, although it involves no tuning or adjusting of sparseness- controlling hyper-parameters.

paragraphs: Sparse learning seeks models that make useful predictions while relying on relatively few active components. This paper introduces a prior that encourages such sparseness without requiring its own adjustable or estimated hyperparameters. The central contribution is therefore a way to favor compact models without separately choosing how strongly this prior should encourage sparsity.

The authors focus on supervised regression and classification, although they identify the prior as potentially useful elsewhere. In these tasks, the challenge is to obtain a compact model while retaining predictive accuracy. Evaluating both error rates and sparseness matters because reducing model size alone would not establish that the resulting predictor remains useful.

Experiments on several public benchmark datasets report state-of-the-art performance. The method outperforms support vector machines and competes with the strongest alternative techniques in both error and sparseness. These are empirical findings for the evaluated tasks. The absence of tuning specifically concerns sparseness-controlling hyperparameters, which is the practical advantage emphasized alongside the reported predictive results.
summary.tldr: A sparsity-inducing prior avoids sparsity hyperparameter tuning while achieving strong benchmark results in regression and classification.

title: Adaptive Sparseness Using Jeffreys Prior

abstract: Time difference of arrival (TDOA) is commonly used to estimate the az- imuth of a source in a microphone array. The most common methods to estimate TDOA are based on ﬁnding extrema in generalized cross- correlation waveforms. In this paper we apply microphone array tech- niques to a manikin head. By considering the entire cross-correlation waveform we achieve azimuth prediction accuracy that exceeds extrema locating methods. We do so by quantizing the azimuthal angle and treating the prediction problem as a multiclass categorization task. We demonstrate the merits of our approach by evaluating the various ap- proaches on Sony’s AIBO robot.

The most common methods to estimate TDOA are based on ﬁnding extrema in generalized cross- correlation waveforms. In this paper we apply microphone array tech- niques to a manikin head. By considering the entire cross-correlation waveform we achieve azimuth prediction accuracy that exceeds extrema locating methods. paragraphs: The paper studies how to estimate a sound source's azimuth, or horizontal direction, from microphone signals. A common approach first estimates the difference in sound arrival time by locating an extremum in a generalized cross-correlation waveform. The authors investigate whether retaining the whole waveform can improve the direction estimate.

They apply microphone-array techniques to a manikin head and recast localization as classification. The azimuth angle is divided into discrete categories, and the task becomes predicting the appropriate category from the cross-correlation waveform. This changes both the information used for prediction and the form of the prediction problem.

The authors report greater azimuth prediction accuracy than methods that locate waveform extrema. They also evaluate the approaches on Sony's AIBO robot to demonstrate the method's merits. The result supports using more of the cross-correlation signal in the evaluated localization setting: its full shape provides a basis for discrimination beyond the single location selected by an extrema-based time-delay estimate.
summary.tldr: Classifying sound direction from the full cross-correlation waveform improves reported azimuth accuracy over extrema-based localization methods.

title: Discriminative Binaural Sound Localization

abstract: We present a new algorithm, Locally Smooth Manifold Learning (LSML), that learns a warping function from a point on an manifold to its neighbors. Important characteristics of LSML include the ability to recover the structure of the manifold in sparsely populated regions and beyond the support of the provided data. Appli- cations of our proposed technique include embedding with a natural out-of-sample extension and tasks such as tangent distance estimation, frame rate up-conversion, video compression and motion transfer.
originalAbstract: We present a new algorithm, Locally Smooth Manifold Learning (LSML), that learns a warping function from a point on an manifold to its neighbors. Important characteristics of LSML include the ability to recover the structure of the manifold in sparsely populated regions and beyond the support of the provided data. Appli- cations of our proposed technique include embedding with a natural out-of-sample extension and tasks such as tangent distance estimation, frame rate up-conversion, video compression and motion transfer.

paragraphs: The paper introduces Locally Smooth Manifold Learning, or LSML, which learns a warping function connecting a point on a manifold to its neighbors. In the image setting, the focus is on learning how to move between nearby points in the underlying structure. The learned object is therefore a local transformation that supports traversal.

The authors identify two important capabilities: recovering manifold structure in sparsely populated regions and extending beyond the support of the supplied data. These capabilities matter because the learned warping function describes relationships that can be used where observations are limited. The method's stated scope includes both movement among nearby examples and structure outside the observed support.

The proposed applications include embedding with a natural extension to new points, tangent-distance estimation, increasing video frame rate, video compression, and motion transfer. These uses connect the local transformation model to both representation and image-sequence tasks. The central contribution is a way to learn manifold movement, with the stated recovery capabilities making that movement useful beyond densely sampled portions of the data.
summary.tldr: LSML learns local warping functions to traverse image manifolds, including sparsely sampled regions and beyond the observed data support.

title: Learning to Traverse Image Manifolds

abstract: When individuals independently recollect events or retrieve facts from memory, how can we aggregate these retrieved memories to reconstruct the actual set of events or facts? In this research, we report the performance of individuals in a series of general knowledge tasks, where the goal is to reconstruct from memory the order of historic events, or the order of items along some physical dimension. We introduce two Bayesian models for aggregating order information based on a Thurstonian approach and Mallows model. Both models assume that each individuals reconstruction is based on either a random permutation of the unobserved ground truth, or by a pure guessing strategy. We apply MCMC to make inferences about the underlying truth and the strategies employed by individuals. The models demonstrate a wisdom of crowds" effect, where the aggregated orderings are closer to the true ordering than the orderings of the best individual."

In this research, we report the performance of individuals in a series of general knowledge tasks, where the goal is to reconstruct from memory the order of historic events, or the order of items along some physical dimension. We introduce two Bayesian models for aggregating order information based on a Thurstonian approach and Mallows model. Both models assume that each individuals reconstruction is based on either a random permutation of the unobserved ground truth, or by a pure guessing strategy. The models demonstrate a wisdom of crowds" effect, where the aggregated orderings are closer to the true ordering than the orderings of the best individual."

paragraphs: People remember the order of historical events or physical quantities imperfectly, but their errors need not be identical. This paper asks whether combining several remembered rankings can recover a more accurate ordering. The data come from general-knowledge tasks requiring participants to reconstruct order from memory.

Two Bayesian aggregation models use Thurstonian and Mallows formulations. Each allows a person’s answer to arise either from a noisy version of the hidden true ordering or from guessing. Markov-chain Monte Carlo jointly infers the underlying order and the strategies that best explain individual responses.

The aggregated rankings are closer to the truth than the best individual ranking, demonstrating a wisdom-of-crowds effect for order information. The contribution shows how an explicit model of memory noise and guessing can extract shared structure from imperfect recollections. Combining answers is valuable here because the model distinguishes informative variation from responses that carry little ordering evidence.
summary.tldr: Bayesian models aggregate noisy remembered rankings into orderings more accurate than those of the best individual participant.

title: The Wisdom of Crowds in the Recollection of Order Information

abstract: Existing methods for recognition of object instances and categories based on quantized local features can perform poorly when local features exist on transparent surfaces, such as glass or plastic objects. There are characteristic patterns to the local appearance of transparent objects, but they may not be well captured by distances to individual examples or by a local pattern codebook obtained by vector quantization. The appearance of a transparent patch is determined in part by the refraction of a background pattern through a transparent medium: the energy from the background usually dominates the patch appearance. We model transparent local patch appearance using an additive model of latent factors: background factors due to scene content, and factors which capture a local edge energy distribution characteristic of the refraction. We implement our method using a novel LDA-SIFT formulation which performs LDA prior to any vector quantization step; we discover latent topics which are characteristic of particular transparent patches and quantize the SIFT space into transparent visual words according to the latent topic dimensions. No knowledge of the background scene is required at test time; we show examples recognizing transparent glasses in a domestic environment.

paragraphs: Transparent objects are difficult to recognize from local image features because their appearance strongly reflects what lies behind them. A patch on glass or plastic contains background structure modified by refraction, and the background often dominates. Consequently, matching patches to individual examples or assigning them to conventional visual codewords can miss patterns characteristic of transparency.

The paper models a transparent patch as an additive combination of hidden factors. Some account for background scene content; others capture the distribution of local edge energy associated with refraction. Its LDA-SIFT formulation applies LDA before vector quantization, discovering latent topics associated with transparent patches. Those topic dimensions then guide the construction of transparent visual words.

This ordering matters because the representation can account for mixed background and refraction contributions before compressing local features into discrete categories. The method requires no knowledge of the background scene at test time. The authors demonstrate examples of recognizing transparent glasses in a domestic environment, illustrating how the learned representation can support recognition when background appearance is a major part of the observed object.
summary.tldr: An additive latent-feature representation separates background and refraction contributions to support transparent-object recognition without knowing the test-time background.

title: An Additive Latent Feature Model for Transparent Object Recognition

abstract: We describe a log-bilinear" model that computes class probabilities by combining an input vector multiplicatively with a vector of binary latent variables. Even though the latent variables can take on exponentially many possible combinations of values, we can efficiently compute the exact probability of each class by marginalizing over the latent variables. This makes it possible to get the exact gradient of the log likelihood. The bilinear score-functions are defined using a three-dimensional weight tensor, and we show that factorizing this tensor allows the model to encode invariances inherent in a task by learning a dictionary of invariant basis functions. Experiments on a set of benchmark problems show that this fully probabilistic model can achieve classification performance that is competitive with (kernel) SVMs, backpropagation, and deep belief nets."
originalAbstract: We describe a log-bilinear" model that computes class probabilities by combining an input vector multiplicatively with a vector of binary latent variables. Even though the latent variables can take on exponentially many possible combinations of values, we can efficiently compute the exact probability of each class by marginalizing over the latent variables. This makes it possible to get the exact gradient of the log likelihood. The bilinear score-functions are defined using a three-dimensional weight tensor, and we show that factorizing this tensor allows the model to encode invariances inherent in a task by learning a dictionary of invariant basis functions. Experiments on a set of benchmark problems show that this fully probabilistic model can achieve classification performance that is competitive with (kernel) SVMs, backpropagation, and deep belief nets."

paragraphs: Gated Softmax Classification models class probabilities through multiplicative interactions between an input vector and binary latent variables. These hidden variables have exponentially many possible joint configurations. The paper’s key computational result is that class probabilities can nevertheless be computed efficiently and exactly by summing out the latent variables.

Exact marginalization also makes the exact log-likelihood gradient available for learning. The model expresses its bilinear scores through a three-dimensional weight tensor. The authors show that factorizing this tensor lets the model learn a dictionary of invariant basis functions, providing a mechanism for encoding invariances inherent in the classification task.

Experiments on benchmark problems find classification performance competitive with kernel support vector machines, backpropagation, and deep belief networks. The stated result is competitiveness, rather than uniform superiority. The broader contribution combines expressive latent interactions with tractable probabilistic calculations: the model can account for many hidden configurations while retaining exact class probabilities and exact learning gradients, and its factorization offers a way to represent task-related invariance.
summary.tldr: A gated probabilistic classifier supports efficient exact latent-variable marginalization and uses tensor factorization to learn task invariances.

title: Gated Softmax Classification

abstract: Latent variable models are a powerful tool for addressing several tasks in machine learning. However, the algorithms for learning the parameters of latent variable models are prone to getting stuck in a bad local optimum. To alleviate this problem, we build on the intuition that, rather than considering all samples simultaneously, the algorithm should be presented with the training data in a meaningful order that facilitates learning. The order of the samples is determined by how easy they are. The main challenge is that often we are not provided with a readily computable measure of the easiness of samples. We address this issue by proposing a novel, iterative self-paced learning algorithm where each iteration simultaneously selects easy samples and learns a new parameter vector. The number of samples selected is governed by a weight that is annealed until the entire training data has been considered. We empirically demonstrate that the self-paced learning algorithm outperforms the state of the art method for learning a latent structural SVM on four applications: object localization, noun phrase coreference, motif finding and handwritten digit recognition.

paragraphs: Learning a latent-variable model can become trapped in a poor local optimum. This paper explores whether training examples can be introduced in an order that makes optimization easier. The motivating idea is to begin with easier examples and gradually include harder ones, but an appropriate measure of difficulty is often unavailable beforehand.

The proposed self-paced algorithm determines that ordering during training. Each iteration jointly selects easy samples and learns a new parameter vector. A weight controls how many examples are selected, and that weight is progressively adjusted until the full training set has been considered. Sample selection and parameter estimation therefore develop together.

Experiments compare the method with the state-of-the-art approach to learning a latent structural SVM across object localization, noun-phrase coreference, motif finding, and handwritten digit recognition. The self-paced method performs better in those four applications. These findings support adaptive example selection as a way to alleviate difficult optimization, without establishing that it always avoids poor local optima.
summary.tldr: Self-paced learning jointly selects easier examples and updates model parameters, gradually expanding training to all samples.

title: Self-Paced Learning for Latent Variable Models

abstract: We analyze the convergence of gradient-based optimization algorithms whose updates depend on delayed stochastic gradient information. The main application of our results is to the development of distributed minimization algorithms where a master node performs parameter updates while worker nodes compute stochastic gradients based on local information in parallel, which may give rise to delays due to asynchrony. Our main contribution is to show that for smooth stochastic problems, the delays are asymptotically negligible. In application to distributed optimization, we show $n$-node architectures whose optimization error in stochastic problems---in spite of asynchronous delays---scales asymptotically as $\order(1 / \sqrt{nT})$, which is known to be optimal even in the absence of delays.
originalAbstract: We analyze the convergence of gradient-based optimization algorithms whose updates depend on delayed stochastic gradient information. The main application of our results is to the development of distributed minimization algorithms where a master node performs parameter updates while worker nodes compute stochastic gradients based on local information in parallel, which may give rise to delays due to asynchrony. Our main contribution is to show that for smooth stochastic problems, the delays are asymptotically negligible. In application to distributed optimization, we show $n$-node architectures whose optimization error in stochastic problems---in spite of asynchronous delays---scales asymptotically as $\order(1 / \sqrt{nT})$, which is known to be optimal even in the absence of delays.

paragraphs: Distributed optimization can use several workers to compute stochastic gradients while a master node updates model parameters. When workers operate asynchronously, a gradient may arrive after the parameters have already changed. This paper analyzes gradient-based optimization with such delayed information, addressing whether the resulting staleness undermines the gains from parallel computation.

The main theoretical finding concerns smooth stochastic problems: delays become negligible asymptotically. This means their influence need not determine the dominant error behavior as computation proceeds. The qualification matters because the claim concerns long-run convergence in the analyzed setting, rather than saying that every delayed update has no effect.

For distributed optimization, the authors exhibit architectures with n nodes whose error scales asymptotically as O(1/√(nT)). That rate is optimal even without delays. The result therefore establishes that asynchronous delays can coexist with optimal asymptotic error scaling. It gives theoretical support for a master-worker arrangement in which parallel gradient computation need not sacrifice the leading convergence rate.
summary.tldr: For smooth stochastic problems, analyzed distributed algorithms achieve optimal asymptotic error scaling despite delayed gradients.

title: Distributed Delayed Stochastic Optimization

abstract: We seek to solve convex optimization problems in composite form: minimize n f (x) := g(x) + h(x), x∈R where g is convex and continuously differentiable and h : Rn → R is a convex but not necessarily differentiable function whose proximal mapping can be evaluated efficiently. We derive a generalization of Newton-type methods to handle such convex but nonsmooth objective functions. We prove such methods are globally convergent and achieve superlinear rates of convergence in the vicinity of an optimal solution. We also demonstrate the performance of these methods using problems of relevance in machine learning and statistics.
originalAbstract: We seek to solve convex optimization problems in composite form: minimize n f (x) := g(x) + h(x), x∈R where g is convex and continuously differentiable and h : Rn → R is a convex but not necessarily differentiable function whose proximal mapping can be evaluated efficiently. We derive a generalization of Newton-type methods to handle such convex but nonsmooth objective functions. We prove such methods are globally convergent and achieve superlinear rates of convergence in the vicinity of an optimal solution. We also demonstrate the performance of these methods using problems of relevance in machine learning and statistics.

paragraphs: The paper considers convex objectives made from two parts: a smooth function g and a convex function h that may be nonsmooth. It assumes that h has a proximal mapping that can be evaluated efficiently. This structure creates an opportunity to handle the smooth and nonsmooth contributions through different operations within the same optimization method.

The authors generalize Newton-type methods to this composite setting. The aim is to bring the fast local behavior associated with Newton methods to objectives that include nondifferentiable terms. The availability of an efficient proximal mapping is central to making the nonsmooth part compatible with the approach.

The paper proves global convergence and superlinear convergence near an optimal solution. These describe distinct aspects of performance: convergence of the method as a whole and an increasingly rapid reduction of error once sufficiently close to a solution. Demonstrations on problems from machine learning and statistics illustrate practical performance alongside the theoretical results for this structured class of convex objectives.
summary.tldr: Proximal Newton-type methods handle composite convex objectives with nonsmooth terms, with global convergence and superlinear convergence near a solution.

title: Proximal Newton-type methods for convex optimization

abstract: We consider streaming, one-pass principal component analysis (PCA), in the high-dimensional regime, with limited memory. Here, $p$-dimensional samples are presented sequentially, and the goal is to produce the $k$-dimensional subspace that best approximates these points. Standard algorithms require $O(p^2)$ memory; meanwhile no algorithm can do better than $O(kp)$ memory, since this is what the output itself requires. Memory (or storage) complexity is most meaningful when understood in the context of computational and sample complexity. Sample complexity for high-dimensional PCA is typically studied in the setting of the {\em spiked covariance model}, where $p$-dimensional points are generated from a population covariance equal to the identity (white noise) plus a low-dimensional perturbation (the spike) which is the signal to be recovered. It is now well-understood that the spike can be recovered when the number of samples, $n$, scales proportionally with the dimension, $p$. Yet, all algorithms that provably achieve this, have memory complexity $O(p^2)$. Meanwhile, algorithms with memory-complexity $O(kp)$ do not have provable bounds on sample complexity comparable to $p$. We present an algorithm that achieves both: it uses $O(kp)$ memory (meaning storage of any kind) and is able to compute the $k$-dimensional spike with $O(p \log p)$ sample-complexity -- the first algorithm of its kind. While our theoretical analysis focuses on the spiked covariance model, our simulations show that our algorithm is successful on much more general models for the data.

paragraphs: Streaming principal component analysis must recover a useful low-dimensional subspace while seeing high-dimensional samples sequentially. Memory is a central obstacle: standard methods require storage quadratic in the input dimension. Merely storing a k-dimensional subspace in p dimensions already requires order kp memory, establishing the output-sized storage target considered here.

The paper presents a one-pass algorithm using order kp storage of any kind. Under the spiked covariance model, it recovers the k-dimensional signal using order p log p samples. In that model, the covariance consists of white noise plus a low-dimensional signal component. The result combines small memory with a sample requirement close to linear in dimension.

This addresses a gap between methods with strong sample guarantees but quadratic memory and methods with output-sized memory lacking comparable sample guarantees. The theoretical analysis is specifically for the spiked covariance setting. Simulations also show success on more general data models, providing empirical evidence beyond the setting covered by the proof without extending the theorem to all such models.
summary.tldr: A one-pass PCA algorithm combines output-sized memory with near-linear sample complexity under the spiked covariance model.

title: Memory Limited, Streaming PCA

abstract: In this work we develop efficient methods for learning random MAP predictors for structured label problems. In particular, we construct posterior distributions over perturbations that can be adjusted via stochastic gradient methods. We show that every smooth posterior distribution would suffice to define a smooth PAC-Bayesian risk bound suitable for gradient methods. In addition, we relate the posterior distributions to computational properties of the MAP predictors. We suggest multiplicative posteriors to learn super-modular potential functions that accompany specialized MAP predictors such as graph-cuts. We also describe label-augmented posterior models that can use efficient MAP approximations, such as those arising from linear program relaxations.

We also describe label-augmented posterior models that can use efficient MAP approximations, such as those arising from linear program relaxations.

paragraphs: Structured prediction produces labels whose parts must be considered together. This paper develops efficient learning methods for randomized maximum-a-posteriori predictors, addressing non-decomposable loss functions. Its approach constructs posterior distributions over perturbations and adjusts those distributions using stochastic gradient methods.

A central theoretical result is that every smooth posterior distribution suffices to define a smooth PAC-Bayesian risk bound suitable for gradient optimization. This provides a connection between the randomization used by a predictor and an objective that can be optimized during learning. The authors also examine how choosing the posterior affects the computational properties of MAP prediction.

Two constructions make that connection concrete. Multiplicative posteriors are proposed for learning super-modular potentials compatible with specialized predictors such as graph cuts. Label-augmented posterior models can instead use efficient MAP approximations, including linear-program relaxations. The contribution therefore joins statistical learning criteria with computational structure, so posterior design can support both trainability and efficient structured prediction.
summary.tldr: Smooth perturbation posteriors enable gradient-based learning of randomized structured predictors while accommodating efficient MAP algorithms.

title: Learning Efficient Random Maximum A-Posteriori Predictors with Non-Decomposable Loss Functions

abstract: This paper addresses the problem of online planning in Markov Decision Processes using only a generative model. We propose a new algorithm which is based on the construction of a forest of single successor state planning trees. For every explored state-action, such a tree contains exactly one successor state, drawn from the generative model. The trees are built using a planning algorithm which follows the optimism in the face of uncertainty principle, in assuming the most favorable outcome in the absence of further information. In the decision making step of the algorithm, the individual trees are combined. We discuss the approach, prove that our proposed algorithm is consistent, and empirically show that it performs better than a related algorithm which additionally assumes the knowledge of all transition distributions.

paragraphs: Online planning in a Markov decision process requires choosing an action while accounting for uncertain future states. This paper addresses the setting where a planner has a generative model that can sample outcomes. The algorithm uses those samples to plan without requiring explicit knowledge of every transition distribution.

The method builds a forest of planning trees. Within each tree, every explored state-action pair has exactly one successor, sampled from the model. Tree construction follows optimism in the face of uncertainty: when information is incomplete, the planner assumes a favorable outcome. At decision time, it combines information from the individual trees to choose an action.

The authors prove consistency of the proposed algorithm and evaluate its practical performance. In their experiments, it outperforms a related method that additionally knows all transition distributions. The result supports the usefulness of aggregating simple sampled trees: a richer description of the environment does not, by itself, ensure better performance for the compared planning algorithm.
summary.tldr: Combining optimistic planning trees with one sampled successor per state-action pair yields a consistent planner using only a generative model.

title: Aggregating Optimistic Planning Trees for Solving Markov Decision Processes

abstract: We formalize the notion of a pseudo-ensemble, a (possibly infinite) collection of child models spawned from a parent model by perturbing it according to some noise process. E.g., dropout (Hinton et al, 2012) in a deep neural network trains a pseudo-ensemble of child subnetworks generated by randomly masking nodes in the parent network. We examine the relationship of pseudo-ensembles, which involve perturbation in model-space, to standard ensemble methods and existing notions of robustness, which focus on perturbation in observation-space. We present a novel regularizer based on making the behavior of a pseudo-ensemble robust with respect to the noise process generating it. In the fully-supervised setting, our regularizer matches the performance of dropout. But, unlike dropout, our regularizer naturally extends to the semi-supervised setting, where it produces state-of-the-art results. We provide a case study in which we transform the Recursive Neural Tensor Network of (Socher et al, 2013) into a pseudo-ensemble, which significantly improves its performance on a real-world sentiment analysis benchmark.

paragraphs: A pseudo-ensemble is a collection of models created by randomly perturbing one parent model. The collection may even be infinite. Dropout provides an example: randomly masking nodes creates different child subnetworks. The paper uses this perspective to study variation in the model itself, alongside ensemble learning and robustness approaches that perturb observations.

The authors introduce a regularizer that encourages the pseudo-ensemble's behavior to remain robust to the noise used to generate its members. The organizing idea is consistency under model perturbations. This provides a training principle that can be applied to a family of child models instead of treating their random differences only as a training device.

In fully supervised learning, the regularizer matches dropout's performance. It also extends naturally to semi-supervised learning, where the authors report state-of-the-art results. A separate sentiment-analysis case study converts a Recursive Neural Tensor Network into a pseudo-ensemble and significantly improves its benchmark performance. These findings show the framework's usefulness across the stated learning settings and one concrete model transformation.
summary.tldr: Regularizing consistency among randomly perturbed child models matches dropout in supervised learning and delivers strong semi-supervised and sentiment-analysis results.

title: Learning with Pseudo-Ensembles

abstract: We propose a new first-order optimization algorithm to solve high-dimensional non-smooth composite minimization problems. Typical examples of such problems have an objective that decomposes into a non-smooth empirical risk part and a non-smooth regularization penalty. The proposed algorithm, called Semi-Proximal Mirror-Prox, leverages the saddle point representation of one part of the objective while handling the other part of the objective via linear minimization over the domain. The algorithm stands in contrast with more classical proximal gradient algorithms with smoothing, which require the computation of proximal operators at each iteration and can therefore be impractical for high-dimensional problems. We establish the theoretical convergence rate of Semi-Proximal Mirror-Prox, which exhibits the optimal complexity bounds for the number of calls to linear minimization oracle. We present promising experimental results showing the interest of the approach in comparison to competing methods.

paragraphs: Many learning objectives combine a data-fitting loss with a regularization penalty, and both components can be nonsmooth. In high dimensions, classical proximal-gradient approaches with smoothing can become impractical because they require a proximal operator at every iteration. This paper proposes a first-order method for handling such composite optimization problems.

Semi-Proximal Mirror-Prox treats the objective's parts through different operations. It uses a saddle-point representation for one part and linear minimization over the domain for the other. This arrangement provides a way to work with the composite structure when repeatedly computing the proximal operations required by more classical methods would be costly.

The authors establish a convergence rate with optimal complexity bounds for the number of calls to a linear minimization oracle. That guarantee concerns a specific computational resource: how often the algorithm must solve its linear minimization subproblem. Experiments provide promising comparisons with competing methods. Together, the theoretical and empirical results support this combination of saddle-point optimization and linear minimization for high-dimensional nonsmooth objectives.
summary.tldr: Semi-Proximal Mirror-Prox combines saddle-point methods and linear minimization with optimal linear-oracle complexity for nonsmooth composite optimization.

title: Semi-Proximal Mirror-Prox for Nonsmooth Composite Minimization

abstract: Stochastic gradient-based Monte Carlo methods such as stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics are useful tools for posterior inference on large scale datasets in many machine learning applications. These methods scale to large datasets by using noisy gradients calculated using a mini-batch or subset of the dataset. However, the high variance inherent in these noisy gradients degrades performance and leads to slower mixing. In this paper, we present techniques for reducing variance in stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics, yielding novel stochastic Monte Carlo methods that improve performance by reducing the variance in the stochastic gradient. We show that our proposed method has better theoretical guarantees on convergence rate than stochastic Langevin dynamics. This is complemented by impressive empirical results obtained on a variety of real world datasets, and on four different machine learning tasks (regression, classification, independent component analysis and mixture modeling). These theoretical and empirical contributions combine to make a compelling case for using variance reduction in stochastic Monte Carlo methods.

paragraphs: Stochastic gradient Monte Carlo methods make posterior inference practical on large datasets by computing gradients from small subsets of observations. This reduces the cost of an update, but the resulting gradients can have high variance. In stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics, that variability can impair performance and slow movement through the target distribution.

The paper introduces variance-reduction techniques for these gradient estimates, yielding new stochastic Monte Carlo methods. The objective is to retain the computational benefits of using subsets while reducing the variability that undermines sampling. This addresses the quality of the information driving each update, which directly influences the method's convergence behavior.

The authors establish better theoretical convergence-rate guarantees than stochastic Langevin dynamics. They also report strong empirical results on real-world datasets spanning regression, classification, independent component analysis, and mixture modeling. These findings supply both analytical and experimental support for variance reduction in stochastic sampling. The range of tested tasks shows its usefulness across several inference problems, while the theoretical result specifically concerns improved convergence guarantees.
summary.tldr: Reducing stochastic-gradient variance improves Langevin sampling's theoretical convergence guarantees and empirical performance across four learning tasks.

title: Variance Reduction in Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics

abstract: A number of recent works have proposed attention models for Visual Question Answering (VQA) that generate spatial maps highlighting image regions relevant to answering the question. In this paper, we argue that in addition to modeling "where to look" or visual attention, it is equally important to model "what words to listen to" or question attention. We present a novel co-attention model for VQA that jointly reasons about image and question attention. In addition, our model reasons about the question (and consequently the image via the co-attention mechanism) in a hierarchical fashion via a novel 1-dimensional convolution neural networks (CNN). Our model improves the state-of-the-art on the VQA dataset from 60.3% to 60.5%, and from 61.6% to 63.3% on the COCO-QA dataset. By using ResNet, the performance is further improved to 62.1% for VQA and 65.4% for COCO-QA.

paragraphs: Visual question answering requires identifying image evidence that addresses a question. Attention models often handle this by highlighting relevant image regions. This paper argues that selecting the relevant parts of the question is equally important: the model needs to determine which language information should guide its interpretation of the image.

The proposed co-attention model reasons jointly about attention over the image and the question. It also processes the question hierarchically using a one-dimensional convolutional neural network. Through co-attention, that hierarchy influences image reasoning as well. The approach therefore connects language selection and visual selection instead of treating the question only as a fixed instruction for locating image regions.

The reported VQA result increases from 60.3% to 60.5%, while COCO-QA increases from 61.6% to 63.3%. Using ResNet raises the reported results further to 62.1% and 65.4%, respectively. These benchmark findings support the usefulness of joint question-image attention, with different improvement sizes across the datasets and an additional benefit reported when ResNet is used.
summary.tldr: Hierarchical co-attention jointly selects relevant question content and image regions, improving reported visual question answering results.

title: Hierarchical Question-Image Co-Attention for Visual Question Answering

abstract: Controlled interventions provide the most direct source of information for learning causal effects. In particular, a dose-response curve can be learned by varying the treatment level and observing the corresponding outcomes. However, interventions can be expensive and time-consuming. Observational data, where the treatment is not controlled by a known mechanism, is sometimes available. Under some strong assumptions, observational data allows for the estimation of dose-response curves. Estimating such curves nonparametrically is hard: sample sizes for controlled interventions may be small, while in the observational case a large number of measured confounders may need to be marginalized. In this paper, we introduce a hierarchical Gaussian process prior that constructs a distribution over the dose-response curve by learning from observational data, and reshapes the distribution with a nonparametric affine transform learned from controlled interventions. This function composition from different sources is shown to speed-up learning, which we demonstrate with a thorough sensitivity analysis and an application to modeling the effect of therapy on cognitive skills of premature infants.

paragraphs: A dose-response curve describes how outcomes change with treatment level. Controlled interventions provide direct causal information, but collecting them can be costly and slow. Observational data may offer additional information, although causal estimation from it requires strong assumptions and can involve accounting for many measured confounders. These difficulties motivate combining the two sources.

The paper introduces a hierarchical Gaussian process prior that first learns a distribution over dose-response curves from observational data. It then reshapes that distribution using a nonparametric affine transformation learned from controlled interventions. This gives each source a distinct role: observational evidence informs the initial curve distribution, and experimental evidence learns how to adjust it.

The authors show that this composition can accelerate learning, supporting the claim through a sensitivity analysis and an application involving therapy and cognitive skills in premature infants. The finding concerns learning the dose-response relationship, rather than establishing a particular therapeutic outcome. The approach matters because it supplies a structured way to use observational information while allowing controlled data to modify what that information suggests.
summary.tldr: A hierarchical Gaussian process combines observationally learned dose-response curves with intervention-based adjustments to accelerate learning.

title: Observational-Interventional Priors for Dose-Response Learning

abstract: Recognizing facial action units (AUs) from spontaneous facial expressions is still a challenging problem. Most recently, CNNs have shown promise on facial AU recognition. However, the learned CNNs are often overfitted and do not generalize well to unseen subjects due to limited AU-coded training images. We proposed a novel Incremental Boosting CNN (IB-CNN) to integrate boosting into the CNN via an incremental boosting layer that selects discriminative neurons from the lower layer and is incrementally updated on successive mini-batches. In addition, a novel loss function that accounts for errors from both the incremental boosted classifier and individual weak classifiers was proposed to fine-tune the IB-CNN. Experimental results on four benchmark AU databases have demonstrated that the IB-CNN yields significant improvement over the traditional CNN and the boosting CNN without incremental learning, as well as outperforming the state-of-the-art CNN-based methods in AU recognition. The improvement is more impressive for the AUs that have the lowest frequencies in the databases.

paragraphs: Recognizing facial action units from spontaneous expressions is difficult when only limited labeled training images are available. Convolutional networks can overfit those images and generalize poorly to unseen people. This paper introduces Incremental Boosting CNN, or IB-CNN, to address that problem by integrating boosting into the network.

Its incremental boosting layer selects discriminative neurons from the layer below and updates across successive mini-batches. The authors also introduce a loss function that accounts for errors made by both the combined boosted classifier and its individual weak classifiers. Fine-tuning therefore considers the quality of the component classifiers alongside the performance of their combination.

Across four benchmark action-unit databases, IB-CNN significantly improves on a traditional CNN and a boosting CNN without incremental learning. It also outperforms the compared state-of-the-art CNN methods. The gains are especially pronounced for action units with the lowest frequencies in the databases. These findings support the usefulness of incremental boosting when labeled examples are limited and some target units appear infrequently.
summary.tldr: IB-CNN integrates incremental boosting into a convolutional network and improves facial action-unit recognition, especially for infrequent units.

title: Incremental Boosting Convolutional Neural Network for Facial Action Unit Recognition

abstract: Recovering high-resolution images from limited sensory data typically leads to a serious ill-posed inverse problem, demanding inversion algorithms that effectively capture the prior information. Learning a good inverse mapping from training data faces severe challenges, including: (i) scarcity of training data; (ii) need for plausible reconstructions that are physically feasible; (iii) need for fast reconstruction, especially in real-time applications. We develop a successful system solving all these challenges, using as basic architecture the repetitive application of alternating proximal and data fidelity constraints. We learn a proximal map that works well with real images based on residual networks with recurrent blocks. Extensive experiments are carried out under different settings: (a) reconstructing abdominal MRI of pediatric patients from highly undersampled k-space data and (b) super-resolving natural face images. Our key findings include: 1. a recurrent ResNet with a single residual block (10-fold repetition) yields an effective proximal which accurately reveals MR image details. 2. Our architecture significantly outperforms conventional non-recurrent deep ResNets by 2dB SNR; it is also trained much more rapidly. 3. It outperforms state-of-the-art compressed-sensing Wavelet-based methods by 4dB SNR, with 100x speedups in reconstruction time.

paragraphs: Recovering detailed images from limited measurements requires prior knowledge because the observed data alone may not determine a unique reconstruction. This paper combines a learned image prior with explicit data-fidelity constraints. Its architecture repeatedly alternates between a learned proximal operation and a step enforcing agreement with the measurements.

The proximal map is learned using residual networks with recurrent blocks. Repetition allows the same learned component to participate in successive reconstruction steps. The authors study abdominal MRI reconstruction from highly undersampled measurements in pediatric patients and super-resolution of natural face images. These applications test the approach in different image-recovery settings.

A single residual block repeated ten times is reported to produce an effective proximal map that reveals MRI details accurately. The architecture improves signal-to-noise ratio by 2 dB over conventional non-recurrent deep residual networks and trains faster. Against state-of-the-art wavelet-based compressed-sensing methods, the reported gains are 4 dB and a hundredfold reconstruction speedup. These experimental findings support combining learned image structure with measurement consistency in a recurrent reconstruction procedure.
summary.tldr: A recurrent learned proximal map alternates with measurement-consistency constraints to deliver accurate, fast image reconstruction in the evaluated settings.

title: Neural Proximal Gradient Descent for Compressive Imaging

abstract: In this paper we propose to use a denoising autoencoder (DAE) prior to simultaneously solve a linear inverse problem and estimate its noise parameter. Existing DAE-based methods estimate the noise parameter empirically or treat it as a tunable hyper-parameter. We instead propose autoencoder guided EM, a probabilistically sound framework that performs Bayesian inference with intractable deep priors. We show that efficient posterior sampling from the DAE can be achieved via Metropolis-Hastings, which allows the Monte Carlo EM algorithm to be used. We demonstrate competitive results for signal denoising, image deblurring and image devignetting. Our method is an example of combining the representation power of deep learning with uncertainty quantification from Bayesian statistics.

Existing DAE-based methods estimate the noise parameter empirically or treat it as a tunable hyper-parameter. We instead propose autoencoder guided EM, a probabilistically sound framework that performs Bayesian inference with intractable deep priors. We show that efficient posterior sampling from the DAE can be achieved via Metropolis-Hastings, which allows the Monte Carlo EM algorithm to be used. We demonstrate competitive results for signal denoising, image deblurring and image devignetting. paragraphs: Linear inverse problems involve recovering a signal from observations that have been transformed and corrupted by noise. A denoising autoencoder can supply a learned prior to guide this recovery. However, existing methods using such priors estimate the noise parameter empirically or leave it as a setting that must be tuned.

Autoencoder guided EM, or AGEM, jointly addresses signal recovery and noise estimation. It provides a Bayesian inference framework for deep priors whose probability calculations are intractable. The authors show how to obtain efficient posterior samples using Metropolis-Hastings, enabling a Monte Carlo version of expectation-maximization to work with the autoencoder prior.

The method produces competitive results on signal denoising, image deblurring, and image devignetting. Its significance is the integration of learned representations with uncertainty-aware statistical inference: the deep prior guides reconstruction while the inference procedure also estimates the noise parameter. The reported applications demonstrate this combination across several recovery tasks without requiring noise to remain an externally tuned hyperparameter.
summary.tldr: AGEM combines denoising autoencoder priors with posterior sampling to reconstruct signals and estimate their noise parameter jointly.

title: AGEM: Solving Linear Inverse Problems via Deep Priors and Sampling

abstract: This paper investigates the evaluation of learned multiagent strategies in the incomplete information setting, which plays a critical role in ranking and training of agents. Traditionally, researchers have relied on Elo ratings for this purpose, with recent works also using methods based on Nash equilibria. Unfortunately, Elo is unable to handle intransitive agent interactions, and other techniques are restricted to zero-sum, two-player settings or are limited by the fact that the Nash equilibrium is intractable to compute. Recently, a ranking method called $\alpha$-Rank, relying on a new graph-based game-theoretic solution concept, was shown to tractably apply to general games. However, evaluations based on Elo or $\alpha$-Rank typically assume noise-free game outcomes, despite the data often being collected from noisy simulations, making this assumption unrealistic in practice. This paper investigates multiagent evaluation in the incomplete information regime, involving general-sum many-player games with noisy outcomes. We derive sample complexity guarantees required to confidently rank agents in this setting. We propose adaptive algorithms for accurate ranking, provide correctness and sample complexity guarantees, then introduce a means of connecting uncertainties in noisy match outcomes to uncertainties in rankings. We evaluate the performance of these approaches in several domains, including Bernoulli games, a soccer meta-game, and Kuhn poker.
originalAbstract: This paper investigates the evaluation of learned multiagent strategies in the incomplete information setting, which plays a critical role in ranking and training of agents. Traditionally, researchers have relied on Elo ratings for this purpose, with recent works also using methods based on Nash equilibria. Unfortunately, Elo is unable to handle intransitive agent interactions, and other techniques are restricted to zero-sum, two-player settings or are limited by the fact that the Nash equilibrium is intractable to compute. Recently, a ranking method called $\alpha$-Rank, relying on a new graph-based game-theoretic solution concept, was shown to tractably apply to general games. However, evaluations based on Elo or $\alpha$-Rank typically assume noise-free game outcomes, despite the data often being collected from noisy simulations, making this assumption unrealistic in practice. This paper investigates multiagent evaluation in the incomplete information regime, involving general-sum many-player games with noisy outcomes. We derive sample complexity guarantees required to confidently rank agents in this setting. We propose adaptive algorithms for accurate ranking, provide correctness and sample complexity guarantees, then introduce a means of connecting uncertainties in noisy match outcomes to uncertainties in rankings. We evaluate the performance of these approaches in several domains, including Bernoulli games, a soccer meta-game, and Kuhn poker.

paragraphs: Ranking agents is difficult when winning relationships form cycles and match outcomes are noisy. Elo cannot represent intransitive interactions, while some equilibrium-based alternatives face restrictions or computational obstacles. Alpha-Rank provides a tractable approach for general games, but evaluations commonly treat observed outcomes as if they were free of noise.

This paper studies ranking when information comes from noisy outcomes in games with many players and potentially different interests. It derives sample-complexity guarantees, addressing how much evidence is needed to rank agents confidently. The authors also propose adaptive ranking algorithms and establish correctness and sampling guarantees for those procedures.

Another contribution connects uncertainty about individual match outcomes with uncertainty about the resulting rankings. This makes the reliability of a ranking part of the evaluation problem itself. The approaches are evaluated on Bernoulli games, a soccer meta-game, and Kuhn poker. Together, the contributions provide a framework for reasoning about evaluation confidence when simulated matches supply incomplete and noisy evidence.
summary.tldr: Adaptive ranking algorithms and sampling guarantees support confident multiagent evaluation from noisy match outcomes.

title: Multiagent Evaluation under Incomplete Information

abstract: In recent studies, several asymptotic upper bounds on generalization errors on deep neural networks (DNNs) are theoretically derived. These bounds are functions of several norms of weights of the DNNs, such as the Frobenius and spectral norms, and they are computed for weights grouped according to either input and output channels of the DNNs. In this work, we conjecture that if we can impose multiple constraints on weights of DNNs to upper bound the norms of the weights, and train the DNNs with these weights, then we can attain empirical generalization errors closer to the derived theoretical bounds, and improve accuracy of the DNNs. To this end, we pose two problems. First, we aim to obtain weights whose different norms are all upper bounded by a constant number. To achieve these bounds, we propose a two-stage renormalization procedure; (i) normalization of weights according to different norms used in the bounds, and (ii) reparameterization of the normalized weights to set a constant and finite upper bound of their norms. In the second problem, we consider training DNNs with these renormalized weights. To this end, we first propose a strategy to construct joint spaces (manifolds) of weights according to different constraints in DNNs. Next, we propose a fine-grained SGD algorithm (FG-SGD) for optimization on the weight manifolds to train DNNs with assurance of convergence to minima. Experimental analyses show that image classification accuracy of baseline DNNs can be boosted using FG-SGD on collections of manifolds identified by multiple constraints.

paragraphs: Some theoretical bounds on neural-network generalization depend on several measures of weight size, including Frobenius and spectral norms. This paper conjectures that jointly constraining these quantities during training could bring empirical errors closer to those bounds and improve accuracy. Image-classification experiments show that applying FG-SGD to collections of manifolds defined by multiple constraints can improve baseline networks' accuracy. The empirical finding supports the usefulness of the training method, while remaining distinct from the motivating conjecture about closeness to theoretical generalization bounds.
summary.tldr: FG-SGD trains neural networks on weight manifolds with multiple norm constraints and improves image-classification accuracy in experiments.

title: Fine-grained Optimization of Deep Neural Networks

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms have demonstrated promising results on complex tasks, yet often require impractical numbers of samples because they learn from scratch. Meta-RL aims to address this challenge by leveraging experience from previous tasks so as to more quickly solve new tasks. However, in practice, these algorithms generally also require large amounts of on-policy experience during the \emph{meta-training} process, making them impractical for use in many problems. To this end, we propose to learn a reinforcement learning procedure in a federated way, where individual off-policy learners can solve the individual meta-training tasks, and then consolidate these solutions into a single meta-learner. Since the central meta-learner learns by imitating the solutions to the individual tasks, it can accommodate either the standard meta-RL problem setting, or a hybrid setting where some or all tasks are provided with example demonstrations. The former results in an approach that can leverage policies learned for previous tasks without significant amounts of on-policy data during meta-training, whereas the latter is particularly useful in cases where demonstrations are easy for a person to provide. Across a number of continuous control meta-RL problems, we demonstrate significant improvements in meta-RL sample efficiency in comparison to prior work as well as the ability to scale to domains with visual observations.

paragraphs: Meta-reinforcement learning tries to make new tasks easier by learning from earlier ones. However, training the meta-learner can itself require large amounts of experience collected under its current policy. This paper targets that training burden, which can undermine the practical benefit of faster adaptation.

The approach distributes the work across individual off-policy learners that solve separate training tasks. A central meta-learner then imitates their solutions, consolidating them into a learned reinforcement learning procedure. Because the central learner learns from solutions, it can also accept demonstrations for some or all tasks. The same framework therefore accommodates both ordinary meta-RL and a mixture of learned task policies and examples.

In the ordinary setting, this enables reuse of previously learned policies without significant on-policy data collection during meta-training. Demonstrations offer another route when people can provide examples easily. Across continuous-control problems, the authors report substantial improvements in meta-RL sample efficiency over prior work and show that the approach can scale to tasks with visual observations.
summary.tldr: Guided meta-policy search improves sample efficiency by training a central meta-learner to imitate separately learned task policies or demonstrations.

title: Guided Meta-Policy Search

abstract: In this paper, we introduce a novel technique for constrained submodular maximization, inspired by barrier functions in continuous optimization. This connection not only improves the running time for constrained submodular maximization but also provides the state of the art guarantee. More precisely, for maximizing a monotone submodular function subject to the combination of a $k$-matchoid and $\ell$-knapsack constraints (for $\ell\leq k$), we propose a potential function that can be approximately minimized. Once we minimize the potential function up to an $\epsilon$ error, it is guaranteed that we have found a feasible set with a $2(k+1+\epsilon)$-approximation factor which can indeed be further improved to $(k+1+\epsilon)$ by an enumeration technique. We extensively evaluate the performance of our proposed algorithm over several real-world applications, including a movie recommendation system, summarization tasks for YouTube videos, Twitter feeds and Yelp business locations, and a set cover problem.

paragraphs: Submodular maximization selects a set whose value exhibits diminishing returns as elements are added. This paper considers a monotone objective under a combination of structural and budget constraints. It introduces a technique inspired by barrier functions in continuous optimization, using a potential function to connect constrained set selection with an approximate minimization problem.

The guarantee applies to a k-matchoid together with ell knapsack constraints, provided ell is no greater than k. Minimizing the proposed potential to within epsilon error guarantees a feasible solution with approximation factor 2(k+1+epsilon). An enumeration technique improves that factor to k+1+epsilon. These factors express a worst-case comparison with the optimal feasible objective value.

The authors state that the technique improves running time and provides a state-of-the-art guarantee. They also evaluate it across movie recommendation, summaries of YouTube videos and Twitter feeds, Yelp business locations, and a set cover problem. The main contribution is a reusable optimization connection: approximate minimization of a carefully constructed potential provides a route to feasible sets with explicit quality guarantees under combined constraints.
summary.tldr: A barrier-inspired potential function yields improved runtime and approximation guarantees for submodular maximization under combined constraints.

title: Submodular Maximization Through Barrier Functions

abstract: Few-shot learning has recently emerged as a new challenge in the deep learning field: unlike conventional methods that train the deep neural networks (DNNs) with a large number of labeled data, it asks for the generalization of DNNs on new classes with few annotated samples. Recent advances in few-shot learning mainly focus on image classification while in this paper we focus on object detection. The initial explorations in few-shot object detection tend to simulate a classification scenario by using the positive proposals in images with respect to certain object class while discarding the negative proposals of that class. Negatives, especially hard negatives, however, are essential to the embedding space learning in few-shot object detection. In this paper, we restore the negative information in few-shot object detection by introducing a new negative- and positive-representative based metric learning framework and a new inference scheme with negative and positive representatives. We build our work on a recent few-shot pipeline RepMet with several new modules to encode negative information for both training and testing. Extensive experiments on ImageNet-LOC and PASCAL VOC show our method substantially improves the state-of-the-art few-shot object detection solutions. Our code is available at https://github.com/yang-yk/NP-RepMet.
