paragraphs: Few-shot object detection asks a model to recognize and locate new object classes from only a few annotated examples. This paper identifies a problem in early approaches that emphasize positive candidate regions while discarding regions that are negative for the class. That simplification loses information the authors regard as essential for learning a useful embedding space.

The proposed method represents both positive and negative examples in a metric-learning framework. It builds on RepMet, adding modules that encode negative information during training and testing. A corresponding inference scheme uses both kinds of representatives when making predictions, so negatives influence the final decision as well as the learned representation.

Hard negatives are particularly relevant because they supply challenging distinctions for the embedding to capture. Experiments on ImageNet-LOC and PASCAL VOC report substantial improvements over state-of-the-art few-shot detection solutions. The findings support treating negative evidence as an explicit part of the detector's learning and prediction process when examples of new classes are scarce.
summary.tldr: Explicit positive and negative representatives improve few-shot object detection by restoring negative evidence during training and prediction.

title: Restoring Negative Information in Few-Shot Object Detection

abstract: The current dominant paradigm in sensorimotor control, whether imitation or reinforcement learning, is to train policies directly in raw action spaces such as torque, joint angle, or end-effector position. This forces the agent to make decision at each point in training, and hence, limits the scalability to continuous, high-dimensional, and long-horizon tasks. In contrast, research in classical robotics has, for a long time, exploited dynamical systems as a policy representation to learn robot behaviors via demonstrations. These techniques, however, lack the flexibility and generalizability provided by deep learning or deep reinforcement learning and have remained under-explored in such settings. In this work, we begin to close this gap and embed dynamics structure into deep neural network-based policies by reparameterizing action spaces with differential equations. We propose Neural Dynamic Policies (NPDs) that make predictions in trajectory distribution space as opposed to prior policy learning methods where action represents the raw control space. The embedded structure allows us to perform end-to-end policy learning under both reinforcement and imitation learning setups. We show that NDPs achieve better or comparable performance to state-of-the-art approaches on many robotic control tasks using both reward-based training and demonstrations. Project video and code are available at: https://shikharbahl.github.io/neural-dynamic-policies/.

paragraphs: Many robot-learning policies directly choose commands such as torques or joint angles at each decision point. This places repeated decision-making demands on the policy, especially for continuous, high-dimensional tasks extending over time. Classical robotics offers another representation through dynamical systems, but the abstract identifies a gap between that structure and the flexibility of deep learning.

Neural Dynamic Policies connect these approaches by using differential equations to reparameterize the action space. The network predicts in a space of trajectory distributions, embedding dynamics into how behavior is represented. This gives the policy a structured way to express motion over time while supporting end-to-end optimization of the neural model.

The framework works with both reinforcement learning from rewards and imitation learning from demonstrations. Across many robotic control tasks, the authors report performance that is better than or comparable to leading approaches. These results support the usefulness of embedding dynamical structure in learned policies without claiming improvement on every task or under every training setup.
summary.tldr: Neural Dynamic Policies embed differential-equation structure into trajectory predictions, enabling end-to-end robot learning from rewards or demonstrations.

title: Neural Dynamic Policies for End-to-End Sensorimotor Learning

abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (RL) agents trained in a limited set of environments tend to suffer overfitting and fail to generalize to unseen testing environments. To improve their generalizability, data augmentation approaches (e.g. cutout and random convolution) are previously explored to increase the data diversity. However, we find these approaches only locally perturb the observations regardless of the training environments, showing limited effectiveness on enhancing the data diversity and the generalization performance. In this work, we introduce a simple approach, named mixreg, which trains agents on a mixture of observations from different training environments and imposes linearity constraints on the observation interpolations and the supervision (e.g. associated reward) interpolations. Mixreg increases the data diversity more effectively and helps learn smoother policies. We verify its effectiveness on improving generalization by conducting extensive experiments on the large-scale Procgen benchmark. Results show mixreg outperforms the well-established baselines on unseen testing environments by a large margin. Mixreg is simple, effective and general. It can be applied to both policy-based and value-based RL algorithms. Code is available at https://github.com/kaixin96/mixreg.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning agents can become too specialized to the environments used during training and perform poorly in unseen ones. The paper examines data augmentation as a remedy. It finds that approaches such as cutout and random convolution make local changes to observations but have limited effectiveness in increasing diversity and improving generalization.

The proposed method, mixreg, trains on mixtures of observations from different training environments. It also interpolates the associated supervision, such as rewards, and imposes linearity constraints linking the mixed observations with that mixed supervision. This couples changes in the training inputs to changes in their learning targets. The authors describe the resulting training as increasing diversity more effectively and encouraging smoother policies.

Experiments on the Procgen benchmark show large improvements over established baselines on unseen testing environments. The method applies to both policy-based and value-based reinforcement learning algorithms. Its significance is that cross-environment mixing provides a simple training intervention with demonstrated generalization benefits, rather than requiring a separate approach for each of those algorithm families.
summary.tldr: Mixreg combines observations and supervision across training environments to improve reinforcement learning generalization on unseen Procgen environments.

title: Improving Generalization in Reinforcement Learning with Mixture Regularization

abstract: Retrosynthesis is the process of recursively decomposing target molecules into available building blocks. It plays an important role in solving problems in organic synthesis planning. To automate or assist in the retrosynthesis analysis, various retrosynthesis prediction algorithms have been proposed. However, most of them are cumbersome and lack interpretability about their predictions. In this paper, we devise a novel template-free algorithm for automatic retrosynthetic expansion inspired by how chemists approach retrosynthesis prediction. Our method disassembles retrosynthesis into two steps: i) identify the potential reaction center of the target molecule through a novel graph neural network and generate intermediate synthons, and ii) generate the reactants associated with synthons via a robust reactant generation model. While outperforming the state-of-the-art baselines by a significant margin, our model also provides chemically reasonable interpretation.

paragraphs: Retrosynthesis works backward from a desired molecule toward building blocks that could be used to make it. Automated predictions can assist this planning, but the authors identify cumbersome methods and unclear prediction rationales as problems with existing approaches. RetroXpert addresses these concerns by separating retrosynthetic expansion into two chemically motivated steps within a template-free method.

First, a graph neural network identifies a potential reaction center in the target molecule and generates intermediate synthons. These intermediates express a proposed decomposition of the target. Second, a reactant-generation model predicts the reactants associated with those synthons. This staged design makes the proposed decomposition an explicit intermediate result connecting the target molecule to the generated reactants.

The authors report that RetroXpert outperforms state-of-the-art baselines by a significant margin and provides chemically reasonable interpretations. The interpretability comes from exposing meaningful stages of the prediction process: where a reaction might occur and which reactants correspond to the resulting intermediates. The reported findings support this decomposition as a useful structure for automatic retrosynthetic expansion.
summary.tldr: RetroXpert predicts reaction centers and intermediate synthons before generating reactants, improving reported retrosynthesis performance while exposing chemically meaningful intermediate decisions.

title: RetroXpert: Decompose Retrosynthesis Prediction Like A Chemist

abstract: Non-linear spectral decompositions of images based on one-homogeneous functionals such as total variation have gained considerable attention in the last few years. Due to their ability to extract spectral components corresponding to objects of different size and contrast, such decompositions enable filtering, feature transfer, image fusion and other applications. However, obtaining this decomposition involves solving multiple non-smooth optimisation problems and is therefore computationally highly intensive. In this paper, we present a neural network approximation of a non-linear spectral decomposition. We report up to four orders of magnitude (×10,000) speedup in processing of mega-pixel size images, compared to classical GPU implementations. Our proposed network, TVspecNET, is able to implicitly learn the underlying PDE and, despite being entirely data driven, inherits invariances of the model based transform. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first approach towards learning a non-linear spectral decomposition of images. Not only do we gain a staggering computational advantage, but this approach can also be seen as a step towards studying neural networks that can decompose an image into spectral components defined by a user rather than a handcrafted functional.

paragraphs: Nonlinear spectral image decomposition separates components associated with objects of different sizes and contrasts. Such components support tasks including filtering, feature transfer, and image fusion. The difficulty is computational: obtaining a decomposition based on total variation normally requires solving multiple nonsmooth optimization problems, making the process expensive.

The paper introduces TVspecNET, a neural network that approximates this decomposition. The authors report that it implicitly learns the underlying partial differential equation and retains invariances of the model-based transform despite being learned entirely from data. The aim is therefore to reproduce useful structure from the mathematical transformation through a much faster learned computation.

For megapixel images, the reported processing speedup reaches up to 10,000 times that of classical GPU implementations. That is a maximum reported improvement, rather than a uniform speedup for every image or setting. Beyond accelerating an existing transform, the authors frame the work as a step toward networks that decompose images into user-defined spectral components, a possible extension beyond components specified by a handcrafted functional.
summary.tldr: TVspecNET learns an approximation to nonlinear spectral image decomposition, reporting speedups of up to 10,000 times.

title: Deeply Learned Spectral Total Variation Decomposition

abstract: We consider three important challenges in conference peer review: (i) reviewers maliciously attempting to get assigned to certain papers to provide positive reviews, possibly as part of quid-pro-quo arrangements with the authors; (ii) "torpedo reviewing," where reviewers deliberately attempt to get assigned to certain papers that they dislike in order to reject them; (iii) reviewer de-anonymization on release of the similarities and the reviewer-assignment code. On the conceptual front, we identify connections between these three problems and present a framework that brings all these challenges under a common umbrella. We then present a (randomized) algorithm for reviewer assignment that can optimally solve the reviewer-assignment problem under any given constraints on the probability of assignment for any reviewer-paper pair. We further consider the problem of restricting the joint probability that certain suspect pairs of reviewers are assigned to certain papers, and show that this problem is NP-hard for arbitrary constraints on these joint probabilities but efficiently solvable for a practical special case. Finally, we experimentally evaluate our algorithms on datasets from past conferences, where we observe that they can limit the chance that any malicious reviewer gets assigned to their desired paper to 50% while producing assignments with over 90% of the total optimal similarity.

paragraphs: Reviewer assignment can be manipulated by people seeking to favor a particular paper or deliberately undermine it. Publishing reviewer-paper similarities and assignment code can also make reviewer identities easier to infer. This paper connects these three problems through a common framework that controls how predictable particular assignments can be.

The authors develop a randomized assignment algorithm that optimally solves the assignment problem under specified limits on the probability of individual reviewer-paper matches. They also study constraints on the joint probability that suspect reviewer pairs receive particular papers. Arbitrary joint constraints make the problem NP-hard, but a practical special case remains efficiently solvable.

Experiments using datasets from past conferences show a useful tradeoff between restricting targeted assignments and preserving reviewer-paper similarity. The algorithms limit a malicious reviewer's chance of receiving a desired paper to 50% while retaining more than 90% of the total optimal similarity. This is evidence that randomized assignments can reduce opportunities for targeted manipulation without sacrificing most of the matching quality in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Randomized reviewer assignments constrain targeted matches while preserving most assignment similarity in evaluations on past conference data.

title: Mitigating Manipulation in Peer Review via Randomized Reviewer Assignments

abstract: In natural language processing (NLP), enormous pre-trained models like BERT have become the standard starting point for training on a range of downstream tasks, and similar trends are emerging in other areas of deep learning. In parallel, work on the lottery ticket hypothesis has shown that models for NLP and computer vision contain smaller matching subnetworks capable of training in isolation to full accuracy and transferring to other tasks. In this work, we combine these observations to assess whether such trainable, transferrable subnetworks exist in pre-trained BERT models. For a range of downstream tasks, we indeed find matching subnetworks at 40% to 90% sparsity. We find these subnetworks at (pre-trained) initialization, a deviation from prior NLP research where they emerge only after some amount of training. Subnetworks found on the masked language modeling task (the same task used to pre-train the model) transfer universally; those found on other tasks transfer in a limited fashion if at all. As large-scale pre-training becomes an increasingly central paradigm in deep learning, our results demonstrate that the main lottery ticket observations remain relevant in this context. Codes available at https://github.com/VITA-Group/BERT-Tickets.

We find these subnetworks at (pre-trained) initialization, a deviation from prior NLP research where they emerge only after some amount of training. Subnetworks found on the masked language modeling task (the same task used to pre-train the model) transfer universally; those found on other tasks transfer in a limited fashion if at all. As large-scale pre-training becomes an increasingly central paradigm in deep learning, our results demonstrate that the main lottery ticket observations remain relevant in this context. Codes available at https://github.com/VITA-Group/BERT-Tickets.

paragraphs: The lottery ticket hypothesis concerns smaller subnetworks that can train in isolation and match the performance of a full model. This paper investigates whether such subnetworks already exist inside pretrained BERT, a common starting point for language tasks. It also asks whether a subnetwork identified using one task remains useful for other tasks.

Across a range of downstream tasks, the authors find matching subnetworks with sparsity between 40% and 90%. These subnetworks are present at the pretrained initialization, before downstream training. That distinction matters: the result concerns a starting point that already contains pretraining knowledge, and differs from earlier language-model findings in which matching subnetworks emerged only after additional training.

Transfer depends strongly on the task used to identify the subnetwork. Those found through masked language modeling, BERT's pretraining task, transfer across the evaluated tasks, while those found through other tasks transfer only narrowly or not at all. The findings extend lottery-ticket observations to pretrained models and show that the selection objective matters for finding broadly reusable sparse subnetworks.
summary.tldr: Pretrained BERT contains matching subnetworks at 40–90% sparsity, with masked-language-modeling subnetworks transferring broadly across the evaluated tasks.

title: The Lottery Ticket Hypothesis for Pre-trained BERT Networks

abstract: Reward-free reinforcement learning (RL) is a framework which is suitable for both the batch RL setting and the setting where there are many reward functions of interest. During the exploration phase, an agent collects samples without using a pre-specified reward function. After the exploration phase, a reward function is given, and the agent uses samples collected during the exploration phase to compute a near-optimal policy. Jin et al. [2020] showed that in the tabular setting, the agent only needs to collect polynomial number of samples (in terms of the number states, the number of actions, and the planning horizon) for reward-free RL. However, in practice, the number of states and actions can be large, and thus function approximation schemes are required for generalization. In this work, we give both positive and negative results for reward-free RL with linear function approximation. We give an algorithm for reward-free RL in the linear Markov decision process setting where both the transition and the reward admit linear representations. The sample complexity of our algorithm is polynomial in the feature dimension and the planning horizon, and is completely independent of the number of states and actions. We further give an exponential lower bound for reward-free RL in the setting where only the optimal $Q$-function admits a linear representation. Our results imply several interesting exponential separations on the sample complexity of reward-free RL.

paragraphs: Reward-free reinforcement learning separates exploration from the choice of reward. An agent first collects data without a specified reward function, then uses that data to compute a near-optimal policy once a reward is supplied. This is useful when a collected dataset must support later planning or several possible objectives.

The paper studies whether linear function approximation can make this process efficient in large state and action spaces. Its positive result assumes a linear Markov decision process, where both transitions and rewards have linear representations. Under that structure, the proposed algorithm needs a number of samples polynomial in feature dimension and planning horizon, independent of the number of states and actions.

The negative result examines the weaker assumption that only the optimal action-value function has a linear representation. In that setting, the authors establish an exponential sample lower bound. Together, the results show that different forms of linear structure can have sharply different consequences for reward-free exploration. A compact optimal value function alone does not supply the same sample-efficiency guarantee as the stronger transition-and-reward representation.
summary.tldr: Reward-free learning has polynomial sample complexity for linear MDPs, while linearity of only the optimal action-value function permits an exponential lower bound.

title: On Reward-Free Reinforcement Learning with Linear Function Approximation

abstract: Noisy labels can impair the performance of deep neural networks. To tackle this problem, in this paper, we propose a new method for filtering label noise. Unlike most existing methods relying on the posterior probability of a noisy classifier, we focus on the much richer spatial behavior of data in the latent representational space. By leveraging the high-order topological information of data, we are able to collect most of the clean data and train a high-quality model. Theoretically we prove that this topological approach is guaranteed to collect the clean data with high probability. Empirical results show that our method outperforms the state-of-the-arts and is robust to a broad spectrum of noise types and levels.

paragraphs: Incorrect training labels can undermine a neural network's predictions. A common filtering strategy judges examples using the probabilities produced by a classifier that has itself learned from noisy labels. This paper proposes a different source of evidence: the spatial organization of examples in the network's learned representation space.

The method uses higher-order topological information, examining structure among represented data rather than relying mainly on individual prediction scores. That structure supports the selection of a largely clean training collection, which is then used to train a high-quality model. The key idea is that relationships across examples can provide useful information about label reliability.

The authors prove a high-probability guarantee for collecting clean data using their topological approach. Their experiments also report stronger performance than the compared state-of-the-art methods and robustness across a broad range of noise types and levels. The findings support topology as a useful basis for filtering labels, with theoretical evidence about clean-data collection complementing empirical evidence about the resulting models.
summary.tldr: A topology-based filter uses the structure of learned representations to identify clean training data amid noisy labels.

title: A Topological Filter for Learning with Label Noise

abstract: The deductive closure of an ideal knowledge base (KB) contains exactly the logical queries that the KB can answer. However, in practice KBs are both incomplete and over-specified, failing to answer some queries that have real-world answers. \emph{Query embedding} (QE) techniques have been recently proposed where KB entities and KB queries are represented jointly in an embedding space, supporting relaxation and generalization in KB inference. However, experiments in this paper show that QE systems may disagree with deductive reasoning on answers that do not require generalization or relaxation. We address this problem with a novel QE method that is more faithful to deductive reasoning, and show that this leads to better performance on complex queries to incomplete KBs. Finally we show that inserting this new QE module into a neural question-answering system leads to substantial improvements over the state-of-the-art.

paragraphs: A knowledge base can answer queries by applying logical reasoning to its stored information. Real knowledge bases are incomplete and over-specified, however, so strict deduction can miss questions with real-world answers. Query embedding methods address this by representing both entities and queries in a shared space, allowing inference to relax or generalize beyond explicit logical consequences.

The paper identifies a problem with that flexibility: existing query embedding systems can disagree with deductive reasoning even when a query needs neither relaxation nor generalization. The authors demonstrate this behavior experimentally and introduce a new embedding method designed to be more faithful to deduction. The aim is to improve the relationship between learned inference and the answers already supported by the knowledge base.

The new method performs better on complex queries over incomplete knowledge bases. When inserted into a neural question-answering system, it also yields substantial improvements over the state of the art. These findings connect faithfulness to practical performance: preserving more of the underlying logical behavior can help learned representations answer questions where missing information still makes generalization useful.
summary.tldr: A query embedding method that better respects deductive reasoning improves complex knowledge-base queries and neural question answering.

title: Faithful Embeddings for Knowledge Base Queries

abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (RL) agents may successfully generalize to new settings if trained on an appropriately diverse set of environment and task configurations. Unsupervised Environment Design (UED) is a promising self-supervised RL paradigm, wherein the free parameters of an underspecified environment are automatically adapted during training to the agent's capabilities, leading to the emergence of diverse training environments. Here, we cast Prioritized Level Replay (PLR), an empirically successful but theoretically unmotivated method that selectively samples randomly-generated training levels, as UED. We argue that by curating completely random levels, PLR, too, can generate novel and complex levels for effective training. This insight reveals a natural class of UED methods we call Dual Curriculum Design (DCD). Crucially, DCD includes both PLR and a popular UED algorithm, PAIRED, as special cases and inherits similar theoretical guarantees. This connection allows us to develop novel theory for PLR, providing a version with a robustness guarantee at Nash equilibria. Furthermore, our theory suggests a highly counterintuitive improvement to PLR: by stopping the agent from updating its policy on uncurated levels (training on less data), we can improve the convergence to Nash equilibria. Indeed, our experiments confirm that our new method, PLR$^{\perp}$, obtains better results on a suite of out-of-distribution, zero-shot transfer tasks, in addition to demonstrating that PLR$^{\perp}$ improves the performance of PAIRED, from which it inherited its theoretical framework.

paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning agents may generalize better when training environments provide appropriate diversity and difficulty. This paper examines how selecting previously generated levels can participate in environment design. It reframes Prioritized Level Replay, or PLR, which selectively revisits random training levels, as a form of unsupervised environment design that adapts training experiences to the agent.

The authors introduce Dual Curriculum Design, a framework containing both PLR and PAIRED as special cases. This connection brings theoretical tools from environment design to replay and yields a PLR version with a robustness guarantee at Nash equilibria. The guarantee is tied to that equilibrium condition, giving a theoretical basis for a method previously motivated mainly by empirical success.

The theory also motivates a counterintuitive change: prevent policy updates on uncurated levels and train through the selected replay curriculum. The resulting PLR-perpendicular method can improve convergence to Nash equilibria despite using less data for updates. Experiments report better out-of-distribution zero-shot transfer results and improved PAIRED performance, supporting selective training as a useful part of environment design.
summary.tldr: A unified theory of replay and environment design motivates selective policy updates that improve reported transfer performance and provide equilibrium-based robustness guarantees.

title: Replay-Guided Adversarial Environment Design

abstract: Random forests have been widely used for their ability to provide so-called importance measures, which give insight at a global (per dataset) level on the relevance of input variables to predict a certain output. On the other hand, methods based on Shapley values have been introduced to refine the analysis of feature relevance in tree-based models to a local (per instance) level. In this context, we first show that the global Mean Decrease of Impurity (MDI) variable importance scores correspond to Shapley values under some conditions. Then, we derive a local MDI importance measure of variable relevance, which has a very natural connection with the global MDI measure and can be related to a new notion of local feature relevance. We further link local MDI importances with Shapley values and discuss them in the light of related measures from the literature. The measures are illustrated through experiments on several classification and regression problems.

paragraphs: Random forests can assign importance scores to input variables across an entire dataset. Such global scores describe overall predictive relevance, but they do not directly explain how relevance varies between individual examples. This paper connects the familiar Mean Decrease of Impurity measure, or MDI, with methods that attribute importance at the individual-instance level.

The authors first show that global MDI scores correspond to Shapley values under certain conditions. That qualification matters: the result does not identify every random forest’s importance scores with Shapley values automatically. They then derive a local MDI measure that has a natural relationship to the global measure and to a new definition of local feature relevance.

The analysis further connects these local scores with Shapley values and discusses their relationship to existing measures. Experiments on classification and regression problems illustrate the proposed quantities. Together, the results provide a theoretical bridge between dataset-level importance and instance-level relevance, helping place two approaches to explaining tree models within a connected framework.
summary.tldr: The paper develops local MDI feature importance and establishes conditional connections between MDI and Shapley values.

title: From global to local MDI variable importances for random forests and when they are Shapley values

abstract: Humans are good at compositional zero-shot reasoning; someone who has never seen a zebra before could nevertheless recognize one when we tell them it looks like a horse with black and white stripes. Machine learning systems, on the other hand, usually leverage spurious correlations in the training data, and while such correlations can help recognize objects in context, they hurt generalization. To be able to deal with underspecified datasets while still leveraging contextual clues during classification, we propose ProtoProp, a novel prototype propagation graph method. First we learn prototypical representations of objects (e.g., zebra) that are independent w.r.t. their attribute labels (e.g., stripes) and vice versa. Next we propagate the independent prototypes through a compositional graph, to learn compositional prototypes of novel attribute-object combinations that reflect the dependencies of the target distribution. The method does not rely on any external data, such as class hierarchy graphs or pretrained word embeddings. We evaluate our approach on AO-Clevr, a synthetic and strongly visual dataset with clean labels, UT-Zappos, a noisy real-world dataset of fine-grained shoe types, and C-GQA, a large-scale object detection dataset modified for compositional zero-shot learning. We show that in the generalized compositional zero-shot setting we outperform state-of-the-art results, and through ablations we show the importance of each part of the method and their contribution to the final results. The code is available on github.

paragraphs: Recognizing an unfamiliar combination of a familiar object and attribute requires separating the components without losing useful context. Training data can make that difficult because objects and attributes often appear together in misleading ways. ProtoProp addresses this compositional zero-shot problem by organizing how component representations are learned and then combined.

First, the method learns object prototypes independent of attribute labels and attribute prototypes independent of object labels. It then propagates these prototypes through a compositional graph to construct representations of new attribute-object combinations. This second stage captures dependencies in the target distribution, allowing context to contribute after the component representations have been separated. No external class hierarchy or pretrained word embeddings are required.

The evaluation spans synthetic visual data, fine-grained shoe images, and a large object dataset adapted for compositional recognition. The authors report outperforming state-of-the-art results in the generalized compositional zero-shot setting. Ablation studies support the contributions of the method's individual parts. The findings favor separating components first and introducing compositional relationships through a dedicated propagation stage.
summary.tldr: ProtoProp learns independent object and attribute prototypes, then propagates them through a graph to recognize unseen combinations.

title: Independent Prototype Propagation for Zero-Shot Compositionality

abstract: Training generative adversarial networks (GANs) with limited real image data generally results in deteriorated performance and collapsed models. To conquer this challenge, we are inspired by the latest observation, that one can discover independently trainable and highly sparse subnetworks (a.k.a., lottery tickets) from GANs. Treating this as an inductive prior, we suggest a brand-new angle towards data-efficient GAN training: by first identifying the lottery ticket from the original GAN using the small training set of real images; and then focusing on training that sparse subnetwork by re-using the same set. We find our coordinated framework to offer orthogonal gains to existing real image data augmentation methods, and we additionally present a new feature-level augmentation that can be applied together with them. Comprehensive experiments endorse the effectiveness of our proposed framework, across various GAN architectures (SNGAN, BigGAN, and StyleGAN-V2) and diverse datasets (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, Tiny-ImageNet, ImageNet, and multiple few-shot generation datasets). Codes are available at: https://github.com/VITA-Group/Ultra-Data-Efficient-GAN-Training.

paragraphs: GANs can perform poorly or collapse when only a small collection of real images is available. This paper approaches that problem through the network being trained, drawing on the observation that GANs can contain highly sparse subnetworks that remain independently trainable. These subnetworks are called lottery tickets, and the authors treat their structure as a useful inductive prior.

The framework first identifies a lottery ticket within the original GAN using the limited real-image dataset. It then trains that sparse subnetwork using the same images again. This makes subnetwork selection part of the response to scarce data. The method does not require a separate, larger image collection for the ticket-discovery stage described in the abstract.

The authors find that this approach provides gains complementary to existing image augmentation methods. They also introduce augmentation at the feature level that can be combined with those methods. Experiments across SNGAN, BigGAN, StyleGAN-V2, and several standard and few-shot datasets support the framework's effectiveness. The stated finding is that choosing what to train can complement modifying the available training examples.
summary.tldr: Selecting and training a sparse GAN subnetwork improves learning from limited images and provides gains complementary to data augmentation.

title: Data-Efficient GAN Training Beyond (Just) Augmentations: A Lottery Ticket Perspective

abstract: This paper studies Imitation Learning from Observations alone (ILFO) where the learner is presented with expert demonstrations that consist only of states visited by an expert (without access to actions taken by the expert). We present a provably efficient model-based framework MobILE to solve the ILFO problem. MobILE involves carefully trading off exploration against imitation - this is achieved by integrating the idea of optimism in the face of uncertainty into the distribution matching imitation learning (IL) framework. We provide a unified analysis for MobILE, and demonstrate that MobILE enjoys strong performance guarantees for classes of MDP dynamics that satisfy certain well studied notions of complexity. We also show that the ILFO problem is strictly harder than the standard IL problem by reducing ILFO to a multi-armed bandit problem indicating that exploration is necessary for solving ILFO efficiently. We complement these theoretical results with experimental simulations on benchmark OpenAI Gym tasks that indicate the efficacy of MobILE. Code for implementing the MobILE framework is available at https://github.com/rahulkidambi/MobILE-NeurIPS2021.

paragraphs: Imitation learning from observations gives a learner the states an expert visited without revealing the expert's actions. This removes information that standard imitation learning can use directly. MobILE tackles this setting with a model-based framework that balances following the expert's observed behavior against exploring the environment to resolve uncertainty.

The method combines distribution-matching imitation learning with optimism in the face of uncertainty. Matching distributions supplies the imitation objective, while optimism provides a way to incorporate exploration. A unified theoretical analysis establishes strong performance guarantees for classes of decision-process dynamics satisfying specified, previously studied notions of complexity.

The paper also establishes that observation-only imitation is strictly harder than standard imitation learning. A connection to a multi-armed bandit problem shows that exploration is necessary for efficient solutions in this setting. Simulations on benchmark OpenAI Gym tasks support MobILE's effectiveness. Together, the results explain why observation-only demonstrations require an exploration strategy and provide a framework with both conditional theoretical guarantees and experimental support.
summary.tldr: MobILE combines optimistic exploration with distribution matching to learn from expert state sequences without expert actions.

title: MobILE: Model-Based Imitation Learning From Observation Alone

abstract: Data with low-dimensional nonlinear structure are ubiquitous in engineering and scientific problems. We study a model problem with such structure---a binary classification task that uses a deep fully-connected neural network to classify data drawn from two disjoint smooth curves on the unit sphere. Aside from mild regularity conditions, we place no restrictions on the configuration of the curves. We prove that when (i) the network depth is large relative to certain geometric properties that set the difficulty of the problem and (ii) the network width and number of samples is polynomial in the depth, randomly-initialized gradient descent quickly learns to correctly classify all points on the two curves with high probability. To our knowledge, this is the first generalization guarantee for deep networks with nonlinear data that depends only on intrinsic data properties. Our analysis proceeds by a reduction to dynamics in the neural tangent kernel (NTK) regime, where the network depth plays the role of a fitting resource in solving the classification problem. In particular, via fine-grained control of the decay properties of the NTK, we demonstrate that when the network is sufficiently deep, the NTK can be locally approximated by a translationally invariant operator on the manifolds and stably inverted over smooth functions, which guarantees convergence and generalization.

paragraphs: The paper studies a concrete case of learning from nonlinear, low-dimensional data: separating points drawn from two disjoint smooth curves on a unit sphere. Apart from mild regularity requirements, the curves can have arbitrary configurations. The goal is to explain when training a deep network succeeds across the entire curves, beyond the sampled training points.

The authors prove that randomly initialized gradient descent quickly learns the correct classification with high probability when several conditions hold. Network depth must be sufficiently large relative to geometric properties governing the problem's difficulty, and both width and sample count must scale polynomially with depth. The guarantee therefore connects successful learning to the geometry of the data and the resources allocated to training.

The analysis uses the neural tangent kernel regime, where training can be studied through an associated kernel. Sufficient depth gives that kernel useful local behavior along the curves and allows stable inversion over smooth functions. This establishes convergence and generalization, with depth acting as a fitting resource for the nonlinear classification problem.
summary.tldr: Under geometric and size conditions, gradient descent provably trains a deep network to classify every point on two disjoint smooth curves.

title: Deep Networks Provably Classify Data on Curves

abstract: We investigate how fairness relaxations scale to flexible classifiers like deep neural networks for images and text. We analyze an easy-to-use and robust way of imposing fairness constraints when training, and through this framework prove that some prior fairness surrogates exhibit degeneracies for non-convex models. We resolve these problems via three new surrogates: an adaptive data re-weighting, and two smooth upper-bounds that are provably more robust than some previous methods. Our surrogates perform comparably to the state-of-the-art on low-dimensional fairness benchmarks, while achieving superior accuracy and stability for more complex computer vision and natural language processing tasks.

We analyze an easy-to-use and robust way of imposing fairness constraints when training, and through this framework prove that some prior fairness surrogates exhibit degeneracies for non-convex models. We resolve these problems via three new surrogates: an adaptive data re-weighting, and two smooth upper-bounds that are provably more robust than some previous methods. Our surrogates perform comparably to the state-of-the-art on low-dimensional fairness benchmarks, while achieving superior accuracy and stability for more complex computer vision and natural language processing tasks.

paragraphs: Fairness constraints often need a tractable substitute, or surrogate, before they can be incorporated into model training. This paper studies how such substitutes behave for flexible classifiers, particularly deep networks processing images and text. Its focus is whether fairness methods remain reliable as the underlying model becomes more complex.

Using a framework for imposing fairness constraints during training, the authors prove that some previous fairness surrogates become degenerate for nonconvex models. They introduce three alternatives to address these problems: one uses adaptive data reweighting, and two use smooth upper bounds. The new upper-bound surrogates have robustness guarantees stronger than those of some earlier approaches, linking the design changes to a theoretical diagnosis.

On low-dimensional fairness benchmarks, the proposed methods perform comparably to the state of the art. On more complex vision and language tasks, they achieve better accuracy and stability. The results indicate that the choice of fairness surrogate matters when moving to flexible classifiers, and that methods adequate on simpler benchmarks may encounter problems in more demanding models.
summary.tldr: Three new fairness surrogates address degeneracies in nonconvex classifiers and improve accuracy and stability on complex image and text tasks.

title: Scalable and Stable Surrogates for Flexible Classifiers with Fairness Constraints

abstract: Machine learning research depends on objectively interpretable, comparable, and reproducible algorithm benchmarks. We advocate the use of curated, comprehensive suites of machine learning tasks to standardize the setup, execution, and reporting of benchmarks. We enable this through software tools that help to create and leverage these benchmarking suites. These are seamlessly integrated into the OpenML platform, and accessible through interfaces in Python, Java, and R. OpenML benchmarking suites (a) are easy to use through standardized data formats, APIs, and client libraries; (b) come with extensive meta-information on the included datasets; and (c) allow benchmarks to be shared and reused in future studies. We then present a first, carefully curated and practical benchmarking suite for classification: the OpenML Curated Classification benchmarking suite 2018 (OpenML-CC18). Finally, we discuss use cases and applications which demonstrate the usefulness of OpenML benchmarking suites and the OpenML-CC18 in particular.

This supports more consistent evaluation practices across studies using the same benchmark resources.
summary.tldr: OpenML benchmarking suites package curated tasks, dataset information, and reusable tools to support consistent and reproducible algorithm comparisons.

title: OpenML Benchmarking Suites

abstract: In this paper, we study a sequential decision-making problem, called Adaptive Sampling for Discovery (ASD). Starting with a large unlabeled dataset, algorithms for ASD adaptively label the points with the goal to maximize the sum of responses.This problem has wide applications to real-world discovery problems, for example drug discovery with the help of machine learning models. ASD algorithms face the well-known exploration-exploitation dilemma. The algorithm needs to choose points that yield information to improve model estimates but it also needs to exploit the model. We rigorously formulate the problem and propose a general information-directed sampling (IDS) algorithm. We provide theoretical guarantees for the performance of IDS in linear, graph and low-rank models. The benefits of IDS are shown in both simulation experiments and real-data experiments for discovering chemical reaction conditions.

paragraphs: This paper studies discovery as a sequence of choices from a large collection of unlabeled candidates. Each selected point is labeled, revealing a response, and the objective is to maximize the total responses collected. This formulation captures settings where evaluating candidates serves an immediate discovery goal, as in searching for useful chemical reaction conditions.

The central difficulty is balancing information gathering against exploiting current predictions. A candidate can be valuable because its response is expected to be high, or because observing it improves estimates that guide later selections. Focusing entirely on either consideration can overlook the other source of value. The authors formalize this problem as Adaptive Sampling for Discovery.

They propose a general information-directed sampling algorithm and establish performance guarantees for linear, graph, and low-rank models. Simulations and experiments using real chemical reaction data demonstrate benefits of the approach. Together, the formulation and results connect model learning directly to cumulative discovery outcomes: the algorithm must account for what a measurement teaches as well as what it yields.
summary.tldr: Information-directed sampling balances learning about candidates with selecting promising ones to improve cumulative discovery outcomes.

title: Adaptive Sampling for Discovery

abstract: Network data are ubiquitous in our daily life, containing rich but often sensitive information. In this paper, we expand the current static analysis of privatised networks to a dynamic framework by considering a sequence of networks with potential change points. We investigate the fundamental limits in consistently localising change points under both node and edge privacy constraints, demonstrating interesting phase transition in terms of the signal-to-noise ratio condition, accompanied by polynomial-time algorithms. The private signal-to-noise ratio conditions quantify the costs of the privacy for change point localisation problems and exhibit a different scaling in the sparsity parameter compared to the non-private counterparts. Our algorithms are shown to be optimal under the edge LDP constraint up to log factors. Under node LDP constraint, a gap exists between our upper bound and lower bound and we leave it as an interesting open problem, echoing the challenges in high-dimensional statistical inference under LDP constraints.

This paper studies locating those change points in sequences of networks under local differential privacy. It considers both node-level and edge-level privacy constraints, extending analysis beyond static private networks.

The authors derive signal-to-noise conditions that describe when consistent localization is possible and identify a phase transition in those conditions. They also provide polynomial-time algorithms. These results quantify how privacy changes the statistical information required to find a shift, including a different dependence on network sparsity from the corresponding non-private problem.

Under edge-level local privacy, the algorithms achieve optimal performance up to logarithmic factors. Under node-level local privacy, the upper and lower bounds do not match, leaving the precise difficulty unresolved. This distinction is part of the paper's contribution: it gives a sharp characterization for edge privacy while exposing an open question for node privacy. The findings connect the chosen privacy constraint to both achievable localization accuracy and the strength of available guarantees.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes privacy costs in network change-point localization, obtaining near-optimal edge-private algorithms while leaving a gap for node privacy.

title: Network change point localisation under local differential privacy

abstract: Calculation of Bayesian posteriors and model evidences typically requires numerical integration. Bayesian quadrature (BQ), a surrogate-model-based approach to numerical integration, is capable of superb sample efficiency, but its lack of parallelisation has hindered its practical applications. In this work, we propose a parallelised (batch) BQ method, employing techniques from kernel quadrature, that possesses an empirically exponential convergence rate.Additionally, just as with Nested Sampling, our method permits simultaneous inference of both posteriors and model evidence.Samples from our BQ surrogate model are re-selected to give a sparse set of samples, via a kernel recombination algorithm, requiring negligible additional time to increase the batch size.Empirically, we find that our approach significantly outperforms the sampling efficiency of both state-of-the-art BQ techniques and Nested Sampling in various real-world datasets, including lithium-ion battery analytics.

paragraphs: Bayesian inference often depends on numerical integration to calculate posterior distributions and model evidence. Bayesian quadrature approaches this task using a surrogate model, which can make efficient use of function evaluations. Its practical value has nevertheless been limited by difficulty exploiting parallel computation. This paper develops a batch version intended to address that bottleneck.

The method uses kernel quadrature techniques and a kernel recombination algorithm. Samples drawn from the surrogate model are reselected into a sparse collection, allowing evaluations to be organized into batches. The authors report that increasing batch size requires negligible additional time for this selection procedure. The same method supports simultaneous inference of the posterior and model evidence.

Across real-world datasets, including lithium-ion battery applications, the approach shows better sampling efficiency than the compared Bayesian quadrature methods and Nested Sampling. The authors also observe an exponential convergence rate empirically. Together, these findings suggest that parallelization and careful sample selection can improve practical integration efficiency; the reported convergence rate is an experimental observation.
summary.tldr: Batch Bayesian quadrature uses kernel recombination to support parallel evaluation and improve sampling efficiency in the reported Bayesian inference experiments.

title: Fast Bayesian Inference with Batch Bayesian Quadrature via Kernel Recombination

abstract: Normalizing flows model probability distributions by learning invertible transformations that transfer a simple distribution into complex distributions. Since the architecture of ResNet-based normalizing flows is more flexible than that of coupling-based models, ResNet-based normalizing flows have been widely studied in recent years. Despite their architectural flexibility, it is well-known that the current ResNet-based models suffer from constrained Lipschitz constants. In this paper, we propose the monotone formulation to overcome the issue of the Lipschitz constants using monotone operators and provide an in-depth theoretical analysis. Furthermore, we construct an activation function called Concatenated Pila (CPila) to improve gradient flow. The resulting model, Monotone Flows, exhibits an excellent performance on multiple density estimation benchmarks (MNIST, CIFAR-10, ImageNet32, ImageNet64). Code is available at https://github.com/mlvlab/MonotoneFlows.

Their architecture must therefore support expressive transformations while preserving invertibility. The paper focuses on flows built from residual networks, which offer more architectural flexibility than coupling-based alternatives but face restrictions on their Lipschitz constants.

These constants describe how strongly a transformation can change when its input changes. The authors propose a formulation using monotone operators to overcome the restrictions affecting existing residual-network flows. They provide a detailed theoretical analysis of this formulation, making the mathematical construction a central part of the contribution rather than relying only on benchmark performance.

The paper also introduces Concatenated Pila, or CPila, an activation function designed to improve gradient flow during learning. The combined model is called Monotone Flows. It reports strong density-estimation performance on MNIST, CIFAR-10, ImageNet32, and ImageNet64. The contribution thus links a different route to invertible transformations with an activation design intended to make those models easier to train.
summary.tldr: Monotone Flows uses monotone operators and a new activation function to address restrictions in residual-network normalizing flows.

title: Invertible Monotone Operators for Normalizing Flows

abstract:
We study the behavior of the Wasserstein-$2$ distance between discrete measures $\mu$ and $
u$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$ when both measures are smoothed by small amounts of Gaussian noise. This procedure, known as Gaussian-smoothed optimal transport, has recently attracted attention as a statistically attractive alternative to the unregularized Wasserstein distance. We give precise bounds on the approximation properties of this proposal in the small noise regime, and establish the existence of a phase transition: we show that, if the optimal transport plan from $\mu$ to $
u$ is unique and a perfect matching, there exists a critical threshold such that the difference between $W_2(\mu, 
u)$ and the Gaussian-smoothed OT distance $W_2(\mu \ast \mathcal{N}_\sigma, 
u\ast \mathcal{N}_\sigma)$ scales like $\exp(-c /\sigma^2)$ for $\sigma$ below the threshold, and scales like $\sigma$ above it. These results establish that for $\sigma$ sufficiently small, the smoothed Wasserstein distance approximates the unregularized distance exponentially well.

u\ast \mathcal{N}_\sigma)$ scales like $\exp(-c /\sigma^2)$ for $\sigma$ below the threshold, and scales like $\sigma$ above it. These results establish that for $\sigma$ sufficiently small, the smoothed Wasserstein distance approximates the unregularized distance exponentially well.

paragraphs: The Wasserstein-2 distance compares distributions through an optimal transport problem. Gaussian smoothing modifies that comparison by adding noise to both distributions before measuring their distance. This paper asks how closely the smoothed distance approximates the original one when the distributions are discrete and the amount of added noise is small.

The authors derive precise approximation bounds and identify a change in behavior across a critical noise threshold. Their stated result assumes that the optimal transport plan is unique and forms a perfect matching. Under that condition, the difference between the original and smoothed distances scales exponentially in the inverse squared noise level below the threshold, and linearly with noise above it.

This distinction matters because reducing noise can improve approximation at very different rates in the two regimes. Below the threshold, sufficiently small noise yields exponentially close agreement with the unsmoothed distance. The result explains a strong approximation property of Gaussian-smoothed transport while tying it to the stated structure of the optimal matching, rather than asserting the same behavior for every pair of distributions.
summary.tldr: Under a unique perfect-matching transport plan, sufficiently small Gaussian noise gives exponentially accurate Wasserstein-distance approximations.

title: Asymptotics of smoothed Wasserstein distances in the small noise regime

abstract: Abstraction has been widely studied as a way to improve the efficiency and generalization of reinforcement learning algorithms. In this paper, we study abstraction in the continuous-control setting. We extend the definition of MDP homomorphisms to encompass continuous actions in continuous state spaces. We derive a policy gradient theorem on the abstract MDP, which allows us to leverage approximate symmetries of the environment for policy optimization. Based on this theorem, we propose an actor-critic algorithm that is able to learn the policy and the MDP homomorphism map simultaneously, using the lax bisimulation metric. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on benchmark tasks in the DeepMind Control Suite. Our method's ability to utilize MDP homomorphisms for representation learning leads to improved performance when learning from pixel observations.

paragraphs: Abstraction can make reinforcement learning more efficient by representing an environment through a simpler decision process. This paper develops that idea for continuous control, where both states and actions can vary continuously. It extends MDP homomorphisms, mappings that connect an original decision process to an abstract one, to this setting.

The authors derive a policy-gradient theorem for the abstract process. This provides a foundation for optimizing policies while taking advantage of approximate symmetries in the environment. Building on the theorem, they introduce an actor-critic algorithm that learns both the policy and the abstraction mapping simultaneously. A lax bisimulation metric guides this joint learning of representations and behavior.

Experiments on DeepMind Control Suite benchmark tasks demonstrate the method's effectiveness. In particular, using these mappings for representation learning improves performance when observations are pixels. The result links the theoretical abstraction machinery to a practical control problem: learning useful decision-making representations directly from visual observations, alongside learning the actions to take.
summary.tldr: The paper extends MDP abstractions to continuous control and jointly learns abstractions and policies, improving performance from pixel observations.

title: Continuous MDP Homomorphisms and Homomorphic Policy Gradient

abstract: For animals to navigate an uncertain world, their brains need to estimate uncertainty at the timescales of sensations and actions. Sampling-based algorithms afford a theoretically-grounded framework for probabilistic inference in neural circuits, but it remains unknown how one can implement fast sampling algorithms in biologically-plausible spiking networks. Here, we propose to leverage the population geometry, controlled by the neural code and the neural dynamics, to implement fast samplers in spiking neural networks. We first show that two classes of spiking samplers---efficient balanced spiking networks that simulate Langevin sampling, and networks with probabilistic spike rules that implement Metropolis-Hastings sampling---can be unified within a common framework. We then show that careful choice of population geometry, corresponding to the natural space of parameters, enables rapid inference of parameters drawn from strongly-correlated high-dimensional distributions in both networks. Our results suggest design principles for algorithms for sampling-based probabilistic inference in spiking neural networks, yielding potential inspiration for neuromorphic computing and testable predictions for neurobiology.

paragraphs: Sampling offers a way for neural circuits to represent uncertainty, but useful inference must happen quickly enough to support sensations and actions. This paper asks how biologically plausible spiking networks could implement fast sampling. Its main idea is to shape population geometry through the neural code and the network's dynamics.

The authors first bring two families of spiking samplers into a common framework. summary.tldr: Choosing suitable population geometry enables fast sampling from strongly correlated distributions in two classes of spiking neural networks.

title: Natural gradient enables fast sampling in spiking neural networks

abstract: We explore how generating a chain of thought---a series of intermediate reasoning steps---significantly improves the ability of large language models to perform complex reasoning. In particular, we show how such reasoning abilities emerge naturally in sufficiently large language models via a simple method called chain of thought prompting, where a few chain of thought demonstrations are provided as exemplars in prompting. Experiments on three large language models show that chain of thought prompting improves performance on a range of arithmetic, commonsense, and symbolic reasoning tasks. The empirical gains can be striking. For instance, prompting a 540B-parameter language model with just eight chain of thought exemplars achieves state of the art accuracy on the GSM8K benchmark of math word problems, surpassing even finetuned GPT-3 with a verifier.

The proposed method supplies a few worked examples containing a sequence of reasoning steps. These demonstrations give the model examples of how to develop an answer through intermediate conclusions.

The authors find that this prompting approach can elicit reasoning abilities in sufficiently large language models. Experiments with three large models show improvements across arithmetic, commonsense, and symbolic reasoning tasks. In the reported settings, including intermediate steps makes prompting a powerful way to draw out capabilities.
summary.tldr: Worked reasoning examples in prompts substantially improve sufficiently large language models' performance on several reasoning tasks.

title: Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models

abstract: Given an input image, and nothing else, our method returns the bounding boxes of objects in the image and phrases that describe the objects. This is achieved within an open world paradigm, in which the objects in the input image may not have been encountered during the training of the localization mechanism. Moreover, training takes place in a weakly supervised setting, where no bounding boxes are provided. To achieve this, our method combines two pre-trained networks: the CLIP image-to-text matching score and the BLIP image captioning tool. Training takes place on COCO images and their captions and is based on CLIP. Then, during inference, BLIP is used to generate a hypothesis regarding various regions of the current image. Our work generalizes weakly supervised segmentation and phrase grounding and is shown empirically to outperform the state of the art in both domains. It also shows very convincing results in the novel task of weakly-supervised open-world purely visual phrase-grounding presented in our work.For example, on the datasets used for benchmarking phrase-grounding, our method results in a very modest degradation in comparison to methods that employ human captions as an additional input.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a system that receives only an image and returns object bounding boxes together with descriptive phrases. It addresses an open-world setting in which objects may be unfamiliar to the trained localization mechanism. Training is weakly supervised: images and captions are available, but bounding-box annotations are not.

The method combines two pretrained networks with different roles. CLIP supplies image-text matching scores for training on COCO images and captions. At inference time, BLIP generates hypotheses about regions in the current image. This combination lets the system produce both descriptions and locations without requiring a human-written caption as an additional input.

The authors report improvements over prior methods in weakly supervised segmentation and phrase grounding. On phrase-grounding benchmarks, removing the need for human captions produces only a modest degradation relative to methods that receive those captions. The findings support a broader task in which the system must determine both what to describe and where it appears from visual input alone.
summary.tldr: Combining CLIP and BLIP enables image-only object localization and description without bounding-box supervision or human captions at inference.

title: What is Where by Looking: Weakly-Supervised Open-World Phrase-Grounding without Text Inputs

abstract: Graph contrastive learning attracts/disperses node representations for similar/dissimilar node pairs under some notion of similarity. It may be combined with a low-dimensional embedding of nodes to preserve intrinsic and structural properties of a graph. COLES, a recent graph contrastive method combines traditional graph embedding and negative sampling into one framework. COLES in fact minimizes the trace difference between the within-class scatter matrix encapsulating the graph connectivity and the total scatter matrix encapsulating negative sampling. In this paper, we propose a more essential framework for graph embedding, called Generalized Laplacian EigeNmaps (GLEN), which learns a graph representation by maximizing the rank difference between the total scatter matrix and the within-class scatter matrix, resulting in the minimum class separation guarantee. However, the rank difference minimization is an NP-hard problem. Thus, we replace the trace difference that corresponds to the difference of nuclear norms by the difference of LogDet expressions, which we argue is a more accurate surrogate for the NP-hard rank difference than the trace difference. While enjoying a lesser computational cost, the difference of LogDet terms is lower-bounded by the Affine-invariant Riemannian metric (AIRM) and Jesen-Bregman the LogDet Divergence (JBLD), and upper-bounded by AIRM scaled by the factor of $\sqrt{m}$. We show that GLEN offers favourable accuracy/scalability compared to state-of-the-art baselines.

paragraphs: Graph embedding maps nodes into representations intended to preserve useful relationships. Contrastive methods encourage similar nodes to stay close and dissimilar nodes to separate. The paper revisits this objective through two scatter matrices: one captures graph connectivity, while the other incorporates the spread associated with negative sampling.

The proposed GLEN framework uses a rank-difference objective to seek a representation with a minimum class-separation guarantee. Direct rank-based optimization is computationally difficult, so the authors replace it with a difference of log-determinant expressions. They argue that this is a more accurate approximation to the rank objective than the trace difference used by the earlier COLES framework.

The analysis also connects the log-determinant difference to established geometric measures between matrices, providing lower and upper bounds involving those measures. These relationships give mathematical structure to the proposed surrogate rather than treating it solely as a convenient numerical replacement. Empirically, GLEN offers favorable accuracy and scalability compared with the tested state-of-the-art baselines, supporting the practical value of reconsidering the objective used to separate graph representations.
summary.tldr: GLEN uses a log-determinant surrogate for a rank-based graph embedding objective and reports favorable accuracy and scalability.

title: Generalized Laplacian Eigenmaps

abstract: Randomized smoothing is one of the most promising frameworks for certifying the adversarial robustness of machine learning models, including Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). Yet, existing randomized smoothing certificates for GNNs are overly pessimistic since they treat the model as a black box, ignoring the underlying architecture. To remedy this, we propose novel gray-box certificates that exploit the message-passing principle of GNNs: We randomly intercept messages and carefully analyze the probability that messages from adversarially controlled nodes reach their target nodes. Compared to existing certificates, we certify robustness to much stronger adversaries that control entire nodes in the graph and can arbitrarily manipulate node features. Our certificates provide stronger guarantees for attacks at larger distances, as messages from farther-away nodes are more likely to get intercepted. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on various models and datasets. Since our gray-box certificates consider the underlying graph structure, we can significantly improve certifiable robustness by applying graph sparsification.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on various models and datasets. paragraphs: Robustness certificates establish conditions under which adversarial changes cannot alter a model's prediction. Existing randomized-smoothing certificates for graph neural networks can be overly pessimistic because they ignore how these networks operate. This paper uses the message-passing architecture to derive certificates that account for how adversarial influence travels through a graph.

The method randomly intercepts messages and analyzes the probability that information from adversarially controlled nodes reaches a target node. This supports guarantees against attackers controlling entire nodes and arbitrarily changing their features. The analysis uses architectural knowledge, making it a gray-box approach rather than treating the prediction system as an opaque function.

The certificates become stronger for attacks originating farther away, because messages traveling from more distant nodes are more likely to be intercepted. Experiments across models and datasets demonstrate the method's effectiveness. The authors also show that graph sparsification can significantly improve certifiable robustness. This connects the guarantee to graph structure: changing the available communication pathways can strengthen the protection that the analysis can establish.
summary.tldr: Randomly intercepting graph messages enables stronger architecture-aware robustness certificates against nodes with arbitrarily manipulated features.

title: Randomized Message-Interception Smoothing: Gray-box Certificates for Graph Neural Networks

abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) have shown superiority in many prediction tasks over graphs due to their impressive capability of capturing nonlinear relations in graph-structured data. However, for node classification tasks, often, only marginal improvement of GNNs has been observed in practice over their linear counterparts. Previous works provide very few understandings of this phenomenon. In this work, we resort to Bayesian learning to give an in-depth investigation of the functions of non-linearity in GNNs for node classification tasks. Given a graph generated from the statistical model CSBM, we observe that the max-a-posterior estimation of a node label given its own and neighbors' attributes consists of two types of non-linearity, the transformation of node attributes and a ReLU-activated feature aggregation from neighbors. The latter surprisingly matches the type of non-linearity used in many GNN models. By further imposing Gaussian assumption on node attributes, we prove that the superiority of those ReLU activations is only significant when the node attributes are far more informative than the graph structure, which nicely explains previous empirical observations. A similar argument is derived when there is a distribution shift of node attributes between the training and testing datasets. Finally, we verify our theory on both synthetic and real-world networks. Our code is available at <https://github.com/Graph-COM/Bayesian_inference_based_GNN.git>.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks can represent nonlinear relationships, yet they sometimes improve only slightly over linear models for node classification. This paper investigates that pattern through Bayesian inference. It asks which nonlinear operations arise when estimating a node's label from its own attributes and the attributes of its neighbors.

For graphs generated by a contextual stochastic block model, the authors identify two nonlinear parts in maximum-a-posteriori label estimation. One transforms node attributes; the other aggregates neighboring features using a ReLU activation. The latter resembles an operation already used in many graph neural networks, connecting their design to a statistical inference procedure.

Under an additional Gaussian assumption on node attributes, the authors prove that the ReLU advantage is significant only when attributes are far more informative than graph structure. They derive a similar argument for shifts in attribute distributions between training and testing. Synthetic and real-network experiments support the theory. The result gives a conditional explanation for modest nonlinear gains, grounded in how information is divided between attributes and connections.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian analysis explains when nonlinear neighbor aggregation offers significant advantages over linear graph models under stated statistical assumptions.

title: Understanding Non-linearity in Graph Neural Networks from the Bayesian-Inference Perspective

abstract: We study the effect of width on the dynamics of feature-learning neural networks across a variety of architectures and datasets. Early in training, wide neural networks trained on online data have not only identical loss curves but also agree in their point-wise test predictions throughout training. For simple tasks such as CIFAR-5m this holds throughout training for networks of realistic widths. We also show that structural properties of the models, including internal representations, preactivation distributions, edge of stability phenomena, and large learning rate effects are consistent across large widths. This motivates the hypothesis that phenomena seen in realistic models can be captured by infinite-width, feature-learning limits. For harder tasks (such as ImageNet and language modeling), and later training times, finite-width deviations grow systematically. Two distinct effects cause these deviations across widths. First, the network output has an initialization-dependent variance scaling inversely with width, which can be removed by ensembling networks. We observe, however, that ensembles of narrower networks perform worse than a single wide network. We call this the bias of narrower width. We conclude with a spectral perspective on the origin of this finite-width bias.
