Early in training on online data, wide networks agree not only in their loss curves but also in predictions for individual test examples. On simpler tasks such as CIFAR-5m, this agreement persists throughout training at widths the authors describe as realistic.

The consistency also appears in internal representations, preactivation distributions, and training phenomena involving stability and large learning rates. These observations motivate the hypothesis that infinite-width theories allowing feature learning can capture behavior in practical networks. The agreement therefore concerns both observable predictions and aspects of the internal learning process.

For harder tasks, including ImageNet and language modeling, differences across widths grow later in training. The authors distinguish initialization-dependent output variance, which decreases inversely with width and can be removed through ensembling, from a remaining disadvantage of narrower networks. Ensembles of narrow networks still perform worse than one wide network. They call this remaining effect finite-width bias and examine its origin through a spectral perspective.
summary.tldr: Wide feature-learning networks often train consistently across widths, but harder tasks reveal a narrow-network disadvantage that ensembling does not remove.

title: Feature-Learning Networks Are Consistent Across Widths At Realistic Scales

abstract: In generative compressed sensing (GCS), we want to recover a signal $\mathbf{x^*}\in\mathbb{R}^n$ from $m$ measurements ($m\ll n$) using a generative prior $\mathbf{x^*}\in G(\mathbb{B}_2^k(r))$, where $G$ is typically an $L$-Lipschitz continuous generative model and $\mathbb{B}_2^k(r)$ represents the radius-$r$ $\ell_2$-ball in $\mathbb{R}^k$. Under nonlinear measurements, most prior results are non-uniform, i.e., they hold with high probability for a fixed $\mathbf{x^*}$ rather than for all $\mathbf{x^*}$ simultaneously. In this paper, we build a unified framework to derive uniform recovery guarantees for nonlinear GCS where the observation model is nonlinear and possibly discontinuous or unknown. Our framework accommodates GCS with 1-bit/uniformly quantized observations and single index model as canonical examples. Specifically, using a single realization of the sensing ensemble and generalized Lasso, all $\mathbf{x^*}\in G(\mathbb{B}_2^k(r))$ can be recovered up to an $\ell_2$-error at most $\epsilon$ using roughly $\tilde{O}({k}/{\epsilon^2})$ samples, with omitted logarithmic factors typically being dominated by $\log L$. Notably, this almost coincides with existing non-uniform guarantees up to logarithmic factors, hence the uniformity costs very little. As part of our technical contributions, we introduce Lipschitz approximation to handle discontinuous observation models. We also develop a concentration inequality that produces tighter bound for product process whose index sets have low metric entropy. Experimental results are presented to corroborate our theory.

paragraphs: Generative compressed sensing reconstructs a high-dimensional signal from relatively few measurements by assuming that the signal belongs to the output range of a generative model. This paper studies nonlinear measurements, including observations that are quantized, discontinuous, or governed by an unknown transformation. Its main concern is whether one measurement setup can support recovery across the entire modeled signal family.

Earlier guarantees often concern a single fixed signal. The authors develop a framework for uniform guarantees: the same realization of the sensing system works simultaneously for all signals in the specified generative range. Using generalized Lasso, recovery to error at most epsilon requires roughly k divided by epsilon squared measurements, apart from logarithmic factors, where k is the latent dimension.

This measurement requirement nearly matches existing guarantees for individual signals, suggesting that uniformity adds little cost within the analyzed setting. The technical tools include Lipschitz approximations for discontinuous observations and a concentration inequality for suitably structured product processes. Experiments provide additional support for the theory.
summary.tldr: A unified framework gives nearly the same measurement requirements for recovering an entire generative signal family as for recovering a single fixed signal.

title: A Unified Framework for Uniform Signal Recovery in Nonlinear Generative Compressed Sensing

abstract: While personalized recommendations systems have become increasingly popular, ensuring user data protection remains a top concern in the development of these learning systems. A common approach to enhancing privacy involves training models using anonymous data rather than individual data. In this paper, we explore a natural technique called "look-alike clustering", which involves replacing sensitive features of individuals with the cluster's average values. We provide a precise analysis of how training models using anonymous cluster centers affects their generalization capabilities. We focus on an asymptotic regime where the size of the training set grows in proportion to the features dimension. Our analysis is based on the Convex Gaussian Minimax Theorem (CGMT) and allows us to theoretically understand the role of different model components on the generalization error. In addition, we demonstrate that in certain high-dimensional regimes, training over anonymous cluster centers acts as a regularization and improves generalization error of the trained models. Finally, we corroborate our asymptotic theory with finite-sample numerical experiments where we observe a perfect match when the sample size is only of order of a few hundreds.

paragraphs: Look-alike clustering replaces an individual's sensitive features with average values from a cluster of similar individuals. The paper studies what this transformation does to a model's ability to generalize. The central question is whether learning from these anonymous representations necessarily sacrifices predictive quality, or whether averaging can sometimes help the learned model.

The authors derive a precise analysis in a high-dimensional asymptotic setting: the number of training examples grows in proportion to the number of features. They use the Convex Gaussian Minimax Theorem to characterize generalization error and understand how different model components contribute to it. This provides a theoretical account of the consequences of replacing individual features with cluster averages.

In certain high-dimensional regimes, the analysis shows that this replacement acts as regularization and improves generalization. The benefit is conditional on the regime studied, rather than a universal property of anonymization. Finite-sample numerical experiments closely match the asymptotic predictions with only a few hundred examples, supporting the theory's relevance beyond an infinite-data limit.
summary.tldr: A high-dimensional analysis shows that replacing sensitive features with cluster averages can improve generalization by acting as regularization in certain regimes.

title: Anonymous Learning via Look-Alike Clustering: A Precise Analysis of Model Generalization

abstract: Recently, the transformer has enabled the speed-oriented trackers to approach state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance with high-speed thanks to the smaller input size or the lighter feature extraction backbone, though they still substantially lag behind their corresponding performance-oriented versions. In this paper, we demonstrate that it is possible to narrow or even close this gap while achieving high tracking speed based on the smaller input size. To this end, we non-uniformly resize the cropped image to have a smaller input size while the resolution of the area where the target is more likely to appear is higher and vice versa. This enables us to solve the dilemma of attending to a larger visual field while retaining more raw information for the target despite a smaller input size. Our formulation for the non-uniform resizing can be efficiently solved through quadratic programming (QP) and naturally integrated into most of the crop-based local trackers. Comprehensive experiments on five challenging datasets based on two kinds of transformer trackers, \ie, OSTrack and TransT, demonstrate consistent improvements over them. In particular, applying our method to the speed-oriented version of OSTrack even outperforms its performance-oriented counterpart by 0.6\% AUC on TNL2K, while running 50\% faster and saving over 55\% MACs. Codes and models are available at https://github.com/Kou-99/ZoomTrack.

paragraphs: Fast visual trackers often reduce input size, sacrificing information that could improve tracking accuracy. ZoomTrack changes how a cropped image is resized so that a small input retains more detail where the target is likely to appear. The aim is to preserve a broad visual field while allocating more of the available resolution to the likely target region.

The resizing is nonuniform: regions with higher target likelihood receive higher resolution, while other regions receive less. The authors formulate this operation as a quadratic programming problem that can be solved efficiently. It can be integrated into most crop-based local trackers, making input preparation the central mechanism for improving the speed–accuracy tradeoff.

Experiments on five datasets using OSTrack and TransT show consistent improvements. On TNL2K, the modified speed-oriented OSTrack exceeds its performance-oriented counterpart by 0.6% AUC while running 50% faster and using over 55% fewer multiply-accumulate operations. This specific result illustrates the paper’s broader finding that target-aware resizing can narrow, and in some evaluated cases close, the accuracy gap associated with smaller tracker inputs.
summary.tldr: ZoomTrack preserves detail near likely target locations through nonuniform resizing, improving the accuracy of fast visual trackers.

title: ZoomTrack: Target-aware Non-uniform Resizing for Efficient Visual Tracking

abstract: Recently, text-to-image models have been thriving. Despite their powerful generative capacity, our research has uncovered a lack of robustness in this generation process. Specifically, the introduction of small perturbations to the text prompts can result in the blending of primary subjects with other categories or their complete disappearance in the generated images. In this paper, we propose **Auto-attack on Text-to-image Models (ATM)**, a gradient-based approach, to effectively and efficiently generate such perturbations. By learning a Gumbel Softmax distribution, we can make the discrete process of word replacement or extension continuous, thus ensuring the differentiability of the perturbation generation. Once the distribution is learned, ATM can sample multiple attack samples simultaneously. These attack samples can prevent the generative model from generating the desired subjects without tampering with the category keywords in the prompt. ATM has achieved a 91.1\% success rate in short-text attacks and an 81.2\% success rate in long-text attacks. Further empirical analysis revealed three attack patterns based on: 1) variability in generation speed, 2) similarity of coarse-grained characteristics, and 3) polysemy of words. The code is available at https://github.com/duchengbin8/Stable_Diffusion_is_Unstable

paragraphs: Small changes to a text prompt can disrupt what a text-to-image model generates. This paper finds that the requested main subject may blend with another category or disappear, even when the subject’s category words remain intact. It introduces Auto-attack on Text-to-image Models, or ATM, to find such perturbations efficiently.

ATM is gradient-based, but replacing or adding words is ordinarily a discrete operation. The method learns a Gumbel Softmax distribution to make that search continuous and differentiable. Once learned, the distribution can produce multiple attack samples at the same time. This gives the method a way to search over prompt modifications while keeping the category keywords unchanged.

The reported attack success rates are 91.1% for short text and 81.2% for long text. Further empirical analysis identifies three patterns associated with the attacks: differences in generation speed, shared coarse characteristics, and words with multiple meanings. The findings expose a robustness weakness in the studied generation process: retaining the intended subject’s name does not reliably preserve that subject when surrounding prompt wording is perturbed.
summary.tldr: ATM finds small prompt changes that can erase or distort intended image subjects without changing their category keywords.

title: Stable Diffusion is Unstable

abstract: Open-set fine-grained retrieval is an emerging challenging task that allows to retrieve unknown categories beyond the training set. The best solution for handling unknown categories is to represent them using a set of visual attributes learnt from known categories, as widely used in zero-shot learning. Though important, attribute modeling usually requires significant manual annotations and thus is labor-intensive. Therefore, it is worth to investigate how to transform retrieval models trained by image-level supervision from category semantic extraction to attribute modeling. To this end, we propose a novel Visual Attribute Parameterization Network (VAPNet) to learn visual attributes from known categories and parameterize them into the retrieval model, without the involvement of any attribute annotations.In this way, VAPNet could utilize its parameters to parse a set of visual attributes from unknown categories and precisely represent them.Technically, VAPNet explicitly attains some semantics with rich details via making use of local image patches and distills the visual attributes from these discovered semantics. Additionally, it integrates the online refinement of these visual attributes into the training process to iteratively enhance their quality. Simultaneously, VAPNet treats these attributes as supervisory signals to tune the retrieval models, thereby achieving attribute parameterization. Extensive experiments on open-set fine-grained retrieval datasets validate the superior performance of our VAPNet over existing solutions.

paragraphs: Open-set fine-grained retrieval must find relevant images from categories that were absent during training. Visual attributes learned from known categories can provide a way to represent those unfamiliar categories. However, explicitly labeling attributes is labor-intensive. This paper asks how a retrieval model trained with image-level supervision can acquire useful attribute representations without those annotations.

The proposed Visual Attribute Parameterization Network, or VAPNet, extracts detailed semantic information from local image patches and distills visual attributes from it. During training, it repeatedly refines the attributes to improve their quality. Those attributes also serve as supervisory signals for tuning the retrieval model, embedding the attribute knowledge into its parameters.

The intended result is a model that can extract and use visual attributes when representing unknown categories. Experiments on open-set fine-grained retrieval datasets report better performance than existing solutions. This supports the approach of learning transferable attribute information from category-supervised images, while avoiding a separate requirement for manually annotated attributes during training.
summary.tldr: VAPNet learns and refines visual attributes without attribute annotations to improve retrieval for categories unseen during training.

title: Learning to Parameterize Visual Attributes for Open-set Fine-grained Retrieval

abstract: Particle-based variational inference methods (ParVIs) such as Stein variational gradient descent (SVGD) update the particles based on the kernelized Wasserstein gradient flow for the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence. However, the design of kernels is often non-trivial and can be restrictive for the flexibility of the method. Recent works show that functional gradient flow approximations with quadratic form regularization terms can improve performance. In this paper, we propose a ParVI framework, called generalized Wasserstein gradient descent (GWG), based on a generalized Wasserstein gradient flow of the KL divergence, which can be viewed as a functional gradient method with a broader class of regularizers induced by convex functions. We show that GWG exhibits strong convergence guarantees. We also provide an adaptive version that automatically chooses Wasserstein metric to accelerate convergence. In experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed framework on both simulated and real data problems.

paragraphs: Particle-based variational inference represents an approximate distribution through a collection of particles and updates their positions to improve the approximation. Methods such as Stein variational gradient descent use a kernelized Wasserstein gradient flow to reduce KL divergence. Choosing a suitable kernel can be difficult and can restrict the flexibility of these methods.

The paper proposes generalized Wasserstein gradient descent, or GWG. Its formulation can be understood as functional gradient optimization with a broader family of regularizers induced by convex functions. This extends the design space beyond the quadratic regularization explored in recent work, offering a more general framework for deciding how the particle distribution should evolve.

The authors establish strong convergence guarantees and introduce an adaptive version that selects the Wasserstein metric automatically to accelerate convergence. Experiments on simulated and real data demonstrate effectiveness and efficiency. The contribution combines a broader mathematical formulation with an adaptive mechanism, connecting choices about the geometry of distribution updates to the behavior of practical particle-based inference.
summary.tldr: GWG broadens the geometry and regularization of particle-based inference, with convergence guarantees and an adaptive metric-selection variant.

title: Particle-based Variational Inference with Generalized Wasserstein Gradient Flow

abstract: We study the problem of $\text{\emph{vector set search}}$ with $\text{\emph{vector set queries}}$. This task is analogous to traditional near-neighbor search, with the exception that both the query and each element in the collection are $\text{\textit{sets}}$ of vectors. We identify this problem as a core subroutine for semantic search applications and find that existing solutions are unacceptably slow. Towards this end, we present a new approximate search algorithm, DESSERT ($\text{\bf D}$ESSERT $\text{\bf E}$ffeciently $\text{\bf S}$earches $\text{\bf S}$ets of $\text{\bf E}$mbeddings via $\text{\bf R}$etrieval $\text{\bf T}$ables). DESSERT is a general tool with strong theoretical guarantees and excellent empirical performance. When we integrate DESSERT into ColBERT, a state-of-the-art semantic search model, we find a 2-5x speedup on the MS MARCO and LoTTE retrieval benchmarks with minimal loss in recall, underscoring the effectiveness and practical applicability of our proposal.

paragraphs: Traditional near-neighbor search compares a query vector against a collection of vectors. This paper studies a more involved version in which both the query and each searchable item are sets of vectors. The authors identify this operation as an important component of semantic search and find existing solutions too slow.

DESSERT is an approximate search algorithm designed specifically for this vector-set problem. Its name refers to searching sets of embeddings through retrieval tables. The paper presents it as a general-purpose tool supported by strong theoretical guarantees and empirical results. Addressing the set-level search operation directly targets the computational burden created when queries and searchable items each have multiple vector representations.

When integrated into the ColBERT semantic search model, DESSERT delivers a two- to five-fold speedup on MS MARCO and LoTTE, with only a small reduction in recall. These results demonstrate a practical speed-versus-retrieval tradeoff in the tested system: substantially faster searches while retaining nearly the same ability to retrieve relevant items.
summary.tldr: DESSERT accelerates approximate search over sets of embeddings, yielding two- to five-fold ColBERT speedups with minimal recall loss.

title: DESSERT: An Efficient Algorithm for Vector Set Search with Vector Set Queries

abstract: This paper advocates a new paradigm Personalized Empirical Risk Minimization (PERM) to facilitate learning from heterogeneous data sources without imposing stringent constraints on computational resources shared by participating devices. In PERM, we aim at learning a distinct model for each client by personalizing the aggregation of local empirical losses by effectively estimating the statistical discrepancy among data distributions, which entails optimal statistical accuracy for all local distributions and overcomes the data heterogeneity issue. To learn personalized models at scale, we propose a distributed algorithm that replaces the standard model averaging with model shuffling to simultaneously optimize PERM objectives for all devices. This also allows to learn distinct model architectures (e.g., neural networks with different number of parameters) for different clients, thus confining to underlying memory and compute resources of individual clients. We rigorously analyze the convergence of proposed algorithm and conduct experiments that corroborates the effectiveness of proposed paradigm.

To learn personalized models at scale, we propose a distributed algorithm that replaces the standard model averaging with model shuffling to simultaneously optimize PERM objectives for all devices. This also allows to learn distinct model architectures (e.g., neural networks with different number of parameters) for different clients, thus confining to underlying memory and compute resources of individual clients. We rigorously analyze the convergence of proposed algorithm and conduct experiments that corroborates the effectiveness of proposed paradigm.

paragraphs: When clients have different data distributions, the same shared learning objective may not serve every client equally well. Personalized Empirical Risk Minimization, or PERM, instead learns a distinct model for each client. It personalizes how local empirical losses are combined by estimating statistical differences among the clients' data distributions.

This makes the aggregation of training evidence specific to the distribution each model must serve. The authors connect this formulation to optimal statistical accuracy for the local distributions. To optimize all clients' objectives at scale, they introduce a distributed algorithm that shuffles models rather than relying on standard model averaging.

The approach also permits clients to use different model architectures, including networks with different parameter counts. That flexibility allows model choices to fit individual devices' memory and computational resources. The paper provides a convergence analysis and experiments supporting the paradigm's effectiveness. Its contribution joins statistical personalization with resource flexibility: both the evidence used for a client and the model assigned to it can differ across the distributed system.
summary.tldr: PERM personalizes distributed learning objectives and uses model shuffling to support clients with different data and computational resources.

title: Distributed Personalized Empirical Risk Minimization

abstract: A digital twin is a virtual replica of a real-world physical phenomena that uses mathematical modeling to characterize and simulate its defining features. By constructing digital twins for disease processes, we can perform in-silico simulations that mimic patients' health conditions and counterfactual outcomes under hypothetical interventions in a virtual setting. This eliminates the need for invasive procedures or uncertain treatment decisions. In this paper, we propose a method to identify digital twin model parameters using only noninvasive patient health data. We approach the digital twin modeling as a composite inverse problem, and observe that its structure resembles pretraining and finetuning in self-supervised learning (SSL). Leveraging this, we introduce a physics-informed SSL algorithm that initially pretrains a neural network on the pretext task of learning a differentiable simulator of a physiological process. Subsequently, the model is trained to reconstruct physiological measurements from noninvasive modalities while being constrained by the physical equations learned in pretraining. We apply our method to identify digital twins of cardiac hemodynamics using noninvasive echocardiogram videos, and demonstrate its utility in unsupervised disease detection and in-silico clinical trials.

title: Med-Real2Sim: Non-Invasive Medical Digital Twins using Physics-Informed Self-Supervised Learning

abstract: Visual text generation has significantly advanced through diffusion models aimed at producing images with readable and realistic text. Recent works primarily use a ControlNet-based framework, employing standard font text images to control diffusion models. Recognizing the critical role of control information in generating high-quality text, we investigate its influence from three perspectives: input encoding, role at different stages, and output features. Our findings reveal that: 1) Input control information has unique characteristics compared to conventional inputs like Canny edges and depth maps. 2) Control information plays distinct roles at different stages of the denoising process. 3) Output control features significantly differ from the base and skip features of the U-Net decoder in the frequency domain. Based on these insights, we propose TextGen, a novel framework designed to enhance generation quality by optimizing control information. We improve input and output features using Fourier analysis to emphasize relevant information and reduce noise. Additionally, we employ a two-stage generation framework to align the different roles of control information at different stages. Furthermore, we introduce an effective and lightweight dataset for training. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in both Chinese and English text generation. The code and dataset are available at https://github.com/CyrilSterling/TextGen.

This paper investigates how that guidance behaves, examining its input encoding, its changing role during denoising, and the features it produces.

They also find that its role changes across denoising stages and that its output features differ in frequency content from the U-Net decoder's base and skip features. These observations motivate TextGen, which uses Fourier analysis to emphasize relevant information and suppress noise in the control features.

Their method achieves state-of-the-art Chinese and English text-generation performance, supporting the idea that improving how control information is represented and scheduled can improve the resulting text images.
summary.tldr: TextGen improves Chinese and English text-image generation by refining control features and matching guidance to different denoising stages.

title: How Control Information Influences Multilingual Text Image Generation and Editing?

abstract: This work presents a unified knowledge protocol, called UKnow, which facilitates knowledge-based studies from the perspective of data. Particularly focusing on visual and linguistic modalities, we categorize data knowledge into five unit types, namely, in-image, in-text, cross-image, cross-text, and image-text, and set up an efficient pipeline to help construct the multimodal knowledge graph from any data collection. Thanks to the logical information naturally contained in knowledge graph, organizing datasets under UKnow format opens up more possibilities of data usage compared to the commonly used image-text pairs. Following UKnow protocol, we collect, from public international news, a large-scale multimodal knowledge graph dataset that consists of 1,388,568 nodes (with 571,791 vision-related ones) and 3,673,817 triplets. The dataset is also annotated with rich event tags, including 11 coarse labels and 9,185 fine labels. Experiments on four benchmarks demonstrate the potential of UKnow in supporting common-sense reasoning and boosting vision-language pre-training with a single dataset, benefiting from its unified form of knowledge organization. Code, dataset, and models will be made publicly available. See Appendix to download the dataset.

paragraphs: UKnow provides a protocol for organizing visual and linguistic knowledge in a shared graph structure. It divides knowledge into five unit types: within an image, within text, across images, across texts, and between images and text. A construction pipeline helps turn data collections into multimodal knowledge graphs following this format.

The motivation is to make more of a dataset's relationships available than a collection of image–text pairs typically exposes. The authors use the protocol to build a dataset from public international news. It contains 1,388,568 nodes, including 571,791 vision-related nodes, and 3,673,817 triplets. Event annotations add 11 coarse labels and 9,185 fine labels, providing another level of organization within the collection.

Experiments on four benchmarks demonstrate the potential of this single dataset to support commonsense reasoning and improve vision-language pretraining. The stated benefit comes from its unified organization of knowledge. The work therefore contributes both a reusable data protocol and a large dataset illustrating how graph-based relationships can support multiple forms of multimodal learning.
summary.tldr: UKnow organizes visual and linguistic relationships into multimodal knowledge graphs that support reasoning and vision-language pretraining.

title: UKnow: A Unified Knowledge Protocol with Multimodal Knowledge Graph Datasets for Reasoning and Vision-Language Pre-Training

abstract: Differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD) has been instrumental in privately training deep learning models by providing a framework to control and track the privacy loss incurred during training. At the core of this computation lies a subsampling method that uses a privacy amplification lemma to enhance the privacy guarantees provided by the additive noise. Fixed size subsampling is appealing for its constant memory usage, unlike the variable sized minibatches in Poisson subsampling. It is also of interest in addressing class imbalance and federated learning. Current computable guarantees for fixed-size subsampling are not tight and do not consider both add/remove and replace-one adjacency relationships. We present a new and holistic Rényi differential privacy (RDP) accountant for DP-SGD with fixed-size subsampling without replacement (FSwoR) and with replacement (FSwR). For FSwoR we consider both add/remove and replace-one adjacency, where we improve on the best current computable bound by a factor of $4$. We also show for the first time that the widely-used Poisson subsampling and FSwoR with replace-one adjacency have the same privacy to leading order in the sampling probability. Our work suggests that FSwoR is often preferable to Poisson subsampling due to constant memory usage. Our FSwR accountant includes explicit non-asymptotic upper and lower bounds and, to the authors' knowledge, is the first such RDP analysis of fixed-size subsampling with replacement for DP-SGD. We analytically and empirically compare fixed size and Poisson subsampling, and show that DP-SGD gradients in a fixed-size subsampling regime exhibit lower variance in practice in addition to memory usage benefits.

This paper develops tighter privacy accounting for fixed-size sampling both with and without replacement.

It improves the best existing computable bound by a factor of four. It also shows that fixed-size sampling without replacement under replace-one adjacency matches Poisson sampling’s privacy behavior to leading order in the sampling probability.

Their analytical and empirical comparisons also find lower gradient variance in practice with fixed-size sampling. Together, these results suggest that sampling without replacement is often an attractive choice: its memory benefits can be accompanied by competitive privacy guarantees and less variable gradient estimates.
summary.tldr: Tighter privacy accounting strengthens the case for fixed-size minibatches in DP-SGD, alongside their memory and observed gradient-variance benefits.

title: Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent with Fixed-Size Minibatches: Tighter RDP Guarantees with or without Replacement

abstract: In this paper, we propose a novel policy optimization framework that maximizes Return on Investment (ROI) of a policy using a fixed dataset within a Markov Decision Process (MDP) equipped with a cost function. ROI, defined as the ratio between the return and the accumulated cost of a policy, serves as a measure of efficiency of the policy. Despite the importance of maximizing ROI in various applications, it remains a challenging problem due to its nature as a ratio of two long-term values: return and accumulated cost. To address this, we formulate the ROI maximizing reinforcement learning problem as a linear fractional programming. We then incorporate the stationary distribution correction (DICE) framework to develop a practical offline ROI maximization algorithm.Our proposed algorithm, ROIDICE, yields an efficient policy that offers a superior trade-off between return and accumulated cost compared to policies trained using existing frameworks.

paragraphs: A policy can earn a large return while consuming substantial resources. ROIDICE studies efficiency by defining return on investment as total return divided by accumulated cost. The goal is to learn a policy that maximizes this ratio using a fixed dataset in a Markov decision process with an explicit cost function.

This objective is difficult because both the numerator and denominator describe long-term outcomes of decisions. The authors formulate the problem as linear fractional programming, giving the ratio objective a mathematical optimization structure. They then combine this formulation with stationary distribution correction, known as DICE, to build a practical offline learning algorithm.

The resulting algorithm targets the relationship between reward and expenditure directly. The authors report that ROIDICE produces policies with a better trade-off between return and accumulated cost than policies trained with existing frameworks. The contribution is therefore both an objective and a method: it makes efficiency the quantity being optimized and provides a way to pursue it from previously collected data.
summary.tldr: ROIDICE learns policies from fixed data by directly maximizing the ratio of long-term return to accumulated cost.

title: ROIDICE: Offline Return on Investment Maximization for Efficient Decision Making

abstract: As the scale of data and models for video understanding rapidly expand, handling long-form video input in transformer-based models presents a practical challenge. Rather than resorting to input sampling or token dropping, which may result in information loss, token merging shows promising results when used in collaboration with transformers. However, the application of token merging for long-form video processing is not trivial. We begin with the premise that token merging should not rely solely on the similarity of video tokens; the saliency of tokens should also be considered. To address this, we explore various video token merging strategies for long-form video classification, starting with a simple extension of image token merging, moving to region-concentrated merging, and finally proposing a learnable video token merging (VTM) algorithm that dynamically merges tokens based on their saliency. Extensive experimental results show that we achieve better or comparable performances on the LVU, COIN, and Breakfast datasets. Moreover, our approach significantly reduces memory costs by 84% and boosts throughput by approximately 6.89 times compared to baseline algorithms.

paragraphs: This paper studies how transformers can process long videos more efficiently by merging their tokens. Sampling the input or dropping tokens may discard information, motivating ways to combine representations. The authors argue that similarity alone is insufficient for deciding which video tokens to merge: their saliency, or importance, should also influence the decision.

The study explores a progression of strategies, beginning with an extension of image token merging and then considering merging concentrated within regions. It culminates in a learnable Video Token Merging algorithm that dynamically uses saliency. The central design choice is to make token reduction sensitive to which parts of the video matter, alongside the relationships among token representations.

Experiments on long-form video classification show better or comparable performance on LVU, COIN, and Breakfast. Relative to baseline algorithms, the approach reduces memory costs by 84% and increases throughput by approximately 6.89 times. These results support saliency-aware merging as a practical way to reduce the cost of long-video processing.
summary.tldr: Learnable saliency-aware video token merging maintains or improves classification performance while sharply reducing memory costs and increasing throughput.

title: Video Token Merging for Long Video Understanding

abstract: The rapid development of Large Language Models (LLMs) has been pivotal in advancing AI, with pre-trained LLMs being adaptable to diverse downstream tasks through fine-tuning. Federated learning (FL) further enhances fine-tuning in a privacy-aware manner by utilizing clients' local data through in-situ computation, eliminating the need for data movement. However, fine-tuning LLMs, given their massive scale of parameters, poses challenges for clients with constrained and heterogeneous resources in FL. Previous methods employed low-rank adaptation (LoRA) for efficient federated fine-tuning but utilized traditional FL aggregation strategies on LoRA adapters. This approach led to mathematically inaccurate aggregation noise, reducing fine-tuning effectiveness and failing to address heterogeneous LoRAs. In this work, we first highlight the mathematical incorrectness of LoRA aggregation in existing federated fine-tuning methods. We introduce a new approach called FLoRA that enables federated fine-tuning on heterogeneous LoRA adapters across clients through a novel stacking-based aggregation method. Our approach is noise-free and seamlessly supports heterogeneous LoRAs. Extensive experiments demonstrate FLoRA's superior performance in both homogeneous and heterogeneous settings, surpassing state-of-the-art methods. We envision this work as a milestone for efficient, privacy-preserving, and accurate federated fine-tuning of LLMs.

paragraphs: Federated fine-tuning lets clients adapt a shared language model using local computation, without moving their training data. Large models make this difficult for clients with limited and unequal resources. Low-rank adaptation reduces the adaptation burden, but combining these smaller adapters across clients introduces its own mathematical challenges.

The paper identifies an aggregation problem in earlier methods: applying traditional federated aggregation strategies to LoRA adapters introduces mathematically inaccurate aggregation noise. Those approaches also fail to accommodate heterogeneous adapters effectively. FLoRA replaces that aggregation mechanism with a stacking-based method designed to combine adapters of different sizes across clients.

The authors describe this aggregation as noise-free with respect to the identified combination error and show that it supports heterogeneous LoRAs. Experiments report better performance than state-of-the-art methods both when clients use homogeneous adapters and when their adapters differ. This makes aggregation itself central to effective federated adaptation: reducing each client's training cost is only part of the problem, because the resulting updates must also be combined correctly.
summary.tldr: FLoRA uses stacking-based aggregation to combine heterogeneous LoRA adapters without the aggregation noise identified in earlier federated fine-tuning methods.

title: FLoRA: Federated Fine-Tuning Large Language Models with Heterogeneous Low-Rank Adaptations

abstract: Large multimodal models (LMMs) are processing increasingly longer and richer inputs. Albeit the progress, few public benchmark is available to measure such development. To mitigate this gap, we introduce LongVideoBench, a question-answering benchmark that features video-language interleaved inputs up to an hour long. Our benchmark includes 3,763 varying-length web-collected videos with their subtitles across diverse themes, designed to comprehensively evaluate LMMs on long-term multimodal understanding. To achieve this, we interpret the primary challenge as to accurately retrieve and reason over detailed multimodal information from long inputs. As such, we formulate a novel video question-answering task termed referring reasoning. Specifically, as part of the question, it contains a referring query that references related video contexts, called referred context. The model is then required to reason over relevant video details from the referred context. Following the paradigm of referring reasoning, we curate 6,678 human-annotated multiple-choice questions in 17 fine-grained categories, establishing one of the most comprehensive benchmarks for long-form video understanding. Evaluations suggest that the LongVideoBench presents significant challenges even for the most advanced proprietary models (e.g. GPT-4o, Gemini-1.5-Pro), while their open-source counterparts show an even larger performance gap. In addition, our results indicate that model performance on the benchmark improves only when they are capable of processing more frames, positioning LongVideoBench as a valuable benchmark for evaluating future-generation long-context LMMs.

paragraphs: LongVideoBench evaluates whether multimodal models can find and reason about detailed information in long videos accompanied by subtitles. It contains 3,763 web videos of varying lengths, with inputs extending to an hour. The benchmark addresses a gap between models' growing capacity to accept long inputs and public evaluations of what they understand from them.

Its central task is referring reasoning. A question points to a relevant context within the video, and the model must reason about details in that context. The benchmark includes 6,678 human-annotated multiple-choice questions spanning 17 categories, combining the challenge of locating relevant material with the challenge of interpreting it.

Evaluations find substantial difficulty even for advanced proprietary models, with open-source models falling further behind. The reported results also indicate that performance improves only when models can process more frames. Within these evaluations, additional frame-processing capacity is therefore a condition associated with improvement, emphasizing the importance of access to detailed visual information over a long input.
summary.tldr: LongVideoBench tests retrieval and reasoning over videos with subtitles lasting up to an hour, revealing substantial challenges for evaluated multimodal models.

title: LongVideoBench: A Benchmark for Long-context Interleaved Video-Language Understanding

abstract: Convolutions (Convs) and multi-head self-attentions (MHSAs) are typically considered alternatives to each other for building vision backbones. Although some works try to integrate both, they apply the two operators simultaneously at the finest pixel granularity. With Convs responsible for per-pixel feature extraction already, the question is whether we still need to include the heavy MHSAs at such a fine-grained level. In fact, this is the root cause of the scalability issue w.r.t. the input resolution for vision transformers. To address this important problem, we propose in this work to use MSHAs and Convs in parallel \textbf{at different granularity levels} instead. Specifically, in each layer, we use two different ways to represent an image: a fine-grained regular grid and a coarse-grained set of semantic slots. We apply different operations to these two representations: Convs to the grid for local features, and MHSAs to the slots for global features. A pair of fully differentiable soft clustering and dispatching modules is introduced to bridge the grid and set representations, thus enabling local-global fusion. Through extensive experiments on various vision tasks, we empirically verify the potential of the proposed integration scheme, named \textit{GLMix}: by offloading the burden of fine-grained features to light-weight Convs, it is sufficient to use MHSAs in a few (e.g., 64) semantic slots to match the performance of recent state-of-the-art backbones, while being more efficient. Our visualization results also demonstrate that the soft clustering module produces a meaningful semantic grouping effect with only IN1k classification supervision, which may induce better interpretability and inspire new weakly-supervised semantic segmentation approaches. Code will be available at \url{https://github.com/rayleizhu/GLMix}.

paragraphs: Combining convolution and attention at fine image resolution can duplicate expensive processing. GLMix gives the two operations different levels of detail to work with. Convolutions extract local features on a regular image grid, while multi-head self-attention models global relationships among a much smaller collection of semantic slots.

Each layer connects these representations through differentiable soft clustering and dispatching modules. Clustering links fine-grained image features to the coarse slot representation, and dispatching enables information exchange back to the grid. This lets local detail and global information interact while concentrating attention computation on a compact representation.

Across the evaluated vision tasks, attention over a small number of slots, such as 64, is sufficient to match recent state-of-the-art backbones with greater efficiency. Visualizations also show meaningful semantic grouping learned using only ImageNet-1K classification supervision. The authors suggest that this grouping may improve interpretability and inspire weakly supervised segmentation approaches; those possibilities are distinct from the demonstrated backbone performance.
summary.tldr: GLMix combines fine-grid convolutions with attention over coarse semantic slots to improve vision-backbone efficiency.

title: Revisiting the Integration of Convolution and Attention for Vision Backbone

abstract: Our objective in this paper is to probe large vision models to determine to what extent they ‘understand’ different physical properties of the 3D scene depicted in an image. To this end, we make the following contributions: (i) We introduce a general and lightweight protocol to evaluate whether features of an off-the-shelf large vision model encode a number of physical ‘properties’ of the 3D scene, by training discriminative classifiers on the features for these properties. The probes are applied on datasets of real images with annotations for the property. (ii) We apply this protocol to properties covering scene geometry, scene material, support relations, lighting, and view-dependent measures, and large vision models including CLIP, DINOv1, DINOv2, VQGAN, Stable Diffusion. (iii) We find that features from Stable Diffusion and DINOv2 are good for discriminative learning of a number of properties, including scene geometry, support relations, shadows and depth, but less performant for occlusion and material, while outperforming DINOv1, CLIP and VQGAN for all properties. (iv) It is observed that different time steps of Stable Diffusion features, as well as different transformer layers of DINO/CLIP/VQGAN, are good at different properties, unlocking potential applications of 3D physical understanding.

The results therefore provide guidance about where useful physical information can be found. The evidence concerns information recoverable by trained probes, giving a concrete interpretation to the paper’s question about physical understanding.
summary.tldr: A lightweight probing protocol finds useful but uneven information about 3D physical properties in large vision models.

title: A General Protocol to Probe Large Vision Models for 3D Physical Understanding

abstract: Generalized eigenvalue problems (GEPs) find applications in various fields of science and engineering. For example, principal component analysis, Fisher's discriminant analysis, and canonical correlation analysis are specific instances of GEPs and are widely used in statistical data processing. In this work, we study GEPs under generative priors, assuming that the underlying leading generalized eigenvector lies within the range of a Lipschitz continuous generative model. Under appropriate conditions, we show that any optimal solution to the corresponding optimization problems attains the optimal statistical rate. Moreover, from a computational perspective, we propose an iterative algorithm called the Projected Rayleigh Flow Method (PRFM) to approximate the optimal solution. We theoretically demonstrate that under suitable assumptions, PRFM converges linearly to an estimated vector that achieves the optimal statistical rate. Numerical results are provided to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

paragraphs: Generalized eigenvalue problems underlie statistical methods including principal component analysis, Fisher’s discriminant analysis, and canonical correlation analysis. The generator is required to be Lipschitz continuous, meaning its outputs change in a controlled way as its inputs change. Under appropriate additional conditions, the authors show that any optimal solution of their formulation achieves the optimal statistical rate. This result concerns the quality of estimation when the assumed generative structure and the theorem’s conditions hold.

To address computation, the paper proposes the Projected Rayleigh Flow Method, an iterative algorithm for approximating that solution. Under suitable assumptions, it converges linearly to an estimated vector that also achieves the optimal statistical rate. Numerical results demonstrate the method’s effectiveness. The work thus connects a structured assumption about the target vector to both statistical guarantees and a practical iterative procedure.
summary.tldr: Generative priors enable statistically optimal generalized eigenvector estimation and a linearly convergent algorithm under suitable assumptions.

title: Generalized Eigenvalue Problems with Generative Priors

abstract: Controllable synthetic data generation can substantially lower the annotation cost of training data. Prior works use diffusion models to generate driving images conditioned on the 3D object layout. However, those models are trained on small-scale datasets like nuScenes, which lack appearance and layout diversity. Moreover, overfitting often happens, where the trained models can only generate images based on the layout data from the validation set of the same dataset. In this work, we introduce a simulator-conditioned scene generation framework called SimGen that can learn to generate diverse driving scenes by mixing data from the simulator and the real world. It uses a novel cascade diffusion pipeline to address challenging sim-to-real gaps and multi-condition conflicts. A driving video dataset DIVA is collected to enhance the generative diversity of SimGen, which contains over 147.5 hours of real-world driving videos from 73 locations worldwide and simulated driving data from the MetaDrive simulator. SimGen achieves superior generation quality and diversity while preserving controllability based on the text prompt and the layout pulled from a simulator. We further demonstrate the improvements brought by SimGen for synthetic data augmentation on the BEV detection and segmentation task and showcase its capability in safety-critical data generation.

paragraphs: Synthetic driving images could reduce the cost of labeled training data, but useful generation needs both diversity and control over scene content. The paper identifies limited appearance and layout diversity, along with overfitting to familiar layouts, as problems in previous diffusion-based approaches trained on small datasets.

Generation remains controlled by a text prompt and a layout obtained from a simulator. The accompanying DIVA dataset includes over 147.5 hours of real driving video from 73 locations worldwide, together with MetaDrive simulation data.

The authors report improved generation quality and diversity while retaining control over the generated scenes. They also demonstrate benefits from synthetic data augmentation for bird's-eye-view detection and segmentation, and show safety-critical scene generation. These results connect visual generation improvements to downstream perception tasks, making the method relevant to producing controllable training examples as well as images.
summary.tldr: SimGen combines real and simulated data to generate diverse, controllable driving scenes and improve perception through synthetic data augmentation.

title: SimGen: Simulator-conditioned Driving Scene Generation

abstract: This paper studies simple bilevel problems, where a convex upper-level function is minimized over the optimal solutions of a convex lower-level problem. We first show the fundamental difficulty of simple bilevel problems, that the approximate optimal value of such problems is not obtainable by first-order zero-respecting algorithms. Then we follow recent works to pursue the weak approximate solutions. For this goal, we propose a novel method by reformulating them into functionally constrained problems. Our method achieves near-optimal rates for both smooth and nonsmooth problems. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first near-optimal algorithm that works under standard assumptions of smoothness or Lipschitz continuity for the objective functions.

paragraphs: A simple bilevel problem has two linked objectives: first identify solutions that optimize a lower-level function, then minimize an upper-level function within that solution set. This paper studies the case where both functions are convex. Even with that structure, the requirement to optimize over another problem’s optimal solutions creates a fundamental computational difficulty.

The authors show that a particular class of methods, first-order zero-respecting algorithms, cannot obtain the approximate optimal value of these problems. They therefore pursue the weaker approximate-solution target considered in recent work. Their method reformulates the bilevel task as a functionally constrained problem, providing a different route to that attainable approximation goal.

The resulting algorithm achieves near-optimal rates for both smooth and nonsmooth problems. The authors describe it, to their knowledge, as the first near-optimal method covering these cases under standard smoothness or Lipschitz-continuity assumptions. The positive result concerns weak approximate solutions, so it fits alongside the impossibility result without claiming to overcome that stronger computational barrier.
summary.tldr: A constrained reformulation yields near-optimal weak approximation rates for convex bilevel problems despite a stronger approximation barrier.

title: Functionally Constrained Algorithm Solves Convex Simple Bilevel Problem

abstract: We study the problem of fitting the high dimensional sparse linear regression model, where the data are provided by strategic or self-interested agents (individuals) who prioritize their privacy of data disclosure. In contrast to the classical setting, our focus is on designing mechanisms that can effectively incentivize most agents to truthfully report their data while preserving the privacy of individual reports. Simultaneously, we seek an estimator which should be close to the underlying parameter. We attempt to solve the problem by deriving a novel private estimator that has a closed-form expression. Based on the estimator, we propose a mechanism which has the following properties via some appropriate design of the computation and payment scheme: (1) the mechanism is $(o(1), O(n^{-\Omega({1})}))$-jointly differentially private, where $n$ is the number of agents; (2) it is an $o(\frac{1}{n})$-approximate Bayes Nash equilibrium for a $(1-o(1))$-fraction of agents to truthfully report their data; (3) the output could achieve an error of $o(1)$ to the underlying parameter; (4) it is individually rational for a $(1-o(1))$ fraction of agents in the mechanism; (5) the payment budget required from the analyst to run the mechanism is $o(1)$. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study on designing truthful (and privacy-preserving) mechanisms for high dimensional sparse linear regression.

paragraphs: This paper studies sparse linear regression when the data come from self-interested people who care about privacy. The setting combines a statistical goal, estimating the underlying parameters accurately, with an incentive problem: participants may prefer to misreport their information. The authors seek a mechanism that protects reports while making truthful participation attractive to most agents.

They derive a private estimator with a closed-form expression and build a computation and payment scheme around it. With an appropriate design, the mechanism satisfies joint differential privacy and makes truthful reporting an approximate Bayes Nash equilibrium for a fraction of agents approaching one. The equilibrium qualification means the incentive guarantee allows a small potential benefit from deviating.

The stated asymptotic results also allow estimation error to approach zero as the number of agents increases. Individual rationality holds for a fraction of participants approaching one, while the analyst's required payment budget tends to zero. These guarantees connect statistical accuracy, privacy, and incentives within one mechanism. Their scope is explicitly approximate and applies to nearly all agents, with the favorable quantities expressed through large-sample rates.
summary.tldr: A private regression estimator and payment mechanism jointly support accurate estimation and approximately truthful participation by nearly all agents.

title: Truthful High Dimensional Sparse Linear Regression

abstract: This paper studies off-policy evaluation (OPE) in the presence of unmeasured confounders. Inspired by the two-way fixed effects regression model widely used in the panel data literature, we propose a two-way unmeasured confounding assumption to model the system dynamics in causal reinforcement learning and develop a two-way deconfounder algorithm that devises a neural tensor network to simultaneously learn both the unmeasured confounders and the system dynamics, based on which a model-based estimator can be constructed for consistent policy value estimation. We illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed estimator through theoretical results and numerical experiments.

We illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed estimator through theoretical results and numerical experiments.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation estimates the value of a policy using data collected under another policy. Unmeasured confounders complicate this task because relevant influences are absent from the recorded variables. This paper studies how to estimate policy value when such hidden influences are part of the system being modeled.

The proposed approach introduces a two-way unmeasured-confounding assumption inspired by two-way fixed-effects regression in panel-data analysis. Under this structured view of confounding, a neural tensor network jointly learns representations of the hidden confounders and the system dynamics. Those learned dynamics then support a model-based estimator of policy value.

The authors provide theoretical results and numerical experiments illustrating the estimator's effectiveness. The stated consistency result concerns estimation within the proposed confounding setup; it does not imply that arbitrary hidden confounding can be removed from any dataset. The contribution is a specific modeling route that connects an explicit assumption about hidden influences to joint dynamics learning and, ultimately, consistent policy-value estimation.
summary.tldr: A two-way confounding assumption and neural tensor network enable model-based off-policy evaluation with a stated consistency result.

title: Two-way Deconfounder for Off-policy Evaluation in Causal Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms are typically based on optimizing a Markov Decision Process (MDP) using the optimal Bellman equation. Recent studies have revealed that focusing the optimization of Bellman equations solely on in-sample actions tends to result in more stable optimization, especially in the presence of function approximation. Upon on these findings, in this paper, we propose an Empirical MDP Iteration (EMIT) framework. EMIT constructs a sequence of empirical MDPs using data from the growing replay memory. For each of these empirical MDPs, it learns an estimated Q-function denoted as $\widehat{Q}$. The key strength is that by restricting the Bellman update to in-sample bootstrapping, each empirical MDP converges to a unique optimal $\widehat{Q}$ function. Furthermore, gradually expanding from the empirical MDPs to the original MDP induces a monotonic policy improvement. Instead of creating entirely new algorithms, we demonstrate that EMIT can be seamlessly integrated with existing online RL algorithms, effectively acting as a regularizer for contemporary Q-learning methods. We show this by implementing EMIT for two representative RL algorithms, DQN and TD3. Experimental results on Atari and MuJoCo benchmarks show that EMIT significantly reduces estimation errors and substantially improves the performance of both algorithms.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning agents often reuse stored experience to estimate how valuable different actions are. This paper builds on findings that Bellman optimization becomes more stable when its updates focus on actions present in the data, particularly when value functions are approximated. Empirical MDP Iteration, or EMIT, turns that principle into a framework for online learning.

The reported results show significantly smaller estimation errors and substantially better performance for both algorithms. These findings support organizing learning around the accumulated experience before expanding the decision process further.
summary.tldr: EMIT learns from expanding empirical decision processes built from replay memory, improving DQN and TD3 in the reported benchmarks.

title: Exploiting the Replay Memory Before Exploring the Environment: Enhancing Reinforcement Learning Through Empirical MDP Iteration

abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have emerged as the predominant approach for learning over graph-structured data. However, most GNNs operate as black-box models and require post-hoc explanations, which may not suffice in high-stakes scenarios where transparency is crucial.In this paper, we present a GNN that is interpretable by design. Our model, Graph Neural Additive Network (GNAN), is a novel extension of the interpretable class of Generalized Additive Models, and can be visualized and fully understood by humans. GNAN is designed to be fully interpretable, offering both global and local explanations at the feature and graph levels through direct visualization of the model. These visualizations describe exactly how the model uses the relationships between the target variable, the features, and the graph. We demonstrate the intelligibility of GNANs in a series of examples on different tasks and datasets. In addition, we show that the accuracy of GNAN is on par with black-box GNNs, making it suitable for critical applications where transparency is essential, alongside high accuracy.

paragraphs: Most graph neural networks require a separate explanation method to make their predictions understandable. This paper introduces the Graph Neural Additive Network, or GNAN, whose design directly exposes how features and graph relationships influence predictions. It extends generalized additive models to learning on graph-structured data.

GNAN is intended to support both global explanations of model behavior and local explanations of individual predictions. Its visualizations operate at the feature and graph levels and describe the model's actual use of relationships among inputs, graph structure, and the target. That direct connection is central to the approach: the visualizations express how the model computes its answers.

The authors demonstrate intelligibility through examples across different tasks and datasets. They also report accuracy on par with black-box graph neural networks in their evaluations. The findings suggest that this architecture can combine transparent behavior with competitive predictive performance. That combination is relevant to applications where users need to understand graph-based decisions as well as obtain accurate predictions.
summary.tldr: GNAN makes graph predictions directly interpretable through an additive architecture while matching black-box GNN accuracy in reported evaluations.

title: The Intelligible and Effective Graph Neural Additive Network

abstract: Most real-world datasets consist of a natural hierarchy between classes or an inherent label structure that is either already available or can be constructed cheaply. However, most existing representation learning methods ignore this hierarchy, treating labels as permutation invariant. Recent work [Zeng et al., 2022] proposes using this structured information explicitly, but the use of Euclidean distance may distort the underlying semantic context [Chen et al., 2013]. In this work, motivated by the advantage of hyperbolic spaces in modeling hierarchical relationships, we propose a novel approach HypStructure: a Hyperbolic Structured regularization approach to accurately embed the label hierarchy into the learned representations. HypStructure is a simple-yet-effective regularizer that consists of a hyperbolic tree-based representation loss along with a centering loss, and can be combined with any standard task loss to learn hierarchy-informed features. Extensive experiments on several large-scale vision benchmarks demonstrate the efficacy of HypStructure in reducing distortion and boosting generalization performance especially under low dimensional scenarios. For a better understanding of structured representation, we perform eigenvalue analysis that links the representation geometry to improved Out-of-Distribution (OOD) detection performance seen empirically.

paragraphs: Labels often have a hierarchy, yet representation learning commonly treats them as unrelated categories. This paper uses that available structure to shape learned features. Its motivation is that Euclidean distance can distort hierarchical semantic relationships, while hyperbolic geometry offers a setting suited to representing such relationships.

The proposed method, HypStructure, is a regularizer combining a hyperbolic tree-based representation loss with a centering loss. It can be added to a standard task loss, allowing the model to learn features informed by the label hierarchy alongside its main objective. The hierarchy therefore influences how examples are represented, rather than serving only as separate label information.

Experiments on several large-scale vision benchmarks show reduced distortion and improved generalization, particularly when representations have few dimensions. The authors also analyze eigenvalues to connect representation geometry with the improved out-of-distribution detection observed experimentally. The results support structured regularization as a way to preserve label relationships and improve the usefulness of learned features, with especially clear benefits in compact representation spaces.
summary.tldr: HypStructure uses hyperbolic regularization to preserve label hierarchies and improve generalization, especially in low-dimensional representations.

title: Learning Structured Representations with Hyperbolic Embeddings

abstract: Mechanistic interpretability methods aim to identify the algorithm a neural network implements, but it is difficult to validate such methods when the true algorithm is unknown. This work presents InterpBench, a collection of semi-synthetic yet realistic transformers with known circuits for evaluating these techniques. We train simple neural networks using a stricter version of Interchange Intervention Training (IIT) which we call Strict IIT (SIIT). Like the original, SIIT trains neural networks by aligning their internal computation with a desired high-level causal model, but it also prevents non-circuit nodes from affecting the model's output. We evaluate SIIT on sparse transformers produced by the Tracr tool and find that SIIT models maintain Tracr's original circuit while being more realistic. SIIT can also train transformers with larger circuits, like Indirect Object Identification (IOI). Finally, we use our benchmark to evaluate existing circuit discovery techniques.

paragraphs: Mechanistic interpretability tries to identify the computation a neural network implements internally. Evaluating such an explanation is difficult when the true computation is unknown. InterpBench addresses this problem with semi-synthetic transformers that have known circuits, providing a reference against which circuit-discovery methods can be checked while retaining more realistic model behavior.

The authors construct these models using Strict Interchange Intervention Training, or SIIT. Like the original training method, SIIT aligns a network's internal computation with a chosen high-level causal model. It adds a stricter requirement: nodes outside the intended circuit must not affect the output. This makes the known circuit a stronger basis for evaluation.

Tests on sparse transformers generated with Tracr show that SIIT preserves their original circuits while making the models more realistic. SIIT can also train transformers with larger circuits, including Indirect Object Identification. The authors then use InterpBench to evaluate existing circuit-discovery techniques, turning controlled knowledge of internal computation into a practical resource for assessing interpretability methods.
summary.tldr: InterpBench provides transformers with known circuits so mechanistic interpretability methods can be evaluated against a controlled computational reference.

title: InterpBench: Semi-Synthetic Transformers for Evaluating Mechanistic Interpretability Techniques

abstract: We propose and study several server-extrapolation strategies for enhancing the theoretical and empirical convergence properties of the popular federated learning optimizer FedProx [Li et al., 2020]. While it has long been known that some form of extrapolation can help in the practice of FL, only a handful of works provide any theoretical guarantees. The phenomenon seems elusive, and our current theoretical understanding remains severely incomplete. In our work, we focus on smooth convex or strongly convex problems in the interpolation regime. In particular, we propose Extrapolated FedProx (FedExProx), and study three extrapolation strategies: a constant strategy (depending on various smoothness parameters and the number of participating devices), and two smoothness-adaptive strategies; one based on the notion of gradient diversity (FedExProx-GraDS), and the other one based on the stochastic Polyak stepsize (FedExProx-StoPS). Our theory is corroborated with carefully constructed numerical experiments.

In particular, we propose Extrapolated FedProx (FedExProx), and study three extrapolation strategies: a constant strategy (depending on various smoothness parameters and the number of participating devices), and two smoothness-adaptive strategies; one based on the notion of gradient diversity (FedExProx-GraDS), and the other one based on the stochastic Polyak stepsize (FedExProx-StoPS). Our theory is corroborated with carefully constructed numerical experiments.

paragraphs: Federated learning combines updates from participating devices through a server. This paper studies server-side extrapolation as a way to improve the convergence of FedProx. Although extrapolation has been useful in practice, the authors identify a gap in theoretical explanations and develop an optimizer called Extrapolated FedProx, or FedExProx.

The analysis covers three strategies for choosing extrapolation. One uses a constant choice determined by smoothness parameters and the number of participating devices. Two adapt to smoothness: FedExProx-GraDS uses gradient diversity, while FedExProx-StoPS uses a stochastic Polyak stepsize. These alternatives provide different ways to control how the server extends the update.

The theoretical setting is restricted to smooth convex or strongly convex problems in the interpolation regime. Within that setting, the paper studies improvements in convergence and supports its theory with carefully constructed numerical experiments. The contribution gives server extrapolation a more explicit mathematical foundation and relates its behavior to concrete strategy choices, with empirical corroboration tailored to the assumptions of the analysis.
summary.tldr: FedExProx studies three server-extrapolation strategies with convergence analysis for smooth convex problems in the interpolation regime.

title: The Power of Extrapolation in Federated Learning

abstract: Computational optimal transport (OT) has received massive interests in the machine learning community, and great advances have been gained in the direction of entropic-regularized OT. The Sinkhorn algorithm, as well as its many improved versions, has become the *de facto* solution to large-scale OT problems. However, most of the existing methods behave like first-order methods, which typically require a large number of iterations to converge. More recently, Newton-type methods using sparsified Hessian matrices have demonstrated promising results on OT computation, but there still remain a lot of unresolved open questions. In this article, we make major new progresses towards this direction: first, we propose a novel Hessian sparsification scheme that promises a strict control of the approximation error; second, based on this sparsification scheme, we develop a *safe* Newton-type method that is guaranteed to avoid singularity in computing the search directions; third, the developed algorithm has a clear implementation for practical use, avoiding most hyperparameter tuning; and remarkably, we provide rigorous global and local convergence analysis of the proposed algorithm, which is lacking in the prior literature. Various numerical experiments are conducted to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm in solving large-scale OT problems.

paragraphs: Entropic-regularized optimal transport is often solved using Sinkhorn and related algorithms. The paper notes that many such approaches behave like first-order methods and can require many iterations. Newton-type methods offer another direction, but making their Hessian computations sparse raises questions about approximation accuracy, numerical solvability, and convergence.

The authors introduce a Hessian sparsification scheme with strict control over approximation error. They use it to construct a Newton-type algorithm guaranteed to avoid singularity when computing search directions. Here, the word safe refers to that numerical property. The method also has a practical implementation that avoids most hyperparameter tuning.

The paper provides rigorous global and local convergence analyses, addressing a gap the authors identify in earlier work on this approach. Numerical experiments demonstrate effectiveness on large-scale optimal transport problems. The contribution joins several requirements that matter together: reducing the Hessian representation, controlling the error introduced by that reduction, keeping direction calculations well-defined, and establishing convergence of the resulting algorithm.
summary.tldr: A sparse Newton method controls Hessian approximation error, avoids singular search-direction computations, and provides convergence guarantees for entropic optimal transport.

title: Safe and Sparse Newton Method for Entropic-Regularized Optimal Transport

abstract: Transformers have achieved state-of-the-art performance across various tasks, but suffer from a notable quadratic complexity in sequence length due to the attention mechanism. In this work, we propose MonarchAttention -- a novel approach to sub-quadratic attention approximation via Monarch matrices, an expressive class of structured matrices. Based on the variational form of softmax, we describe an efficient optimization-based algorithm to compute an approximate projection of softmax attention onto the class of Monarch matrices with $\Theta(N\sqrt{N} d)$ computational complexity and $\Theta(Nd)$ memory/IO complexity. Unlike previous approaches, MonarchAttention is both (1) transferable, yielding minimal performance loss with no additional training, even when replacing every attention layer of the transformer, and (2) hardware-efficient, utilizing the highest-throughput tensor core units on modern GPUs. With optimized kernels, MonarchAttention achieves substantial speed-ups in wall-time over FlashAttention-2: $1.4\times$ for shorter sequences $(N=256)$, $4.5\times$ for medium-length sequences $(N=4K)$, and $8.2\times$ for longer sequences $(N=16K)$. We demonstrate the quality of MonarchAttention on diverse tasks and architectures in vision and language problems, showing that it flexibly and accurately approximates softmax attention in a variety of contexts.
