paragraphs: Standard transformer attention becomes expensive as sequence length grows because its computation scales quadratically. MonarchAttention approximates softmax attention using Monarch matrices, a structured matrix family. The goal is an approximation that transfers to existing transformers without additional training and runs efficiently on modern GPU hardware.

The method uses the variational form of softmax to construct an optimization algorithm for an approximate projection onto Monarch matrices. For sequence length N and dimension d, its computation scales as Θ(N√N d), with Θ(Nd) memory and input/output complexity. Optimized kernels use high-throughput tensor cores, connecting the mathematical reduction in work to the hardware that executes it.

The authors report minimal performance loss without additional training, including when replacing every attention layer. Against FlashAttention-2, measured wall-time speedups are 1.4 times at sequence length 256, 4.5 times at 4K, and 8.2 times at 16K. Evaluations span vision and language tasks and multiple architectures. These results support the approach’s combination of practical acceleration and accurate approximation across the tested contexts.
summary.tldr: MonarchAttention replaces softmax attention with a hardware-efficient structured approximation that accelerates tested transformers without additional training.

title: MonarchAttention: Zero-Shot Conversion to Fast, Hardware-Aware Structured Attention

abstract: Dense metric depth estimation has witnessed great developments in recent years. While single-image-based methods have demonstrated commendable performance in certain circumstances, they may encounter challenges regarding scale ambiguities and visual illusions in real world. Traditional depth-from-focus methods are constrained by low sampling rates during data acquisition. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach to enhance dense metric depth estimation by fusing events with image foundation models via a prompting approach. Specifically, we build Event-based Differential Focus Volumes (EDFV) using events triggered through focus sweeping, which are subsequently transformed into sparse metric depth maps. These maps are then utilized for prompting dense depth estimation via our proposed Event-based Depth Prompting Network. We further construct synthetic and real-captured datasets to facilitate the training and evaluation of both frame-based and event-based methods. Quantitative and qualitative results, including both in-domain and zero-shot experiments, demonstrate the superior performance of our method compared to existing approaches. Code and data will be available at https://github.com/liboyu02/EDFV/.

paragraphs: Estimating actual distances from a single image can be difficult because visual appearance may leave scale ambiguous or create misleading depth cues. Traditional methods that infer depth by changing focus face a different constraint: low acquisition sampling rates. This paper combines event-based focus information with image foundation models to improve dense metric depth estimation.

The method gathers events triggered while focus is swept and organizes them into Event-based Differential Focus Volumes. These volumes are converted into sparse maps of metric depth. An Event-based Depth Prompting Network then uses those maps to guide dense depth prediction. The sparse measurements supply distance information, while the prompted model produces a depth estimate across the image.

The authors also construct synthetic and real-captured datasets for training and comparing frame-based and event-based approaches. Their quantitative and qualitative evaluations report superior performance over existing methods in both in-domain and zero-shot experiments. The contribution is a way to connect focus-derived metric information with the dense prediction abilities of image models through prompting.
summary.tldr: Event measurements collected during focus sweeping provide sparse metric depth prompts that improve dense depth prediction.

title: Dense Metric Depth Estimation via Event-based Differential Focus Volume Prompting

abstract: Foundation models trained on large-scale de-identified electronic health records (EHRs) hold promise for clinical applications. However, their capacity to memorize patient information raises important privacy concerns. In this work, we introduce a suite of black-box evaluation tests to assess privacy-related memorization risks in foundation models trained on structured EHR data. Our framework includes methods for probing memorization at both the embedding and generative levels, and aims to distinguish between model generalization and harmful memorization in clinically relevant settings. We contextualize memorization in terms of its potential to compromise patient privacy, particularly for vulnerable subgroups. We validate our approach on a publicly available EHR foundation model and release an open-source toolkit to facilitate reproducible and collaborative privacy assessments in healthcare AI.

paragraphs: Foundation models trained on de-identified electronic health records may still memorize patient information. This paper develops ways to assess that risk in models trained on structured medical records. Its central concern is whether retained information could compromise patient privacy, with particular attention to vulnerable subgroups.

The authors introduce a suite of black-box tests that probe memorization at two levels: embeddings and generated outputs. Examining both broadens the assessment beyond what a model explicitly generates. The framework aims to distinguish useful generalization from harmful memorization in clinically relevant settings, making the privacy implications of retained information central to the evaluation.

The approach is validated on a publicly available EHR foundation model, and the authors release an open-source toolkit for reproducible assessments. The stated contribution is an evaluation framework and its demonstrated application, rather than a quantified claim about how commonly healthcare models expose records. By making the tests reusable, the work supports collaborative investigation of privacy risks in this class of models.
summary.tldr: The paper introduces black-box tests for privacy-related memorization in healthcare foundation models, covering both embeddings and generated outputs.

title: An Investigation of Memorization Risk in Healthcare Foundation Models

abstract: Envision an AI capable of functioning in human-like settings, moving beyond mere observation to actively understand, anticipate, and proactively respond to unfolding events. Towards this vision, we focus on the innovative task where, given ego-streaming video input, an assistant proactively answers diverse, evolving questions at the opportune moment, while maintaining synchronized perception and reasoning. This task embodies three key properties: (1) Proactive Coherence, (2) Just-in-Time Responsiveness, and (3) Synchronized Efficiency. To evaluate and address these properties, we first introduce ESTP-Bench (Ego Streaming Proactive Benchmark) alongside the ESTP-F1 metric—a novel framework designed for their rigorous assessment. Secondly, we propose a comprehensive technical pipeline to enable models to tackle this challenging task. This pipeline comprises: (1) a data engine, (2) a multi-stage training strategy, and (3) a proactive dynamic compression technique. Our proposed model effectively addresses these critical properties while achieving state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance on the standard COIN benchmark.

paragraphs: An assistant watching a first-person video stream must handle events while they unfold. This paper studies a task in which the assistant proactively answers changing questions at appropriate moments. Success requires more than understanding individual frames: the system must keep its perception and reasoning synchronized while deciding when a response is useful.

The authors organize the task around three properties: coherent proactive behavior, timely responsiveness, and efficient synchronization. They introduce ESTP-Bench and the ESTP-F1 metric to assess these properties together. This makes response timing and ongoing coordination part of the evaluation, alongside the assistant's ability to respond to the evolving visual situation.

Their technical pipeline combines a data engine, training in multiple stages, and a proactive dynamic compression technique. Together, these components support the proposed streaming-video behavior. The abstract reports that the resulting model effectively addresses the task's three properties and achieves state-of-the-art performance on COIN. The work therefore contributes both an evaluation framework for proactive streaming assistance and a model pipeline intended to meet it.
summary.tldr: The paper introduces a benchmark and model pipeline for first-person video assistants that proactively answer evolving questions at suitable moments.

title: Eyes Wide Open: Ego Proactive Video-LLM for Streaming Video

abstract: The development of reasoning capabilities represents a critical frontier in large language models (LLMs) research, where reinforcement learning (RL) and process reward models (PRMs) have emerged as predominant methodological frameworks. Contrary to conventional wisdom, empirical evidence from DeepSeek-R1 demonstrates that pure RL training focused on mathematical problem-solving can progressively enhance reasoning abilities without PRM integration, challenging the perceived necessity of process supervision. In this study, we conduct a systematic investigation of the relationship between RL training and PRM capabilities. Our findings demonstrate that problem-solving proficiency and process supervision capabilities represent complementary dimensions of reasoning that co-evolve synergistically during pure RL training. In particular, current PRMs underperform simple baselines like majority voting when applied to state-of-the-art models such as DeepSeek-R1 and QwQ-32B. To address this limitation, we propose Self-PRM, an introspective framework in which models autonomously evaluate and rerank their generated solutions through self-reward mechanisms. Although Self-PRM consistently improves the accuracy of the benchmark (particularly with larger sample sizes), analysis exposes persistent challenges: The approach exhibits low precision (<10\%) on difficult problems, frequently misclassifying flawed solutions as valid. These analyses underscore the need for combined training with process supervision and continued RL scaling to enhance reward alignment and introspective accuracy. We hope these findings provide actionable insights for building more reliable and self-aware complex reasoning models.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether reinforcement learning for mathematical problem solving also develops the ability to evaluate reasoning processes. Process reward models provide this kind of supervision explicitly. The authors find that problem-solving ability and process-evaluation capability develop together during pure reinforcement learning, making their relationship more nuanced than separate training roles suggest.

They also find that current process reward models perform worse than simple majority voting when used with strong reasoning models such as DeepSeek-R1 and QwQ-32B. To address this, they introduce Self-PRM, in which a model evaluates and reranks its own generated solutions through self-reward mechanisms.

Self-PRM consistently improves benchmark accuracy, especially when more candidate solutions are available. However, its precision on difficult problems remains below 10%, and it often accepts flawed solutions as valid. The results therefore support both emerging self-evaluation capability and a substantial reliability gap. The authors argue for combining process supervision with further reinforcement-learning scaling to improve reward alignment and introspective accuracy.
summary.tldr: Problem-solving reinforcement learning develops self-evaluation abilities, but Self-PRM’s accuracy gains coexist with poor precision on difficult problems.

title: Is PRM Necessary? Problem-Solving RL Implicitly Induces PRM Capability in LLMs

abstract: Recent foundational models for tabular data, such as TabPFN, excel at adapting to new tasks via in-context learning but remain constrained to a fixed, pre-defined number of target dimensions—often necessitating costly ensembling strategies. We trace this constraint to a deeper architectural shortcoming: these models lack target-equivariance, so that permuting target-dimension orderings alters their predictions. This deficiency gives rise to an irreducible “equivariance gap,” an error term that introduces instability in predictions. We eliminate this gap by designing a fully target-equivariant architecture—ensuring permutation invariance via equivariant encoders, decoders, and a bi-attention mechanism. Empirical evaluation on standard classification benchmarks shows that, on datasets with more classes than those seen during pre-training, our model matches or surpasses existing methods while incurring lower computational overhead.

paragraphs: Tabular foundation models such as TabPFN can adapt to new tasks through examples supplied in context. However, their architectures often assume a fixed number of target dimensions. The paper connects this restriction to a deeper problem: changing the order of target dimensions can change predictions in ways that should not depend on that ordering.

The authors describe the resulting instability as an irreducible equivariance gap. EquiTabPFN removes this gap through an architecture whose encoders, decoders, and bi-attention mechanism respect permutations of target dimensions. Intuitively, rearranging the targets should produce the corresponding rearrangement of outputs while preserving the underlying prediction. Building this behavior into the architecture addresses the source of the ordering problem.

On standard classification benchmarks, the model matches or exceeds existing methods when datasets contain more classes than were encountered during pretraining. It also uses less computation in those evaluations. These findings connect the architectural guarantee to a practical benefit: handling larger target sets with lower overhead, in a setting where existing approaches often rely on costly ensembles.
summary.tldr: EquiTabPFN removes target-ordering instability and handles more classes than seen in pretraining with competitive accuracy and lower computational overhead.

title: EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network

abstract: Few-shot learning (FSL) aims to classify unseen examples (query set) into labeled data (support set) through low-dimensional embeddings. However, the diversity and unpredictability of environments and capture devices make FSL more challenging in real-world applications. In this paper, we propose Dual Support Query Shift (DSQS), a novel challenge in FSL that integrates two key issues: inter-set shifts (between support and query sets) and intra-set shifts (within each set), which significantly hinder model performance. To tackle these challenges, we introduce a Dual Alignment framework (DUAL), whose core insight is that clean features can improve optimal transportation (OT) alignment. Firstly, DUAL leverages a robust embedding function enhanced by a repairer network trained with perturbed and adversarially generated “hard” examples to obtain clean features. Additionally, it incorporates a two-stage OT approach with a negative entropy regularizer, which aligns support set instances, minimizes intra-class distances, and uses query data as anchor nodes to achieve effective distribution alignment. We provide a theoretical bound of DUAL and experimental results on three image datasets, compared against 10 state-of-the-art baselines, showing that DUAL achieves a remarkable average performance improvement of 25.66%. Our code is available at https://github.com/siyang-jiang/DUAL.

paragraphs: Few-shot classification uses a small labeled support set to classify new query examples. Changes in environments or capture devices can create differences between the two sets, as well as variation within each set. The paper combines these difficulties into a challenge called Dual Support Query Shift.

DUAL addresses the challenge by improving features before aligning their distributions. A repairer network learns from perturbed examples and adversarially generated hard examples to help produce cleaner representations. A two-stage optimal transport procedure then aligns support instances, brings same-class representations closer together, and uses query examples as anchors. A negative entropy regularizer is part of this alignment procedure.

The authors provide a theoretical bound and compare the method with ten leading baselines on three image datasets. They report an average performance improvement of 25.66%. The result supports the central idea that feature repair and distribution alignment can reinforce each other when shifts occur both within and between the available example sets.
summary.tldr: DUAL combines feature repair and two-stage distribution alignment to improve few-shot classification under shifts within and between example sets.

title: Dual Alignment Framework for Few-shot Learning with Inter-Set and Intra-Set Shifts

abstract: We present Ambient Protein Diffusion, a framework for training protein diffusion models that generates structures with unprecedented diversity and quality. State-of-the-art generative models are trained on computationally derived structures from AlphaFold2 (AF), as experimentally determined structures are relatively scarce. The resulting models are therefore limited by the quality of synthetic datasets. Since the accuracy of AF predictions degrades with increasing protein length and complexity, de novo generation of long, complex proteins remains challenging. Ambient Protein Diffusion overcomes this problem by treating low-confidence AF structures as corrupted data. Rather than simply filtering out low-quality AF structures, our method adjusts the diffusion objective for each structure based on its corruption level, allowing the model to learn from both high and low quality structures. Empirically, ambient protein diffusion yields major improvements: on proteins with 700 residues, diversity increases from 45% to 85% from the previous state-of-the-art, and designability improves from 70% to 88%.

paragraphs: Protein generators often learn from structures predicted by AlphaFold2 because experimentally determined structures are relatively scarce. This creates a quality problem: errors in the predicted training structures can constrain what the generator learns. The abstract highlights long, complex proteins as particularly challenging because AlphaFold2 predictions become less accurate as protein length and complexity increase.

Ambient Protein Diffusion treats low-confidence predicted structures as corrupted observations. Instead of discarding them, it changes the diffusion training objective according to each structure's corruption level. The model can therefore learn from structures of varying quality while accounting for their differing reliability. The central contribution is a way to use imperfect training material without treating every predicted structure as equally trustworthy.

For proteins containing 700 residues, the authors report diversity rising from 45% to 85% relative to the previous state of the art, alongside designability increasing from 70% to 88%. These empirical results support the approach for the reported long-protein setting. They connect the treatment of noisy training structures to improvements in both the variety and designability of generated structures.
summary.tldr: Ambient Protein Diffusion adjusts training to account for unreliable predicted structures, improving reported diversity and designability for long proteins.

title: Ambient Proteins - Training Diffusion Models on Noisy Structures

abstract: Bilevel reinforcement learning (BRL) has emerged as a powerful framework for aligning generative models, yet its theoretical foundations, especially sample complexity bounds, remain underexplored. In this work, we present the first sample complexity bound for BRL, establishing a rate of $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-3})$ in continuous state-action spaces. Traditional MDP analysis techniques do not extend to BRL due to its nested structure and non-convex lower-level problems. We overcome these challenges by leveraging the Polyak-Łojasiewicz (PL) condition and the MDP structure to obtain closed-form gradients, enabling tight sample complexity analysis. Our analysis also extends to general bi-level optimization settings with non-convex lower levels, where we achieve state-of-the-art sample complexity results of $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-3})$ improving upon existing bounds of $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-6})$. Additionally, we address the computational bottleneck of hypergradient estimation by proposing a fully first-order, Hessian-free algorithm suitable for large-scale problems.

paragraphs: Bilevel reinforcement learning nests one learning problem inside another, making its data requirements harder to analyze than those of a standard Markov decision process. The difficulty is compounded when the inner problem is non-convex. This paper establishes a sample-complexity bound of O(ε⁻³) for bilevel reinforcement learning in continuous state and action spaces.

The analysis uses the Polyak–Łojasiewicz condition together with the structure of the Markov decision process to obtain closed-form gradients. That condition is a substantive part of the theoretical setup, so the result should be understood within the analyzed setting. The authors also extend their approach to general bilevel optimization with non-convex inner problems, improving existing O(ε⁻⁶) bounds to O(ε⁻³).

A separate algorithmic contribution addresses the cost of estimating hypergradients, which express how outer objectives depend on inner optimization. The proposed method uses only first-order information and avoids Hessian computations. Together, the results strengthen theoretical understanding of sampling requirements and provide a computational approach intended to accommodate large-scale bilevel problems.
summary.tldr: Using the Polyak–Łojasiewicz condition, this work establishes O(ε⁻³) sample-complexity bounds and a Hessian-free algorithm for bilevel learning.

title: On the Sample Complexity Bounds of Bilevel Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have recently achieved remarkable progress in video understanding. However, their effectiveness in real-time streaming scenarios remains limited due to storage constraints of historical visual features and insufficient real-time spatiotemporal reasoning. To address these challenges, we propose StreamForest, a novel architecture specifically designed for streaming video understanding. Central to StreamForest is the Persistent Event Memory Forest, a memory mechanism that adaptively organizes video frames into multiple event-level tree structures. This process is guided by penalty functions based on temporal distance, content similarity, and merge frequency, enabling efficient long-term memory retention under limited computational resources. To enhance real-time perception, we introduce a Fine-grained Spatiotemporal Window, which captures detailed short-term visual cues to improve current scene perception. Additionally, we present OnlineIT, an instruction-tuning dataset tailored for streaming video tasks. OnlineIT significantly boosts MLLM performance in both real-time perception and future prediction. To evaluate generalization in practical applications, we introduce ODV-Bench, a new benchmark focused on real-time streaming video understanding in autonomous driving scenarios. Experimental results demonstrate that StreamForest achieves the state-of-the-art performance, with accuracies of 77.3% on StreamingBench, 60.5% on OVBench, and 55.6% on OVO-Bench. In particular, even under extreme visual token compression (limited to 1024 tokens), the model retains 96.8% of its average accuracy in eight benchmarks relative to the default setting. These results underscore the robustness, efficiency, and generalizability of StreamForest for streaming video understanding.

This process is guided by penalty functions based on temporal distance, content similarity, and merge frequency, enabling efficient long-term memory retention under limited computational resources. To enhance real-time perception, we introduce a Fine-grained Spatiotemporal Window, which captures detailed short-term visual cues to improve current scene perception. Additionally, we present OnlineIT, an instruction-tuning dataset tailored for streaming video tasks. OnlineIT significantly boosts MLLM performance in both real-time perception and future prediction. To evaluate generalization in practical applications, we introduce ODV-Bench, a new benchmark focused on real-time streaming video understanding in autonomous driving scenarios. Experimental results demonstrate that StreamForest achieves the state-of-the-art performance, with accuracies of 77.3% on StreamingBench, 60.5% on OVBench, and 55.6% on OVO-Bench. These results underscore the robustness, efficiency, and generalizability of StreamForest for streaming video understanding.

The architecture is designed around the need to preserve useful history while continuing to reason about incoming video under limited computational resources.

A Fine-grained Spatiotemporal Window separately captures detailed short-term cues. The paper also introduces OnlineIT for streaming-video instruction tuning and ODV-Bench for evaluation in autonomous-driving scenarios, extending the contribution beyond the memory architecture.

Reported accuracies are 77.3% on StreamingBench, 60.5% on OVBench, and 55.6% on OVO-Bench. With visual memory compressed to 1,024 tokens, the model retains 96.8% of its default-setting average accuracy across eight benchmarks. That last figure is a relative retention measure, showing how much evaluated performance survives compression. Together, the findings support the architecture's balance between long-term memory and current-scene detail.
summary.tldr: StreamForest combines event-organized memory with detailed short-term perception to understand streaming video under tight memory budgets.

title: StreamForest: Efficient Online Video Understanding with Persistent Event Memory

abstract: While end-to-end video-to-audio generation has greatly improved, producing high-fidelity audio that authentically captures the nuances of visual content remains challenging. Like professionals in the creative industries, this generation requires sophisticated reasoning about items such as visual dynamics, acoustic environments, and temporal relationships. We present **ThinkSound**, a novel framework that leverages Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning to enable stepwise, interactive audio generation and editing for videos. Our approach decomposes the process into three complementary stages: foundational foley generation that creates semantically coherent soundscapes, interactive object-centric refinement through precise user interactions, and targeted editing guided by natural language instructions. At each stage, a multimodal large language model generates contextually aligned CoT reasoning that guides a unified audio foundation model. Furthermore, we introduce **AudioCoT**, a comprehensive dataset with structured reasoning annotations that establishes connections between visual content, textual descriptions, and sound synthesis. Experiments demonstrate that ThinkSound achieves state-of-the-art performance in video-to-audio generation across both audio metrics and CoT metrics, and excels in the out-of-distribution Movie Gen Audio benchmark. The project page is available at https://ThinkSound-Project.github.io.

paragraphs: Creating sound for a video requires interpreting motion, acoustic surroundings, and the timing of events. ThinkSound organizes this process around explicit stepwise reasoning generated by a multimodal language model. That reasoning guides an audio foundation model, connecting the interpretation of a scene to the sound produced for it.

The framework has three stages. It first generates a coherent base soundscape through foundational foley generation. Users can then refine sound around particular objects through precise interactions. Finally, natural-language instructions guide targeted edits. Each stage uses contextually aligned reasoning, allowing generation and revision to share a common audio model. The authors also introduce AudioCoT, a dataset with structured reasoning annotations connecting visual content, text descriptions, and sound synthesis.

Experiments report state-of-the-art video-to-audio performance on both audio and reasoning metrics, alongside strong results on the out-of-distribution Movie Gen Audio benchmark. These findings support the framework’s combination of reasoning and interactive refinement in the evaluated settings. Its contribution is both a staged production workflow and training data that explicitly links scene interpretation to audio generation.
summary.tldr: ThinkSound uses multimodal stepwise reasoning to guide video sound generation, object-focused refinement, and language-directed editing.

title: ThinkSound: Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in Multimodal LLMs for Audio Generation and Editing

abstract: We study quantum algorithms based on quantum (sub)gradient estimation using noisy function evaluation oracles, and demonstrate the first dimension-independent query complexities (up to poly-logarithmic factors) for zeroth-order convex optimization in both smooth and nonsmooth settings. Interestingly, only using noisy function evaluation oracles, we match the first-order query complexities of classical gradient descent, thereby exhibiting exponential separation between quantum and classical zeroth-order optimization. We then generalize these algorithms to work in non-Euclidean settings by using quantum (sub)gradient estimation to instantiate mirror descent and its variants, including dual averaging and mirror prox. By leveraging a connection between semidefinite programming and eigenvalue optimization, we use our quantum mirror descent method to give a new quantum algorithm for solving semidefinite programs, linear programs, and zero-sum games. We identify a parameter regime in which our zero-sum games algorithm is faster than any existing classical or quantum approach.

paragraphs: Zeroth-order optimization works from function evaluations rather than directly supplied gradients. This paper develops quantum methods that estimate gradients or subgradients using noisy function-evaluation access. It studies both smooth convex objectives and nonsmooth ones, where ordinary gradients may not exist everywhere.

The main result is query complexity that is independent of dimension apart from polylogarithmic factors. Using only noisy function values, the methods match the first-order query complexity of classical gradient descent. The authors establish an exponential separation between quantum and classical zeroth-order optimization. This comparison concerns oracle queries, the calls made to obtain function information.

The authors also extend quantum gradient estimation to non-Euclidean optimization through mirror descent, dual averaging, and mirror prox. Connecting semidefinite programming with eigenvalue optimization yields algorithms for semidefinite programs, linear programs, and zero-sum games. For zero-sum games, they identify a parameter regime where their algorithm is faster than existing classical and quantum approaches. The result is explicitly tied to that regime, rather than asserting an advantage for every game.
summary.tldr: Quantum gradient estimation enables nearly dimension-independent query complexity for convex optimization using noisy function values.

title: Fast Zeroth-Order Convex Optimization with Quantum Gradient Methods

abstract: Risk-averse total-reward Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) offer a promising framework for modeling and solving undiscounted infinite-horizon objectives. Existing model-based algorithms for risk measures like the entropic risk measure (ERM) and entropic value-at-risk (EVaR) are effective in small problems, but require full access to transition probabilities. We propose a Q-learning algorithm to compute the optimal stationary policy for total-reward ERM and EVaR objectives with strong convergence and performance guarantees. The algorithm and its optimality are made possible by ERM's dynamic consistency and elicitability. Our numerical results on tabular domains demonstrate quick and reliable convergence of the proposed Q-learning algorithm to the optimal risk-averse value function.

paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning with risk-averse objectives based on total reward over an undiscounted, infinite horizon. The focus is on the entropic risk measure and entropic value-at-risk. Existing model-based algorithms can handle small problems, but they require complete access to transition probabilities, making that information requirement a central obstacle.

The authors propose a Q-learning algorithm for computing an optimal stationary policy for these objectives. Two properties of the entropic risk measure support the construction and its optimality: dynamic consistency and elicitability. These properties are central to making the proposed learning approach work for the stated risk-sensitive total-reward setting.

The paper supplies strong convergence and performance guarantees, together with numerical experiments in tabular domains. Those experiments show quick and reliable convergence to the optimal risk-averse value function. The contribution is both algorithmic and theoretical: it provides a Q-learning route for objectives previously addressed by algorithms needing full transition probabilities, while its reported numerical evidence concerns tabular problems.
summary.tldr: A Q-learning algorithm learns optimal stationary policies for risk-averse, undiscounted total-reward objectives with convergence and performance guarantees.

title: Risk-Averse Total-Reward Reinforcement Learning

abstract: While existing image‑guided composition methods may help insert a foreground object onto a user-specified region of a background image, achieving natural blending inside the region with the rest of the image unchanged, we observe that these existing methods often struggle in synthesizing seamless interaction-aware compositions when the task involves human-object interactions. In this paper, we first propose HOComp, a novel approach for compositing a foreground object onto a human-centric background image, while ensuring harmonious interactions between the foreground object and the background person and their consistent appearances. Our approach includes two key designs: (1) MLLMs-driven Region-based Pose Guidance (MRPG), which utilizes MLLMs to identify the interaction region as well as the interaction type (e.g., holding and lefting) to provide coarse-to-fine constraints to the generated pose for the interaction while incorporating human pose landmarks to track action variations and enforcing fine-grained pose constraints; and (2) Detail-Consistent Appearance Preservation (DCAP), which unifies a shape-aware attention modulation mechanism, a multi-view appearance loss, and a background consistency loss to ensure consistent shapes/textures of the foreground and faithful reproduction of the background human. We then propose the first dataset, named Interaction-aware Human-Object Composition (IHOC), for the task. Experimental results on our dataset show that HOComp effectively generates harmonious human-object interactions with consistent appearances, and outperforms relevant methods qualitatively and quantitatively.

paragraphs: Placing an object into an image of a person requires more than making its edges blend into the background. The person's pose must support a plausible interaction, while both the object and person retain consistent appearances. HOComp addresses this interaction-aware composition problem through coordinated pose guidance and appearance preservation.

Its pose component uses multimodal large language models to identify the interaction region and type. These decisions provide coarse-to-fine guidance, supplemented by human pose landmarks that track action changes and constrain finer details. Its appearance component combines shape-aware attention modulation with losses for multi-view appearance and background consistency. These mechanisms aim to preserve the object's shape and texture while faithfully reproducing the background person.

The authors also introduce IHOC, a dataset for interaction-aware human-object composition. Experiments on that dataset show more harmonious interactions and consistent appearances, with qualitative and quantitative improvements over relevant methods. The findings support treating human pose and visual identity as linked requirements of composition, rather than assessing an inserted object solely by how naturally it blends into a selected region.
summary.tldr: HOComp combines interaction-specific pose guidance and appearance preservation to create more coherent human-object image compositions.

title: HOComp: Interaction-Aware Human-Object Composition

abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models provide a powerful approach to training control policies for physical systems, such as robots, by combining end-to-end learning with transfer of semantic knowledge from web-scale vision-language model (VLM) training. However, the constraints of real-time control are often at odds with the design of VLMs: the most powerful VLMs have tens or hundreds of billions of parameters, presenting an obstacle to real-time inference, and operate on discrete tokens rather than the continuous-valued outputs that are required for controlling robots. To address this challenge, recent VLA models have used specialized modules for efficient continuous control, such as action experts or continuous output heads, which typically require adding new untrained parameters to the pretrained VLM backbone. While these modules improve real-time and control capabilities, it remains an open question whether they preserve or degrade the semantic knowledge contained in the pretrained VLM, and what effect they have on the VLA training dynamics. In this paper, we study this question in the context of VLAs that include a continuous diffusion or flow matching action expert, showing that naively including such experts significantly harms both training speed and knowledge transfer. We provide an extensive analysis of various design choices, their impact on performance and knowledge transfer, and propose a technique for insulating the VLM backbone during VLA training that mitigates this issue. Videos are available at https://pi.website/research/knowledge_insulation and open-source model weights are available at https://github.com/Physical-Intelligence/openpi.

This creates a practical mismatch: powerful pretrained models can be too large for real-time control, and their discrete token outputs differ from the continuous commands robots require. Specialized action modules address these control requirements by adding new parameters to the pretrained system.

The paper examines what happens when those modules are continuous action experts based on diffusion or flow matching. The authors find that simply attaching such experts can substantially slow training and harm knowledge transfer. This makes the interaction between the new control module and the existing backbone an important part of the learning problem.

Through an extensive analysis of design choices, the authors study their effects on performance and preservation of semantic knowledge. They propose a technique that insulates the vision-language backbone during action-model training, mitigating the observed problems. The contribution is a way to improve how pretrained understanding and newly learned control are combined, addressing training dynamics as well as the demands of robot action generation.
summary.tldr: Insulating a pretrained vision-language backbone mitigates the training slowdown and impaired knowledge transfer caused by naively adding continuous action experts.

title: Knowledge Insulating Vision-Language-Action Models: Train Fast, Run Fast, Generalize Better

abstract: We consider the problem of federated learning (FL) with graph-structured data distributed across multiple clients. In particular, we address the common scenario of interconnected subgraphs, where interconnections between clients significantly influence the learning process. Existing approaches suffer from critical limitations, either requiring the exchange of sensitive node embeddings, thereby posing privacy risks, or relying on computationally-intensive steps, which hinders scalability. To tackle these challenges, we propose FedLap, a novel framework that leverages global structure information via Laplacian smoothing in the spectral domain to effectively capture inter-node dependencies while ensuring privacy and scalability. We provide a formal analysis of the privacy of FedLap, demonstrating that it preserves privacy. Notably, FedLap is the first subgraph FL scheme with strong privacy guarantees. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed method achieves competitive or superior utility compared to existing techniques.

paragraphs: When a graph is distributed across multiple clients, each client's subgraph can remain connected to subgraphs held elsewhere. These cross-client connections influence learning, so treating the pieces independently can miss relevant dependencies. Existing methods either exchange sensitive node embeddings or rely on expensive computation, creating privacy or scalability concerns.

FedLap incorporates global structural information through Laplacian smoothing in the spectral domain. The framework uses this graph-based operation to capture dependencies between nodes while addressing the challenges of distributed data. Its design aims to retain the benefits of understanding the wider graph without the privacy risks associated with exchanging sensitive embeddings.

The paper provides a formal privacy analysis and presents FedLap as the first subgraph federated-learning scheme with strong privacy guarantees. Experiments on benchmark datasets report competitive or superior utility compared with existing techniques. The contribution is the combination of global graph structure, a formally analyzed privacy property, and an approach designed for scalability. The results indicate that preserving privacy in this setting can coexist with useful predictive performance.
summary.tldr: FedLap uses spectral Laplacian smoothing to learn across interconnected client subgraphs with formal privacy guarantees and competitive performance.

title: Subgraph Federated Learning via Spectral Methods

abstract: Contemporary large models often exhibit behaviors suggesting the presence of low-level primitives that compose into modules with richer functionality, but these fundamental building blocks remain poorly understood. We investigate this compositional structure in linear layers by asking: \textit{can we identify/synthesize linear transformations from a minimal set of geometric primitives?} Using Clifford algebra, we show that linear layers can be expressed as compositions of bivectors---geometric objects encoding oriented planes---and introduce a differentiable algorithm that decomposes them into products of rotors. This construction uses only $\mathcal{O}(\log^2 d)$ parameters, versus $\mathcal{O}(d^2)$ required by dense matrices. Applied to the key, query, and value projections in LLM attention layers, our rotor-based layers match the performance of strong baselines such as block-Hadamard and low-rank approximations. Our findings provide an algebraic perspective on how these geometric primitives can compose into higher-level functions within deep models.

The motivation is compositionality: simple operations may combine to produce richer functions, but the underlying primitives remain poorly understood. Linear layers provide a concrete setting in which to study this idea algebraically.

title: Composing Linear Layers from Irreducibles

abstract: Programming assistants powered by large language models have transformed software development, yet most benchmarks focus narrowly on code generation tasks. Recent efforts like InfiBench and StackEval attempt to address this gap using Stack Overflow data but remain limited to single-turn interactions in isolated contexts, require significant manual curation, and fail to represent complete project environments. We introduce CodeAssistBench (CAB), the first benchmark framework for evaluating multi-turn programming assistance in realistic settings that address questions grounded in actual codebases. Unlike existing programming Q&A benchmarks, CAB automatically generates scalable datasets from GitHub issues tagged with questions using configurable parameters (e.g., repository creation date, star count, programming languages), and includes automatic containerization of codebases for evaluation. It then evaluates models through simulated users in these containerized environments with full codebase access. Using this framework, we constructed a test set of 3,286 real-world programming questions across 214 repositories, spanning seven programming languages and diverse problem domains. Our evaluation of leading LLMs reveals a substantial capability gap: while models perform well on Stack Overflow questions with success rates of 70-83%, they resolve only up to 16.49% of CAB's issues from recent repositories (post-training cutoff). This discrepancy highlights the challenges of providing assistance in complex, project-specific contexts versus answering standalone questions. Our fully automated framework enables continuous benchmark expansion and is available at https://github.com/amazon-science/CodeAssistBench/.

CodeAssistBench evaluates that broader form of assistance. Its questions come from actual GitHub issues, and models work with access to the relevant codebase rather than only an isolated problem statement.

title: CodeAssistBench (CAB): Dataset & Benchmarking for Multi-turn Chat-Based Code Assistance

abstract: Recent works have highlighted the optimization difficulties encountered by gradient descent in training the first and last layer of transformer-based language models, which are overcome by optimizers such as Adam. The problem appears linked to the heavy-tailed distribution of words in text data, where the frequency of the $k$th most frequent word $\pi_k$ is proportional to $1/k$, following Zipf's law. To better understand the impact of the data distribution on training performance, we study a linear bigram model for next-token prediction when the tokens follow a power-law $\pi_k \propto 1/k^\alpha$ parameterized by the exponent $\alpha$. We derive optimization scaling laws for deterministic gradient descent and sign descent as a proxy for Adam as a function of the power $\alpha \geq 0$. This setting differs from existing theoretical investigations in scaling laws which assume that the eigenvalues of the data decay as a power with power $\alpha > 1$. This assumption effectively makes the problem "finite dimensional" as most of the loss comes from a few of the largest eigencomponents. In comparison, we show that the problem is more difficult when the data have heavier tails. The case $\alpha = 1$ as found in text is ``worst-case'' for gradient descent, in that the number of iterations required to reach a small relative error scales almost linearly with dimension. While the performance of sign descent also depends on the dimension, for Zipf-distributed data the number of iterations scales only with the square-root of the dimension, leading to a large improvement over gradient descent for large vocabularies.

paragraphs: This paper examines how unequal token frequencies affect optimization in a linear bigram model for next-token prediction. Token probabilities follow a power law controlled by an exponent, including the Zipf-like case where frequency is inversely proportional to rank. This simplified setting helps isolate how the data distribution changes the difficulty of training.

The authors derive iteration-scaling laws for deterministic gradient descent and sign descent, using the latter as a proxy for Adam. Their analysis includes heavier-tailed distributions than those emphasized in earlier theory. When probability mass is less concentrated among a few components, the optimization problem becomes harder because a small set of dominant components accounts for less of the loss.

Within this setting, the Zipf case is worst-case for gradient descent: reaching a small relative error requires an iteration count that grows almost linearly with dimension. Sign descent needs iterations growing only with the square root of dimension in that case. The result provides a theoretical explanation for a substantial optimizer advantage at large vocabulary sizes in the studied model.
summary.tldr: For a linear bigram model with Zipf-distributed tokens, sign descent has substantially better dimension-dependent iteration scaling than gradient descent.

title: Scaling Laws for Gradient Descent and Sign Descent for Linear Bigram Models under Zipf’s Law

abstract: We propose VASA-3D, an audio-driven, single-shot 3D head avatar generator. This research tackles two major challenges: capturing the subtle expression details present in real human faces, and reconstructing an intricate 3D head avatar from a single portrait image. To accurately model expression details, VASA-3D leverages the motion latent of VASA-1, a method that yields exceptional realism and vividness in 2D talking heads. A critical element of our work is translating this motion latent to 3D, which is accomplished by devising a 3D head model that is conditioned on the motion latent. Customization of this model to a single image is achieved through an optimization framework that employs numerous video frames of the reference head synthesized from the input image. The optimization takes various training losses robust to artifacts and limited pose coverage in the generated training data. Our experiment shows that VASA-3D produces realistic 3D talking heads that cannot be achieved by prior art, and it supports the online generation of 512x512 free-viewpoint videos at up to 75 FPS, facilitating more immersive engagements with lifelike 3D avatars.

paragraphs: VASA-3D creates an audio-driven three-dimensional head avatar from one portrait. The problem combines two difficult requirements: reconstructing a detailed head from limited visual evidence and preserving the subtle expressions that make speech animation convincing. The method builds on the motion representation used by VASA-1 for realistic two-dimensional talking heads.

To transfer that motion into three dimensions, the authors construct a 3D head model conditioned on the motion representation. They customize it to the portrait by optimizing against numerous video frames synthesized from that image. The reported experiments show realistic 3D talking heads beyond what prior methods achieve in the comparison. The system also supports online generation of 512-by-512 free-viewpoint video at up to 75 frames per second. The contribution links expressive motion learned for 2D generation with a personalized 3D representation, enabling the animated head to be viewed from changing viewpoints while responding to audio.
summary.tldr: VASA-3D turns a single portrait into an expressive, audio-driven 3D head avatar with fast free-viewpoint rendering.

title: VASA-3D: Lifelike Audio-Driven Gaussian Head Avatars from a Single Image

abstract: We study the tradeoff between sample complexity and round complexity in *on-demand sampling*, where the learning algorithm adaptively samples from $k$ distributions over a limited number of rounds. In the realizable setting of Multi-Distribution Learning (MDL), we show that the optimal sample complexity of an $r$-round algorithm scales approximately as $dk^{\Theta(1/r)} / \epsilon$. For the general agnostic case, we present an algorithm that achieves near-optimal sample complexity of $\widetilde O((d + k) / \epsilon^2)$ within $\widetilde O(\sqrt{k})$ rounds. Of independent interest, we introduce a new framework, Optimization via On-Demand Sampling (OODS), which abstracts the sample-adaptivity tradeoff and captures most existing MDL algorithms. We establish nearly tight bounds on the round complexity in the OODS setting. The upper bounds directly yield the $\widetilde O(\sqrt{k})$-round algorithm for agnostic MDL, while the lower bounds imply that achieving sub-polynomial round complexity would require fundamentally new techniques that bypass the inherent hardness of OODS.

paragraphs: When learning from several distributions, an algorithm can use earlier observations to decide where to collect more data. This paper studies how much that adaptivity helps when sampling is restricted to a limited number of rounds. The central tradeoff is between the total number of samples and opportunities to revise sampling decisions.

For realizable multi-distribution learning, the optimal sample complexity scales approximately as d times k raised to Θ(1/r), divided by ε, where k is the number of distributions and r the number of rounds. The dependence on k therefore changes with the available adaptivity. In the agnostic setting, the authors give an algorithm with near-optimal sample complexity of approximately (d+k)/ε² using approximately √k rounds, with logarithmic factors suppressed.

The paper also introduces Optimization via On-Demand Sampling, a framework encompassing most existing algorithms for this learning problem. Nearly tight round-complexity bounds explain both the new algorithm and a barrier: obtaining sub-polynomial rounds would require techniques that bypass this framework's hardness. That lower-bound implication is tied to the framework, rather than an unrestricted impossibility claim.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes sample–round tradeoffs in multi-distribution learning and identifies a framework-specific barrier to substantially reducing adaptive rounds.

title: Sample-Adaptivity Tradeoff in On-Demand Sampling

abstract: Natural Language to SQL (NL2SQL) enables intuitive interactions with databases by transforming natural language queries into structured SQL statements. Despite recent advancements in enhancing human-computer interaction within database applications, significant challenges persist, particularly regarding the inference performance in complex scenarios involving multi-table joins and nested queries. Current methodologies primarily utilize supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to train the NL2SQL model, which may limit adaptability and interpretability in new environments (e.g., finance and healthcare). In order to enhance the reasoning performance of the NL2SQL model in the above complex situations, we introduce SQL-R1, a novel NL2SQL reasoning model trained by the reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms. We design a specialized RL-based reward function tailored for NL2SQL tasks and discussed the impact of cold start and synthetic data on the effectiveness of intensive training. In addition, we achieve competitive accuracy using only a tiny amount of synthetic NL2SQL data for augmented training and further explore data engineering for RL. In existing experiments, SQL-R1 achieves execution accuracy of 88.6\% and 67.1\% on the benchmark Spider and BIRD, respectively. The code is available at https://github.com/IDEA-FinAI/SQL-R1.

paragraphs: SQL-R1 translates natural-language database questions into SQL, focusing on difficult cases such as queries that join several tables or contain nested queries. The paper argues that the dominant reliance on supervised fine-tuning may constrain adaptation and interpretability in new environments. It explores reinforcement learning as a way to strengthen reasoning for these complex SQL tasks.

The authors design a reward function specifically for natural-language-to-SQL training. They also examine how cold-start training and synthetic data affect the effectiveness of intensive training, making data preparation part of the investigation. The abstract reports competitive accuracy with only a small amount of synthetic data used for augmentation. This places attention on how training signals and augmented examples work together.

In the reported experiments, SQL-R1 achieves execution accuracy of 88.6% on Spider and 67.1% on BIRD. These results evaluate generated queries through execution, connecting the training approach to functional database-query performance. The contribution combines a reasoning model trained with reinforcement learning, a task-specific reward, and an investigation of the data choices supporting that training.
summary.tldr: SQL-R1 uses a task-specific reinforcement-learning reward to strengthen natural-language-to-SQL reasoning, reporting competitive benchmark execution accuracy.

title: SQL-R1: Training Natural Language to SQL Reasoning Model By Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Patients with epilepsy can manifest short, sub-clinical epileptic “bursts” in addition to full-blown clinical seizures. We believe the relationship between these two classes of events—something not previously studied quantitatively—could yield important insights into the nature and intrinsic dynamics of seizures. A goal of our work is to parse these complex epileptic events into distinct dynamic regimes. A challenge posed by the intracranial EEG (iEEG) data we study is the fact that the number and placement of electrodes can vary between patients. We develop a Bayesian nonparametric Markov switching process that allows for (i) shared dynamic regimes between a variable numbers of channels, (ii) asynchronous regime-switching, and (iii) an unknown dictionary of dynamic regimes. We encode a sparse and changing set of dependencies between the channels using a Markov-switching Gaussian graphical model for the innovations process driving the channel dynamics. We demonstrate the importance of this model in parsing and out-of-sample predictions of iEEG data. We show that our model produces intuitive state assignments that can help automate clinical analysis of seizures and enable the comparison of sub-clinical bursts and full clinical seizures.

paragraphs: Epileptic activity includes short subclinical bursts as well as full clinical seizures. This paper aims to divide those events into distinct dynamic regimes so their patterns can be studied and compared. Intracranial EEG creates a modeling challenge because patients can have different numbers of electrodes in different locations.

The authors develop a Bayesian nonparametric Markov switching process that shares regimes across varying numbers of channels. Channels can switch regimes asynchronously, and the collection of regimes is not fixed in advance. A switching Gaussian graphical model represents sparse, changing dependencies in the innovations process, the part driving new changes in the channel dynamics.

The paper demonstrates the model's importance for parsing recordings and predicting held-out iEEG data. Its state assignments are described as intuitive and potentially useful for automating parts of clinical seizure analysis. They also enable comparison of subclinical bursts with full seizures. The proposed scientific benefit is a better description of event dynamics; the abstract does not claim to establish the underlying relationship between those event classes.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian switching model parses correlated iEEG channels into shared dynamic regimes, supporting comparison of subclinical bursts and seizures.

title: Parsing epileptic events using a Markov switching process model for correlated time series

abstract: We present a novel approach to learning an HMM whose outputs are distributed according to a parametric family. This is done by \em decoupling the learning task into two steps: first estimating the output parameters, and then estimating the hidden states transition probabilities. The first step is accomplished by fitting a mixture model to the output stationary distribution. Given the parameters of this mixture model, the second step is formulated as the solution of an easily solvable convex quadratic program. We provide an error analysis for the estimated transition probabilities and show they are robust to small perturbations in the estimates of the mixture parameters. Finally, we support our analysis with some encouraging empirical results.
originalAbstract: We present a novel approach to learning an HMM whose outputs are distributed according to a parametric family. This is done by \em decoupling the learning task into two steps: first estimating the output parameters, and then estimating the hidden states transition probabilities. The first step is accomplished by fitting a mixture model to the output stationary distribution. Given the parameters of this mixture model, the second step is formulated as the solution of an easily solvable convex quadratic program. We provide an error analysis for the estimated transition probabilities and show they are robust to small perturbations in the estimates of the mixture parameters. Finally, we support our analysis with some encouraging empirical results.

paragraphs: A hidden Markov model describes observations through hidden states and the probabilities of moving between them. This paper studies models whose observations belong to a parametric distribution family. Its main strategy separates learning what each hidden state emits from learning how the hidden state changes over time, producing a two-stage estimation procedure.

First, the method fits a mixture model to the stationary distribution of the observations. This estimates the output-distribution parameters. Given those estimates, the second stage learns hidden-state transition probabilities through a convex quadratic program that the authors describe as easy to solve. Separating the stages gives the transition estimation problem a particularly tractable form.

The paper analyzes errors in the estimated transition probabilities, including the consequences of imperfect output estimates. It shows robustness to small perturbations in the mixture parameters. That result matters because the second stage necessarily depends on quantities estimated in the first. Encouraging empirical results support the analysis, complementing the theoretical account of how estimation errors carry through the procedure.
summary.tldr: A two-stage HMM learner estimates output distributions first, then learns transitions through convex optimization with robustness to small first-stage errors.

title: On learning parametric-output HMMs

abstract: We consider a multi-armed bandit problem where the reward distributions are indexed by two sets –one for arms, one for type– and can be partitioned into a small number of clusters according to the type. First, we consider the setting where all reward distributions are known and all types have the same underlying cluster, the type’s identity is, however, unknown. Second, we study the case where types may come from different classes, which is significantly more challenging. Finally, we tackle the case where the reward distributions are completely unknown. In each setting, we introduce specific algorithms and derive non-trivial regret performance. Numerical experiments show that, in the most challenging agnostic case, the proposed algorithm achieves excellent performance in several difficult scenarios.
originalAbstract: We consider a multi-armed bandit problem where the reward distributions are indexed by two sets –one for arms, one for type– and can be partitioned into a small number of clusters according to the type. First, we consider the setting where all reward distributions are known and all types have the same underlying cluster, the type’s identity is, however, unknown. Second, we study the case where types may come from different classes, which is significantly more challenging. Finally, we tackle the case where the reward distributions are completely unknown. In each setting, we introduce specific algorithms and derive non-trivial regret performance. Numerical experiments show that, in the most challenging agnostic case, the proposed algorithm achieves excellent performance in several difficult scenarios.

paragraphs: The paper studies a bandit problem in which reward distributions depend on both the chosen arm and an underlying type. Types organize those distributions into a small number of clusters. This adds hidden structure to the decision problem: selecting rewarding arms is connected to understanding which type or class governs the rewards.

The authors separate three levels of uncertainty. First, reward distributions are known and types share an underlying cluster, but the type’s identity is unknown. Next, types may belong to different classes, creating a more challenging problem. Finally, the reward distributions themselves are completely unknown. This progression distinguishes uncertainty about identity from uncertainty about the reward model.

For each setting, the paper introduces specific algorithms and derives nontrivial regret guarantees. Numerical experiments focus on the most challenging agnostic case and show excellent performance in several difficult scenarios. The contribution is therefore a set of methods matched to different available knowledge, together with theoretical and empirical evidence that the latent structure can be addressed.
summary.tldr: The paper develops bandit algorithms and regret guarantees for rewards organized by hidden types and clusters.

title: Latent Bandits.

abstract: Maximum a posteriori (MAP) inference over discrete Markov random fields is a central task spanning a wide spectrum of real-world applications but known to be NP-hard for general graphs. In this paper, we propose a novel semidefinite relaxation formulation (referred to as SDR) to estimate the MAP assignment. Algorithmically, we develop an accelerated variant of the alternating direction method of multipliers (referred to as SDPAD-LR) that can effectively exploit the special structure of SDR. Encouragingly, the proposed procedure allows solving SDR for large-scale problems, e.g. problems comprising hundreds of thousands of variables with multiple states on a grid graph. Compared with prior SDP solvers, SDPAD-LR is capable of attaining comparable accuracy while exhibiting remarkably improved scalability. This contradicts the commonly held belief that semidefinite relaxation can only been applied on small-scale problems. We have evaluated the performance of SDR on various benchmark datasets including OPENGM2 and PIC. Experimental results demonstrate that for a broad class of problems, SDPAD-LR outperforms state-of-the-art algorithms in producing better MAP assignments.

paragraphs: Maximum a posteriori inference seeks the most probable assignment in a probabilistic model. For discrete Markov random fields on general graphs, this problem is NP-hard. The paper introduces a semidefinite relaxation, called SDR, to estimate the assignment and focuses on making this approach computationally practical for large problems.

Its solver, SDPAD-LR, is an accelerated variant of the alternating direction method of multipliers. It exploits the special structure of the proposed relaxation. The authors report solving grid-graph problems with hundreds of thousands of variables, each having multiple states. Compared with previous semidefinite-programming solvers, it reaches comparable accuracy with substantially improved scalability.

Evaluations include the OPENGM2 and PIC benchmarks. For a broad class of problems, the method produces better MAP assignments than leading comparison algorithms. These results challenge the idea that semidefinite relaxation is confined to small instances. The contribution is the pairing of a relaxation with a solver designed around its structure, enabling large-scale approximate inference without claiming to solve general NP-hard MAP inference exactly.
summary.tldr: A structured semidefinite relaxation and accelerated solver make approximate MAP inference practical on large discrete graphical models.

title: Scalable Semidefinite Relaxation for Maximum A Posterior Estimation

abstract: We investigate numerical integration of ordinary differential equations (ODEs) for Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC). High-quality integration is crucial for designing efficient and effective proposals for HMC. While the standard method is leapfrog (Stormer-Verlet) integration, we propose the use of an exponential integrator, which is robust to stiff ODEs with highly-oscillatory components. This oscillation is difficult to reproduce using leapfrog integration, even with carefully selected integration parameters and preconditioning. Concretely, we use a Gaussian distribution approximation to segregate stiff components of the ODE. We integrate this term analytically for stability and account for deviation from the approximation using variation of constants. We consider various ways to derive Gaussian approximations and conduct extensive empirical studies applying the proposed “exponential HMC” to several benchmarked learning problems. We compare to state-of-the-art methods for improving leapfrog HMC and demonstrate the advantages of our method in generating many effective samples with high acceptance rates in short running times.

paragraphs: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo relies on numerically solving differential equations to propose new samples. The quality of that numerical integration directly affects sampling efficiency. This paper focuses on stiff equations with rapidly oscillating components, which the usual leapfrog integrator can struggle to reproduce even with carefully chosen parameters and preconditioning.

The proposed exponential integrator uses a Gaussian approximation to separate out stiff components of the dynamics. It integrates that part analytically for stability, then uses variation of constants to account for departures from the approximation. This makes the Gaussian approximation a tool for organizing the numerical calculation while retaining a treatment of the remaining dynamics.

The authors explore several ways to obtain the Gaussian approximation and evaluate exponential HMC on benchmark learning problems. Comparisons with methods for improving leapfrog HMC show advantages in producing effective samples, maintaining high acceptance rates, and keeping runtime short. These are empirical findings about the studied problems, supporting the value of changing the integration method itself.
summary.tldr: Exponential HMC analytically handles stiff dynamics identified through a Gaussian approximation, improving sampling efficiency in the reported experiments.

title: Exponential Integration for Hamiltonian Monte Carlo

abstract: We introduce interacting particle Markov chain Monte Carlo (iPMCMC), a PMCMC method based on an interacting pool of standard and conditional sequential Monte Carlo samplers. Like related methods, iPMCMC is a Markov chain Monte Carlo sampler on an extended space. We present empirical results that show significant improvements in mixing rates relative to both non-interacting PMCMC samplers and a single PMCMC sampler with an equivalent memory and computational budget. An additional advantage of the iPMCMC method is that it is suitable for distributed and multi-core architectures.

Like related methods, iPMCMC is a Markov chain Monte Carlo sampler on an extended space. We present empirical results that show significant improvements in mixing rates relative to both non-interacting PMCMC samplers and a single PMCMC sampler with an equivalent memory and computational budget. An additional advantage of the iPMCMC method is that it is suitable for distributed and multi-core architectures.

paragraphs: The paper introduces interacting particle Markov chain Monte Carlo, or iPMCMC. Its central design is a pool of standard and conditional sequential Monte Carlo samplers that interact. As with related particle MCMC methods, the overall algorithm is a Markov chain Monte Carlo sampler defined on an extended space.

The empirical question is whether interaction improves how effectively the sampler moves through its distribution. The authors report significant improvements in mixing rates compared with non-interacting particle MCMC samplers. They also compare against a single particle MCMC sampler given an equivalent computational and memory budget, reporting improved mixing in that comparison as well.

The budget-matched comparison matters because it evaluates the interacting design against an alternative with comparable resources. The reported benefit therefore goes beyond simply allocating more memory or computation in that experiment. The method is also suitable for distributed and multicore architectures, aligning its pool-based structure with parallel hardware. Together, these findings support interaction as a useful way to organize particle MCMC computation.
summary.tldr: Interacting particle MCMC combines multiple samplers and empirically improves mixing, including against a single sampler with matched resources.

title: Interacting Particle Markov Chain Monte Carlo

abstract: Gaussian Processes (GPs) provide a general and analytically tractable way of modeling complex time-varying, nonparametric functions. The Automatic Bayesian Covariance Discovery (ABCD) system constructs natural-language description of time-series data by treating unknown time-series data nonparametrically using GP with a composite covariance kernel function. Unfortunately, learning a composite covariance kernel with a single time-series data set often results in less informative kernel that may not give qualitative, distinctive descriptions of data. We address this challenge by proposing two relational kernel learning methods which can model multiple time-series data sets by finding common, shared causes of changes. We show that the relational kernel learning methods find more accurate models for regression problems on several real-world data sets; US stock data, US house price index data and currency exchange rate data.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether modeling several time series together can reveal structure that is difficult to recognize in one series alone. Its starting point is Gaussian process regression, which represents complex changes over time through a covariance kernel. The Automatic Bayesian Covariance Discovery system combines kernels to model a series and produce a natural-language description of its behavior.

The difficulty is that learning a composite kernel from a single series can yield a model whose description is not especially informative or distinctive. The authors propose two relational kernel learning methods that connect multiple time series through shared sources of change. This makes relationships among the series part of the modeling problem, rather than treating each series as an isolated collection of observations.

The reported experiments find more accurate regression models on US stocks, US house price indices, and currency exchange rates. These findings support the value of learning shared structure across related series. The contribution connects the search for descriptive time-series structure with improved regression accuracy on the evaluated real-world datasets.
summary.tldr: Two relational kernel learning methods improve regression by finding shared structure across multiple time series.

title: Automatic Construction of Nonparametric Relational Regression Models for Multiple Time Series

abstract: Convolutional neural networks provide visual features that perform remarkably well in many computer vision applications. However, training these networks requires significant amounts of supervision; this paper introduces a generic framework to train such networks, end-to-end, with no supervision. We propose to fix a set of target representations, called Noise As Targets (NAT), and to constrain the deep features to align to them. This domain agnostic approach avoids the standard unsupervised learning issues of trivial solutions and collapsing of the features. Thanks to a stochastic batch reassignment strategy and a separable square loss function, it scales to millions of images. The proposed approach produces representations that perform on par with the state-of-the-arts among unsupervised methods on ImageNet and Pascal VOC.

However, training these networks requires significant amounts of supervision; this paper introduces a generic framework to train such networks, end-to-end, with no supervision. paragraphs: Convolutional networks can learn useful visual features, but supervised training depends on substantial labeled data. This paper proposes an end-to-end training framework that uses no supervision. It fixes a collection of target representations, called Noise As Targets, and trains the network's features to align with them.

The fixed targets and alignment constraints are designed to avoid trivial solutions and feature collapse, where the learned representations cease to meaningfully distinguish inputs. A stochastic batch reassignment strategy organizes how examples are matched to targets. Combined with a separable squared loss, this allows the approach to scale to millions of images.

The authors report that the resulting representations perform comparably to leading unsupervised methods on ImageNet and Pascal VOC. The framework is described as domain agnostic, so its training principle does not depend on task-specific supervision. Its significance is that fixed noise targets can support useful representation learning when paired with a training scheme that prevents collapse and remains computationally scalable.
summary.tldr: Aligning image features with fixed noise targets enables scalable unsupervised training with competitive reported representation quality.

title: Unsupervised Learning by Predicting Noise

abstract: Finding statistically significant high-order interactions in predictive modeling is important but challenging task because the possible number of high-order interactions is extremely large (e.g., $> 10^{17}$). In this paper we study feature selection and statistical inference for sparse high-order interaction models. Our main contribution is to extend recently developed selective inference framework for linear models to high-order interaction models by developing a novel algorithm for efficiently characterizing the selection event for the selective inference of high-order interactions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm by applying it to an HIV drug response prediction problem.

In this paper we study feature selection and statistical inference for sparse high-order interaction models.
