paragraphs: High-order interactions capture predictive relationships involving combinations of several variables. Finding statistically significant interactions is difficult because the number of possible combinations can be enormous, exceeding 10¹⁷ in the setting described by the authors. This paper studies both selecting a sparse collection of interactions and performing statistical inference about them.

The main contribution extends a selective-inference framework developed for linear models to high-order interaction models. Selective inference accounts for the event that led particular features to be chosen. The authors develop an algorithm that efficiently characterizes this selection event for high-order interactions, addressing a computational obstacle created by the huge candidate space.

The algorithm is applied to an HIV drug-response prediction problem, where the authors demonstrate its effectiveness. The contribution concerns the connection between model selection and statistical assessment: identifying an interaction for a predictive model and evaluating its significance are linked tasks. By making the relevant selection event tractable to characterize, the method brings selective inference to a setting with exceptionally many possible interactions.
summary.tldr: An efficient selection-event algorithm extends selective inference to sparse models with enormous numbers of possible high-order interactions.

title: Selective Inference for Sparse High-Order Interaction Models

abstract: Latent space models (LSMs) provide a principled and effective way to extract hidden patterns from observed data. To cope with two challenges in LSMs: (1) how to capture infrequent patterns when pattern frequency is imbalanced and (2) how to reduce model size without sacrificing their expressiveness, several studies have been proposed to “diversify” LSMs, which design regularizers to encourage the components therein to be “diverse”. In light of the limitations of existing approaches, we design a new diversity-promoting regularizer by considering two factors: uncorrelation and evenness, which encourage the components to be uncorrelated and to play equally important roles in modeling data. Formally, this amounts to encouraging the covariance matrix of the components to have more uniform eigenvalues. We apply the regularizer to two LSMs and develop an efficient optimization algorithm. Experiments on healthcare, image and text data demonstrate the effectiveness of the regularizer.

paragraphs: Latent space models aim to uncover hidden patterns in observed data. The paper focuses on two challenges: representing uncommon patterns when frequencies are imbalanced, and reducing model size while preserving expressive power. Both motivate encouraging diversity among the components that make up the model's hidden representation.

The proposed regularizer combines uncorrelation with evenness. Uncorrelation encourages components to carry less overlapping information, while evenness encourages them to play similarly important roles in modeling the data. The authors express this joint goal by encouraging the component covariance matrix to have more uniform eigenvalues, providing a mathematical target for the desired diversity.

They apply the regularizer to two latent space models and develop an efficient optimization algorithm. Experiments involving healthcare, image, and text data demonstrate its effectiveness. The distinctive contribution is to treat diversity as both separation among components and balance in their contributions, bringing the two considerations into a single regularization approach motivated by compactness and coverage of infrequent patterns.
summary.tldr: A diversity regularizer encourages latent components to be uncorrelated and similarly influential by making covariance eigenvalues more uniform.

title: Uncorrelation and Evenness: a New Diversity-Promoting Regularizer

abstract: Learning to coordinate between multiple agents is an important problem in many reinforcement learning problems. Key to learning to coordinate is exploiting loose couplings, i.e., conditional independences between agents. In this paper we study learning in repeated fully cooperative games, multi-agent multi-armed bandits (MAMABs), in which the expected rewards can be expressed as a coordination graph. We propose multi-agent upper confidence exploration (MAUCE), a new algorithm for MAMABs that exploits loose couplings, which enables us to prove a regret bound that is logarithmic in the number of arm pulls and only linear in the number of agents. We empirically compare MAUCE to sparse cooperative Q-learning, and a state-of-the-art combinatorial bandit approach, and show that it performs much better on a variety of settings, including learning control policies for wind farms.

paragraphs: The paper studies repeated cooperative decisions in which multiple agents choose actions and pursue a shared reward. These problems are modeled as multi-agent multi-armed bandits. The key structural assumption is that expected rewards can be represented by a coordination graph, capturing conditional independences that make some agent interactions separable from others.

The proposed algorithm, Multi-Agent Upper Confidence Exploration, or MAUCE, exploits these loose couplings during learning. Rather than treating every combination of agents’ actions as an unrelated possibility, it uses the structure of their dependencies. This matters because coordination becomes harder as the number of agents grows, and useful structure can reduce the burden of exploration.

The authors prove a regret bound that grows logarithmically with the number of arm pulls and only linearly with the number of agents. Regret measures the accumulated reward shortfall from learning rather than already knowing the best choices. Empirically, MAUCE substantially outperforms sparse cooperative Q-learning and a combinatorial bandit method across several settings, including wind-farm control.
summary.tldr: MAUCE exploits coordination-graph structure to learn cooperative actions with favorable regret bounds and strong empirical results.

title: Learning to Coordinate with Coordination Graphs in Repeated Single-Stage Multi-Agent Decision Problems

abstract: Understanding the learning dynamics of neural networks is one of the key issues for the improvement of optimization algorithms as well as for the theoretical comprehension of why deep neural nets work so well today. In this paper, we introduce a random matrix-based framework to analyze the learning dynamics of a single-layer linear network on a binary classification problem, for data of simultaneously large dimension and size, trained by gradient descent. Our results provide rich insights into common questions in neural nets, such as overfitting, early stopping and the initialization of training, thereby opening the door for future studies of more elaborate structures and models appearing in today’s neural networks.

paragraphs: This paper develops a random matrix framework for understanding how training evolves over time. It studies a single-layer linear network performing binary classification with gradient descent. The data setting has both a large number of observations and a large number of dimensions, bringing the analysis into a regime suited to random matrix methods.

The focus is learning dynamics rather than only the final trained model. The resulting analysis provides insights into overfitting, early stopping, and initialization. These questions concern different parts of the same process: where training begins, how it progresses, and when continued optimization may cease to be useful for generalization.

The scope of the established framework is the specified linear network and classification problem. The authors present it as a foundation for future analysis of more elaborate neural architectures and models. Its significance is that a tractable high-dimensional setting can reveal structure in training behavior and offer a starting point for studying questions that also arise in deeper networks.
summary.tldr: A random matrix framework analyzes gradient-descent dynamics in a high-dimensional linear classifier, informing questions about initialization, overfitting, and early stopping.

title: The Dynamics of Learning: A Random Matrix Approach

abstract: We develop nested automatic differentiation (AD) algorithms for exact inference and learning in integer latent variable models. Recently, Winner, Sujono, and Sheldon showed how to reduce marginalization in a class of integer latent variable models to evaluating a probability generating function which contains many levels of nested high-order derivatives. We contribute faster and more stable AD algorithms for this challenging problem and a novel algorithm to compute exact gradients for learning. These contributions lead to significantly faster and more accurate learning algorithms, and are the first AD algorithms whose running time is polynomial in the number of levels of nesting.

paragraphs: Integer latent variable models contain hidden quantities that take integer values. In a class of these models, summing over the hidden possibilities can be reduced to evaluating a probability generating function. The computational challenge is that this function involves many levels of nested, high-order derivatives, making differentiation central to both inference and learning.

This paper develops automatic differentiation algorithms tailored to that nested structure. The algorithms improve speed and numerical stability for the inference calculation. The authors also introduce a method for computing exact gradients for learning, connecting the ability to evaluate the model with the ability to adjust its parameters.

The resulting learning algorithms are reported to be significantly faster and more accurate. A central theoretical contribution is polynomial running time in the number of nesting levels, which the authors identify as a first for automatic differentiation algorithms of this kind. The result addresses the growth of computational effort with nesting depth within the stated model class, making the generating-function approach more effective for exact inference and learning.
summary.tldr: New nested automatic differentiation algorithms enable faster, more stable exact inference and gradient-based learning in a class of integer latent variable models.

title: Learning in Integer Latent Variable Models with Nested Automatic Differentiation

abstract: We propose a method to learn deep ReLU-based classifiers that are provably robust against norm-bounded adversarial perturbations on the training data. For previously unseen examples, the approach is guaranteed to detect all adversarial examples, though it may flag some non-adversarial examples as well. The basic idea is to consider a convex outer approximation of the set of activations reachable through a norm-bounded perturbation, and we develop a robust optimization procedure that minimizes the worst case loss over this outer region (via a linear program). Crucially, we show that the dual problem to this linear program can be represented itself as a deep network similar to the backpropagation network, leading to very efficient optimization approaches that produce guaranteed bounds on the robust loss. The end result is that by executing a few more forward and backward passes through a slightly modified version of the original network (though possibly with much larger batch sizes), we can learn a classifier that is provably robust to any norm-bounded adversarial attack. We illustrate the approach on a number of tasks to train classifiers with robust adversarial guarantees (e.g. for MNIST, we produce a convolutional classifier that provably has less than 5.8% test error for any adversarial attack with bounded $\ell_\infty$ norm less than $\epsilon = 0.1$).

paragraphs: This paper trains ReLU classifiers using guarantees about adversarial perturbations whose size is bounded by a norm. It considers the internal activations reachable under those perturbations and encloses them in a convex outer approximation. Optimizing against this larger region provides bounds on the loss that an allowed adversary could cause.

The robust objective minimizes worst-case loss over the outer region through a linear program. The authors show that the corresponding dual problem can itself be represented as a deep network resembling backpropagation. This representation enables efficient optimization using additional forward and backward passes, although substantially larger batches may be needed.

In the MNIST example, a convolutional classifier has certified test error below 5.8% for attacks with infinity-norm perturbation below 0.1. The result illustrates a guarantee over the specified perturbation set, rather than evidence limited to success against particular attack algorithms.
summary.tldr: A convex relaxation of reachable activations enables efficient robust training and certified guarantees against norm-bounded adversarial perturbations.

title: Provable Defenses against Adversarial Examples via the Convex Outer Adversarial Polytope

abstract: Off-policy learning, the task of evaluating and improving policies using historic data collected from a logging policy, is important because on-policy evaluation is usually expensive and has adverse impacts. One of the major challenge of off-policy learning is to derive counterfactual estimators that also has low variance and thus low generalization error. In this work, inspired by learning bounds for importance sampling problems, we present a new counterfactual learning principle for off-policy learning with bandit feedbacks. Our method regularizes the generalization error by minimizing the distribution divergence between the logging policy and the new policy, and removes the need for iterating through all training samples to compute sample variance regularization in prior work. With neural network policies, our end-to-end training algorithms using variational divergence minimization showed significant improvement over conventional baseline algorithms and is also consistent with our theoretical results.

paragraphs: Off-policy learning improves a decision policy using historical data gathered by a different logging policy. This is useful when evaluating new decisions directly is expensive or has adverse consequences. A central challenge is controlling the variance of counterfactual estimates so that conclusions from logged data generalize reliably.

The paper introduces a learning principle for bandit feedback inspired by bounds for importance sampling. It regularizes generalization error by minimizing a distribution divergence between the logging policy and the new policy. This makes the relationship between the two policies part of the optimization objective, linking policy learning to the statistical stability of its estimates.

The approach avoids the need to pass through all training samples to compute the sample-variance regularization used in earlier work. For neural-network policies, the authors develop end-to-end training algorithms based on variational divergence minimization. Their experiments show significant improvements over conventional baselines, consistent with the theoretical results. The contribution combines an alternative way to control generalization with a training procedure that removes a particular computational burden of variance regularization.
summary.tldr: Divergence-based regularization supports off-policy neural policy learning while avoiding full-data sample-variance calculations used by earlier methods.

title: Variance Regularized Counterfactual Risk Minimization via Variational Divergence Minimization

abstract: We propose a conditional gradient framework for a composite convex minimization template with broad applications. Our approach combines smoothing and homotopy techniques under the CGM framework, and provably achieves the optimal convergence rate. We demonstrate that the same rate holds if the linear subproblems are solved approximately with additive or multiplicative error. In contrast with the relevant work, we are able to characterize the convergence when the non-smooth term is an indicator function. Specific applications of our framework include the non-smooth minimization, semidefinite programming, and minimization with linear inclusion constraints over a compact domain. Numerical evidence demonstrates the benefits of our framework.

paragraphs: This paper develops a framework for convex optimization problems whose objectives combine different kinds of terms, including nonsmooth ones. It uses conditional gradient methods, which organize optimization around linear subproblems. The aim is to accommodate a broad collection of problems within a single framework while retaining a provable convergence rate.

The approach combines smoothing with homotopy: it makes difficult terms smoother and changes the approximation as optimization proceeds. The authors prove that their framework achieves an optimal convergence rate. They also show that this rate survives when the linear subproblems are solved approximately, under the additive or multiplicative error formulations they analyze. This makes approximate subproblem solutions part of the theoretical framework.

A further contribution is a convergence characterization when the nonsmooth term is an indicator function, allowing constraints to enter the formulation. Applications include nonsmooth minimization, semidefinite programming, and linear inclusion constraints over a compact domain. Numerical results support the framework’s benefits alongside its theoretical guarantees.
summary.tldr: A conditional gradient framework combines smoothing and homotopy to achieve optimal convergence rates, including with approximate linear subproblem solutions.

title: A Conditional Gradient Framework for Composite Convex Minimization with Applications to Semidefinite Programming

abstract: Dynamic neural networks are becoming increasingly common, and yet it is hard to implement them efficiently. On-the-fly operation batching for such models is sub-optimal and suffers from run time overheads, while writing manually batched versions can be hard and error-prone. To address this we extend TensorFlow with pfor, a parallel-for loop optimized using static loop vectorization. With pfor, users can express computation using nested loops and conditional constructs, but get performance resembling that of a manually batched version. Benchmarks demonstrate speedups of one to two orders of magnitude on range of tasks, from jacobian computation, to Graph Neural Networks.

paragraphs: Dynamic neural networks can be difficult to implement efficiently because their computations do not always fit a straightforward manually batched form. Grouping operations during execution adds runtime overhead, while writing batched implementations by hand can be difficult and error-prone. The paper addresses this programming and performance problem within TensorFlow.

The authors introduce pfor, a parallel-for loop optimized through static loop vectorization. Users can write computations with nested loops and conditional constructs, while the system transforms the loop computation into a vectorized form. The intended benefit is to preserve a convenient way of expressing the computation while obtaining performance resembling a manually batched implementation.

Benchmarks report speedups of one to two orders of magnitude across tasks ranging from Jacobian computation to graph neural networks. These results demonstrate benefits across different kinds of computation in the evaluated suite. The contribution is an automatic batching mechanism that moves optimization into the static transformation of loops, reducing the need for users to construct efficient batched versions themselves.
summary.tldr: TensorFlow’s pfor automatically vectorizes loop computations, delivering reported benchmark speedups of one to two orders of magnitude.

title: Static Automatic Batching In TensorFlow

abstract: We introduce HyperGAN, a generative model that learns to generate all the parameters of a deep neural network. HyperGAN first transforms low dimensional noise into a latent space, which can be sampled from to obtain diverse, performant sets of parameters for a target architecture. We utilize an architecture that bears resemblance to generative adversarial networks, but we evaluate the likelihood of generated samples with a classification loss. This is equivalent to minimizing the KL-divergence between the distribution of generated parameters, and the unknown true parameter distribution. We apply HyperGAN to classification, showing that HyperGAN can learn to generate parameters which solve the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets with competitive performance to fully supervised learning, while also generating a rich distribution of effective parameters. We also show that HyperGAN can also provide better uncertainty estimates than standard ensembles. This is evidenced by the ability of HyperGAN-generated ensembles to detect out of distribution data as well as adversarial examples.

paragraphs: HyperGAN learns to generate complete sets of parameters for a deep neural network with a chosen architecture. Instead of producing a single trained parameter set, it aims to produce a distribution containing many effective ones. Low-dimensional noise is first transformed into a latent space, from which parameter sets can be sampled.

The architecture resembles a generative adversarial network, but generated samples are assessed through a classification loss. The authors describe this objective as equivalent to minimizing KL divergence between the generated parameter distribution and an unknown true parameter distribution. The training signal thus connects parameter generation to the classification task the resulting networks must solve.

On MNIST and CIFAR-10, HyperGAN generates networks with performance competitive with fully supervised learning while retaining a rich distribution of effective parameters. The authors also report that ensembles of generated networks can give better uncertainty estimates than standard ensembles. Evidence comes from detecting data outside the training distribution and adversarial examples. These findings link diversity among generated models with both classification performance and useful uncertainty information.
summary.tldr: HyperGAN generates diverse, effective neural-network parameter sets and can improve ensemble uncertainty estimates in the reported classification experiments.

title: HyperGAN: A Generative Model for Diverse, Performant Neural Networks

abstract: In this paper, we provide an explicit theoretical connection between Sparse subspace clustering (SSC) and spectral clustering (SC) from the perspective of learning a data similarity matrix. We show that spectral clustering with Gaussian kernel can be viewed as sparse subspace clustering with entropy-norm (SSC+E). Compared to SSC, SSC+E can obtain an analytical, symmetrical, nonnegative and nonlinearly-representational similarity matrix. Besides, SSC+E makes use of Gaussian kernel to compute the sparse similarity matrix of objects, which can avoid the complex computation of the sparse optimization program of SSC. Finally, we provide the experimental analysis to compare the efficiency and effectiveness of sparse subspace clustering and spectral clustering on ten benchmark data sets. The theoretical and experimental analysis can well help users for the selection of high-dimensional data clustering algorithms.

Besides, SSC+E makes use of Gaussian kernel to compute the sparse similarity matrix of objects, which can avoid the complex computation of the sparse optimization program of SSC. paragraphs: Sparse subspace clustering and spectral clustering both depend on relationships encoded in a data similarity matrix. This paper develops an explicit theoretical connection between them through that shared object. It shows that spectral clustering with a Gaussian kernel can be interpreted as sparse subspace clustering with an entropy-norm, which the authors call SSC+E.

Under this interpretation, SSC+E provides an analytical similarity matrix that is symmetric, nonnegative, and capable of nonlinear representation. It uses the Gaussian kernel to compute sparse similarities between objects, avoiding the complex sparse optimization program associated with conventional sparse subspace clustering. The connection therefore concerns both the mathematical meaning of the methods and the computation used to construct similarities.

The authors compare efficiency and effectiveness on ten benchmark datasets. Their theoretical and experimental analysis is intended to guide the choice of clustering algorithms for high-dimensional data. The abstract presents a relationship and a comparative study, rather than a universal ranking of the methods. Its main value is explaining how a familiar kernel construction fits within a subspace-clustering perspective.
summary.tldr: Gaussian-kernel spectral clustering can be viewed as entropy-norm sparse subspace clustering, connecting their similarity matrices and computational approaches.

title: Sparse Subspace Clustering with Entropy-Norm

abstract: We introduce a family of multilayer graph kernels and establish new links between graph convolutional neural networks and kernel methods. Our approach generalizes convolutional kernel networks to graph-structured data, by representing graphs as a sequence of kernel feature maps, where each node carries information about local graph substructures. On the one hand, the kernel point of view offers an unsupervised, expressive, and easy-to-regularize data representation, which is useful when limited samples are available. On the other hand, our model can also be trained end-to-end on large-scale data, leading to new types of graph convolutional neural networks. We show that our method achieves competitive performance on several graph classification benchmarks, while offering simple model interpretation. Our code is freely available at https://github.com/claying/GCKN.

paragraphs: This paper connects two approaches to learning from graphs: kernel methods and graph convolutional neural networks. It introduces multilayer graph kernels by extending convolutional kernel networks to graph-structured inputs. A graph is represented through successive kernel feature maps, with each node carrying information about local structures in the graph.

The connection offers two ways to use the model. From the kernel perspective, it supplies an expressive representation that can be learned without supervision and is straightforward to regularize. The authors emphasize its usefulness when training samples are limited. The same framework can also be trained end-to-end on large datasets, yielding new forms of graph convolutional networks.

On several graph classification benchmarks, the method achieves competitive performance and offers simple model interpretation. These findings support the value of a common framework that accommodates both unsupervised representations and end-to-end learning. Its significance lies in linking local graph structure, kernel representations, and neural training within one family of models, rather than requiring a separate construction for each approach.
summary.tldr: Multilayer graph kernels connect interpretable, unsupervised graph representations with graph neural networks that can also train end-to-end.

title: Convolutional Kernel Networks for Graph-Structured Data

abstract: Building rich machine learning datasets in a scalable manner often necessitates a crowd-sourced data collection pipeline. In this work, we use human studies to investigate the consequences of employing such a pipeline, focusing on the popular ImageNet dataset. We study how specific design choices in the ImageNet creation process impact the fidelity of the resulting dataset—including the introduction of biases that state-of-the-art models exploit. Our analysis pinpoints how a noisy data collection pipeline can lead to a systematic misalignment between the resulting benchmark and the real-world task it serves as a proxy for. Finally, our findings emphasize the need to augment our current model training and evaluation toolkit to take such misalignment into account.

paragraphs: Large image datasets often rely on crowdsourced collection because gathering rich data at scale is difficult. This paper uses human studies to examine what that process means for ImageNet. Its focus is how decisions made during dataset creation affect how faithfully the resulting benchmark represents image classification.

The analysis connects specific collection choices to biases that strong models exploit. It shows how noise in a collection pipeline can produce a systematic mismatch between a benchmark and the real-world task it is intended to represent. This makes the construction process relevant to interpreting model performance, rather than treating the dataset as a neutral measurement instrument.

The findings call for training and evaluation methods that account for this mismatch. Their significance is that progress on a benchmark needs to be understood in light of how its examples and labels were collected. The paper provides evidence that dataset design can shape what models learn and what benchmark success tells us about the broader task.
summary.tldr: Human studies of ImageNet show how crowdsourced dataset design can introduce exploitable biases and misalign benchmark performance with the intended task.

title: From ImageNet to Image Classification: Contextualizing Progress on Benchmarks

abstract: A landmark challenge for AI is to learn flexible, powerful representations from small numbers of examples. On an important class of tasks, hypotheses in the form of programs provide extreme generalization capabilities from surprisingly few examples. However, whereas large natural few-shot learning image benchmarks have spurred progress in meta-learning for deep networks, there is no comparably big, natural program-synthesis dataset that can play a similar role. This is because, whereas images are relatively easy to label from internet meta-data or annotated by non-experts, generating meaningful input-output examples for program induction has proven hard to scale. In this work, we propose a new way of leveraging unit tests and natural inputs for small programs as meaningful input-output examples for each sub-program of the overall program. This allows us to create a large-scale naturalistic few-shot program-induction benchmark and propose new challenges in this domain. The evaluation of multiple program induction and synthesis algorithms points to shortcomings of current methods and suggests multiple avenues for future work.

paragraphs: Programs can express hypotheses that generalize from very few examples, making program learning an important test of flexible intelligence. Progress is harder to measure without large, meaningful benchmarks. This paper addresses the difficulty of producing input-output examples for program induction at a scale comparable to the datasets available for few-shot image learning.

The proposed construction uses unit tests and natural inputs for small programs to obtain meaningful examples for their subprograms. This turns material associated with an overall program into evidence for learning its constituent parts. The approach provides a way to scale dataset creation while keeping examples connected to naturalistic program behavior.

Using this construction, the authors create a large benchmark for few-shot program induction and introduce new challenges within that setting. They evaluate multiple induction and synthesis algorithms and find shortcomings in current methods. The main contribution is therefore both a dataset-building method and an evaluation resource: it enables systematic comparison and exposes opportunities for further work, rather than claiming that learning programs from few examples is already solved.
summary.tldr: A benchmark built from unit tests and natural program inputs makes few-shot program learning easier to evaluate at scale and reveals shortcomings in existing methods.

title: A large-scale benchmark for few-shot program induction and synthesis

abstract: Conformal Predictors (CP) are wrappers around ML models, providing error guarantees under weak assumptions on the data distribution. They are suitable for a wide range of problems, from classification and regression to anomaly detection. Unfortunately, their very high computational complexity limits their applicability to large datasets. In this work, we show that it is possible to speed up a CP classifier considerably, by studying it in conjunction with the underlying ML method, and by exploiting incremental&decremental learning. For methods such as k-NN, KDE, and kernel LS-SVM, our approach reduces the running time by one order of magnitude, whilst producing exact solutions. With similar ideas, we also achieve a linear speed up for the harder case of bootstrapping. Finally, we extend these techniques to improve upon an optimization of k-NN CP for regression. We evaluate our findings empirically, and discuss when methods are suitable for CP optimization.

Their usefulness spans classification, regression, and anomaly detection, but their computational demands can make large datasets difficult to handle. This paper asks how much of that work can be reduced by exploiting the underlying prediction method.

The approach uses incremental and decremental learning: updating computations when data are added or removed. Rather than treating conformal prediction as a separate layer whose costs are fixed, the authors study it together with methods such as nearest neighbors, kernel density estimation, and kernel least-squares support vector machines. For these methods, they report an order-of-magnitude reduction in running time while retaining exact solutions.

Related ideas yield a linear speedup for the more difficult bootstrapping case. The paper also extends the techniques to improve an existing optimization for nearest-neighbor conformal regression. Empirical evaluation supports the findings, and the authors discuss which underlying methods suit this optimization strategy. The contribution is computational acceleration that preserves the computed conformal solutions.
summary.tldr: Incremental and decremental updates substantially accelerate conformal prediction for several underlying models while preserving exact solutions.

title: Exact Optimization of Conformal Predictors via Incremental and Decremental Learning

abstract: Algorithmic stability is a key characteristic to ensure the generalization ability of a learning algorithm. Among different notions of stability, \emph{uniform stability} is arguably the most popular one, which yields exponential generalization bounds. However, uniform stability only considers the worst-case loss change (or so-called sensitivity) by removing a single data point, which is distribution-independent and therefore undesirable. There are many cases that the worst-case sensitivity of the loss is much larger than the average sensitivity taken over the single data point that is removed, especially in some advanced models such as random feature models or neural networks. Many previous works try to mitigate the distribution independent issue by proposing weaker notions of stability, however, they either only yield polynomial bounds or the bounds derived do not vanish as sample size goes to infinity. Given that, we propose \emph{locally elastic stability} as a weaker and distribution-dependent stability notion, which still yields exponential generalization bounds. We further demonstrate that locally elastic stability implies tighter generalization bounds than those derived based on uniform stability in many situations by revisiting the examples of bounded support vector machines, regularized least square regressions, and stochastic gradient descent.

paragraphs: Algorithmic stability studies how much a learned model’s loss changes when a training example is removed. Uniform stability measures the worst possible change, regardless of the data distribution. That can make its generalization bounds pessimistic when the worst-case sensitivity is much larger than the sensitivity typically encountered under the distribution.

This paper introduces locally elastic stability, a weaker notion that incorporates distribution-dependent behavior. It still yields exponential generalization bounds. Preserving that form of guarantee matters because earlier weaker notions could produce only polynomial bounds or bounds that failed to vanish as the sample size increased.

The authors revisit bounded support vector machines, regularized least-squares regression, and stochastic gradient descent to demonstrate tighter bounds than uniform stability provides in many situations. The improvement is not asserted for every learning problem. Its significance is that a stability analysis can account for how data are distributed while retaining strong concentration guarantees, making the resulting generalization assessment more informative in the demonstrated cases.
summary.tldr: Locally elastic stability incorporates the data distribution while retaining exponential generalization bounds and tightening them in many analyzed cases.

title: Toward Better Generalization Bounds with Locally Elastic Stability

abstract: We present a new framework SoundDet, which is an end-to-end trainable and light-weight framework, for polyphonic moving sound event detection and localization. Prior methods typically approach this problem by preprocessing raw waveform into time-frequency representations, which is more amenable to process with well-established image processing pipelines. Prior methods also detect in segment-wise manner, leading to incomplete and partial detections. SoundDet takes a novel approach and directly consumes the raw, multichannel waveform and treats the spatio-temporal sound event as a complete “sound-object" to be detected. Specifically, SoundDet consists of a backbone neural network and two parallel heads for temporal detection and spatial localization, respectively. Given the large sampling rate of raw waveform, the backbone network first learns a set of phase-sensitive and frequency-selective bank of filters to explicitly retain direction-of-arrival information, whilst being highly computationally and parametrically efficient than standard 1D/2D convolution. A dense sound event proposal map is then constructed to handle the challenges of predicting events with large varying temporal duration. Accompanying the dense proposal map are a temporal overlapness map and a motion smoothness map that measure a proposal’s confidence to be an event from temporal detection accuracy and movement consistency perspective. Involving the two maps guarantees SoundDet to be trained in a spatio-temporally unified manner. Experimental results on the public DCASE dataset show the advantage of SoundDet on both segment-based evaluation and our newly proposed event-based evaluation system.

paragraphs: SoundDet detects and locates overlapping, moving sound events directly from multichannel audio waveforms. The paper treats each event as a complete object extending through time and space. This addresses the partial detections associated with segment-wise approaches and avoids first converting the waveform into a time-frequency representation for an image-processing pipeline.

The lightweight, end-to-end framework combines a shared backbone with separate temporal-detection and spatial-localization heads. Its learned filters preserve phase and frequency information needed to retain direction-of-arrival cues, while improving computational and parameter efficiency over standard convolutions. A dense proposal map provides candidate events across widely varying durations.

Two accompanying maps assess proposals through temporal overlap and motion smoothness. These connect confidence to both event timing and consistency of movement, unifying temporal and spatial training. Experiments on the public DCASE dataset show advantages under segment-based evaluation and the authors’ new event-based evaluation. The results support processing sounds as complete moving events rather than assessing their temporal and spatial structure in isolation.
summary.tldr: SoundDet jointly detects and localizes complete moving sound events from raw multichannel audio, showing advantages on DCASE evaluations.

title: SoundDet: Polyphonic Moving Sound Event Detection and Localization from Raw Waveform

abstract: Gradient regularization is a neural network defense technique that requires no prior knowledge of an adversarial attack and that brings only limited increase in training computational complexity. A form of complex-valued neural network (CVNN) is proposed to improve the performance of gradient regularization on classification tasks of real-valued input in adversarial settings. The activation derivatives of each layer of the CVNN are dependent on the combination of inputs to the layer, and locally stable representations can be learned for inputs the network is trained on. Furthermore, the properties of the CVNN parameter derivatives resist decrease of performance on the standard objective that is caused by competition with the gradient regularization objective. Experimental results show that the performance of gradient regularized CVNN surpasses that of real-valued neural networks with comparable storage and computational complexity. Moreover, gradient regularized complex-valued networks exhibit robust performance approaching that of real-valued networks trained with multi-step adversarial training.

paragraphs: Gradient regularization is a defense that does not require prior knowledge of a particular adversarial attack and adds only limited training computation. This paper asks whether changing the network’s numerical representation can make that defense more effective. It proposes a complex-valued neural network for classification problems whose inputs remain real-valued.

In the proposed network, activation derivatives depend on combinations of inputs to each layer. This allows locally stable representations to be learned around inputs used in training. The authors also identify properties of parameter derivatives that resist damage to the standard classification objective when it competes with the gradient-regularization objective. The design therefore addresses both stability and the interaction between training goals.

Experiments show better performance than gradient-regularized real-valued networks with comparable storage and computational requirements. Robust performance also approaches that of real-valued networks trained using multi-step adversarial training. These results support complex-valued network design as a way to strengthen gradient regularization while retaining its relatively limited computational overhead.
summary.tldr: A complex-valued network strengthens gradient regularization, improving reported robustness over comparable real-valued networks and approaching multi-step adversarial training.

title: Improving Gradient Regularization using Complex-Valued Neural Networks

abstract: We present a simple and effective self-supervised learning approach for speech recognition. The approach learns a model to predict the masked speech signals, in the form of discrete labels generated with a random-projection quantizer. In particular the quantizer projects speech inputs with a randomly initialized matrix, and does a nearest-neighbor lookup in a randomly-initialized codebook. Neither the matrix nor the codebook are updated during self-supervised learning. Since the random-projection quantizer is not trained and is separated from the speech recognition model, the design makes the approach flexible and is compatible with universal speech recognition architecture. On LibriSpeech our approach achieves similar word-error-rates as previous work using self-supervised learning with non-streaming models, and provides lower word-error-rates than previous work with streaming models. On multilingual tasks the approach also provides significant improvement over wav2vec 2.0 and w2v-BERT.

paragraphs: This paper presents self-supervised speech learning in which a model predicts discrete labels for masked speech signals. The labels come from a simple random-projection quantizer. This provides a prediction target for learning from speech without requiring the quantizer itself to learn a representation.

The quantizer first projects speech inputs through a randomly initialized matrix, then assigns labels through nearest-neighbor lookup in a randomly initialized codebook. Both components remain fixed throughout self-supervised learning. Separating this fixed label generator from the speech-recognition model makes the approach flexible and compatible with a universal speech-recognition architecture.

On LibriSpeech, the method achieves word-error rates similar to earlier self-supervised work with non-streaming models and lower rates than earlier work with streaming models. On multilingual tasks, it also delivers significant improvements over wav2vec 2.0 and w2v-BERT. The results show that a fixed random quantizer can supply effective training targets in these settings, with the reported advantages depending on the recognition setting and comparison.
summary.tldr: A fixed random-projection quantizer supplies effective masked-prediction targets for self-supervised speech recognition.

title: Self-supervised learning with random-projection quantizer for speech recognition

abstract: We consider the problem of signal estimation in generalized linear models defined via rotationally invariant design matrices. Since these matrices can have an arbitrary spectral distribution, this model is well suited for capturing complex correlation structures which often arise in applications. We propose a novel family of approximate message passing (AMP) algorithms for signal estimation, and rigorously characterize their performance in the high-dimensional limit via a state evolution recursion. Our rotationally invariant AMP has complexity of the same order as the existing AMP derived under the restrictive assumption of a Gaussian design; our algorithm also recovers this existing AMP as a special case. Numerical results showcase a performance close to Vector AMP (which is conjectured to be Bayes-optimal in some settings), but obtained with a much lower complexity, as the proposed algorithm does not require a computationally expensive singular value decomposition.

paragraphs: The paper studies recovering a signal in generalized linear models whose design matrices are rotationally invariant. Such matrices can have arbitrary spectral distributions, allowing the model to express complex correlation structures. This broadens the setting beyond the Gaussian-design assumption used by an existing form of approximate message passing.

The authors introduce a family of approximate message-passing algorithms for this broader matrix class. They rigorously describe the algorithms’ performance in the high-dimensional limit through a state-evolution recursion, a sequence of equations tracking their behavior. The method has the same order of computational complexity as the Gaussian-design algorithm and includes that earlier algorithm as a special case.

Numerical experiments show performance close to Vector AMP while using much less computation, because the proposed method avoids an expensive singular value decomposition. Vector AMP is conjectured to be Bayes-optimal in some settings; proximity to its numerical performance does not establish that property for the new method. The stated benefit is broader correlation modeling with efficient computation and rigorous asymptotic characterization.
summary.tldr: A new AMP family handles rotationally invariant designs with rigorous high-dimensional analysis and avoids the costly decomposition required by Vector AMP.

title: Estimation in Rotationally Invariant Generalized Linear Models via Approximate Message Passing

abstract: The Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC) (Chollet, 2019) and its most recent language-complete instantiation (LARC) has been postulated as an important step towards general AI. Yet, even state-of-the-art machine learning models struggle to achieve meaningful performance on these problems, falling behind non-learning based approaches. We argue that solving these tasks requires extreme generalization that can only be achieved by proper accounting for core knowledge priors. As a step towards this goal, we focus on geometry priors and introduce LatFormer, a model that incorporates lattice symmetry priors in attention masks. We show that, for any transformation of the hypercubic lattice, there exists a binary attention mask that implements that group action. Hence, our study motivates a modification to the standard attention mechanism, where attention weights are scaled using soft masks generated by a convolutional network. Experiments on synthetic geometric reasoning show that LatFormer requires 2 orders of magnitude fewer data than standard attention and transformers. Moreover, our results on ARC and LARC tasks that incorporate geometric priors provide preliminary evidence that these complex datasets do not lie out of the reach of deep learning models.

paragraphs: Abstract geometric reasoning tasks can require generalization from very little data. This paper investigates whether attention models can learn such tasks more efficiently when they incorporate knowledge about grid geometry. The authors introduce LatFormer, which builds lattice symmetry priors into attention masks, aiming to supply useful structure for reasoning over geometric transformations.

The theoretical motivation is a representation result: each transformation of the hypercubic lattice has a binary attention mask implementing its group action. Building on that connection, LatFormer scales attention weights with soft masks produced by a convolutional network. This provides a learnable mechanism for bringing geometric structure into the attention computation.

On synthetic geometric reasoning tasks, the authors report that LatFormer requires two orders of magnitude less data than standard attention and transformers. They also study ARC and LARC tasks involving geometric priors. Those results provide preliminary evidence that deep learning can make progress on these demanding datasets. The evidence supports the value of geometric priors in the tested tasks, while the broader argument about core knowledge remains a motivating position.
summary.tldr: LatFormer incorporates lattice symmetries into attention and reports roughly 100-fold lower data requirements on synthetic geometric reasoning tasks.

title: Infusing Lattice Symmetry Priors in Attention Mechanisms for Sample-Efficient Abstract Geometric Reasoning

abstract: For reinforcement learning systems to be widely adopted, their users must understand and trust them. We present a theoretical analysis of explaining reinforcement learning using Shapley values, following a principled approach from game theory for identifying the contribution of individual players to the outcome of a cooperative game. We call this general framework Shapley Values for Explaining Reinforcement Learning (SVERL). Our analysis exposes the limitations of earlier uses of Shapley values in reinforcement learning. We then develop an approach that uses Shapley values to explain agent performance. In a variety of domains, SVERL produces meaningful explanations that match and supplement human intuition.

We present a theoretical analysis of explaining reinforcement learning using Shapley values, following a principled approach from game theory for identifying the contribution of individual players to the outcome of a cooperative game. paragraphs: Understanding why a reinforcement learning agent performs as it does is important for users deciding whether to trust it. This paper studies explanations based on Shapley values, a game-theoretic approach for assigning contributions to participants in a cooperative outcome. The authors develop a general framework called Shapley Values for Explaining Reinforcement Learning, or SVERL.

The contribution begins with a theoretical analysis of how this attribution idea applies to reinforcement learning. That analysis exposes limitations in earlier uses of Shapley values in this setting. The authors then develop an approach directed specifically at explaining agent performance, making the outcome being explained central to the attribution framework.

Across a variety of domains, SVERL produces explanations that the authors describe as meaningful and consistent with human intuition, while also adding information beyond that intuition. This provides practical support for the framework alongside its theoretical analysis. The paper's significance lies in connecting a principled contribution-allocation method to explanations of reinforcement learning performance and examining whether the resulting explanations make sense to people.
summary.tldr: SVERL develops a theoretically grounded use of Shapley values to explain reinforcement learning agent performance.

title: Explaining Reinforcement Learning with Shapley Values

abstract: We study $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-differentially private (DP) stochastic convex optimization under an $r$-th quantile loss function taking the form $c(u) = ru^+ + (1-r)(-u)^+$. The function is non-smooth, and we propose to approximate it with a smooth function obtained by convolution smoothing, which enjoys both structure and bandwidth flexibility and can address outliers. This leads to a better approximation than those obtained from existing methods such as Moreau Envelope. We then design private algorithms based on DP stochastic gradient descent and objective perturbation, and show that both algorithms achieve (near) optimal excess generalization risk $O(\max\{\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}, \frac{\sqrt{d\ln(1/\delta)}}{n\varepsilon}\})$. Through objective perturbation, we further derive an upper bound $O(\max\{\sqrt{\frac{d}{n}}, \sqrt{\frac{d\ln(1/\delta)}{n\varepsilon}}\})$ on the parameter estimation error under mild assumptions on data generating processes. Some applications in private quantile regression and private inventory control will be discussed.

paragraphs: Quantile loss assigns different penalties to positive and negative errors, making it useful when the target is a chosen quantile. Its sharp corner creates a nonsmooth optimization problem. This paper studies how to optimize that loss while satisfying differential privacy, so learning must balance statistical accuracy with protection of individual data.

The authors replace the original loss with a smooth approximation constructed through convolution. This gives flexibility in both the smoothing structure and bandwidth, and the approach can address outliers. They report a better approximation than existing approaches such as the Moreau envelope. Using the smoothed loss, they develop private algorithms based on stochastic gradient descent and objective perturbation.

Both algorithms receive near-optimal or optimal excess generalization risk bounds that account for sample size, dimension, and privacy parameters. For objective perturbation, the paper additionally bounds parameter estimation error under mild assumptions on how the data are generated. Applications include private quantile regression and inventory control, connecting the analysis to settings where asymmetric prediction errors influence decisions.
summary.tldr: Flexible smoothing of quantile loss enables differentially private optimization with optimal or near-optimal generalization risk guarantees.

title: Differentially Private Stochastic Convex Optimization under a Quantile Loss Function

abstract: In this paper, we present improved learning-augmented algorithms for the multi-option ski rental problem. Learning-augmented algorithms take ML predictions as an added part of the input and incorporates these predictions in solving the given problem. Due to their unique strength that combines the power of ML predictions with rigorous performance guarantees, they have been extensively studied in the context of online optimization problems. Even though ski rental problems are one of the canonical problems in the field of online optimization, only deterministic algorithms were previously known for multi-option ski rental, with or without learning augmentation. We present the first randomized learning-augmented algorithm for this problem, surpassing previous performance guarantees given by deterministic algorithms. Our learning-augmented algorithm is based on a new, provably best-possible randomized competitive algorithm for the problem. Our results are further complemented by lower bounds for deterministic and randomized algorithms, and computational experiments evaluating our algorithms’ performance improvements.

paragraphs: Learning-augmented algorithms use machine-learning predictions as additional input while retaining rigorous performance guarantees. This paper studies that combination for the multi-option ski rental problem, a problem in online optimization where decisions must be made without complete knowledge of the future. Previously known algorithms for this setting were deterministic, both with and without prediction assistance.

The authors develop the first randomized learning-augmented algorithm for the problem. Its construction builds on a new randomized competitive algorithm whose guarantee is proved best possible. Randomization therefore supplies the foundation for improving the prediction-assisted method, rather than being introduced only as an experimental variation.

The resulting learning-augmented guarantees surpass those of prior deterministic algorithms. The paper also supplies lower bounds for deterministic and randomized approaches, helping establish the limits against which these guarantees should be judged. Computational experiments evaluate the performance improvements. Together, the theoretical bounds and experiments show how prediction assistance and randomization can be combined in this particular online decision problem.
summary.tldr: A randomized prediction-assisted algorithm improves guarantees for multi-option ski rental using a best-possible randomized competitive algorithm.

title: Improved Learning-Augmented Algorithms for the Multi-Option Ski Rental Problem via Best-Possible Competitive Analysis

abstract: The successes of artificial neural networks (ANNs) are largely attributed to mimicking the human brain structures. Recent advances in neuroscience revealed that neurons interact with each other through various kinds of connectivity patterns to process information, in which the common connectivity patterns are also called circuit motifs. However, many existing ANNs can only model one or two circuit motifs in their architectures, so that their performance may drastically vary among different types of machine learning tasks. In this paper, we propose a new type of neural network inspired by the architectures of neuronal circuits, namely Circuit Neural Network (CircuitNet). In CircuitNet, a group of densely connected neurons, namely circuit motif unit (CMU), form the basic unit of the network, which is capable of modeling universal circuit motifs by adjusting the weights within the CMUs. Compared with traditional feed-forward networks, CircuitNet has the ability to model more types of neuron connections such as feed-back and lateral motifs. Inspired by the locally dense and globally sparse structure of the human brain, several iterations of signal transmission among different CMUs are achieved by sparse connections through the input ports and output ports of different CMUs. Experiments have demonstrated that CircuitNet can outperform popular neural network architectures in function approximation, reinforcement learning, image classification, and time series forecasting tasks.

paragraphs: Neurons can interact through many recurring connection patterns, called circuit motifs. This paper argues that neural network architectures restricted to only a few such patterns may vary substantially in performance across tasks. CircuitNet is designed to support a broader range of connections within one general architecture.

Its basic building block is a densely connected group of neurons called a circuit motif unit. Adjusting weights inside these units allows them to model different motifs, including feedback and lateral connections beyond those available in traditional feed-forward networks. Connections between units are sparse and pass through designated input and output ports, supporting several rounds of signal transmission.

This design combines dense local interaction with sparse communication across the network. Experiments show that CircuitNet can outperform popular architectures on function approximation, reinforcement learning, image classification, and time series forecasting. The findings support the usefulness of flexible connectivity across several task types. The architectural contribution is a reusable unit whose internal weights can express varied interaction patterns while participating in a larger sparsely connected system.
summary.tldr: CircuitNet combines dense, flexible circuit units with sparse connections between them and reports improvements across several kinds of learning tasks.

title: CircuitNet: A Generic Neural Network to Realize Universal Circuit Motif Modeling

abstract: We study the problem of private vector mean estimation in the shuffle model of privacy where $n$ users each have a unit vector $v^{(i)} \in \mathbb{R}^d$. We propose a new multi-message protocol that achieves the optimal error using $O(\min(n\varepsilon^2,d))$ messages per user. Moreover, we show that any (unbiased) protocol that achieves optimal error must require each user to send $\Omega(\min(n\varepsilon^2,d)/\log(n))$ messages, demonstrating the optimality of our message complexity up to logarithmic factors. Additionally, we study the single-message setting and design a protocol that achieves mean squared error $O(dn^{d/(d+2)}\varepsilon^{-4/(d+2)})$. Moreover, we show that any single-message protocol must incur mean squared error $\Omega(dn^{d/(d+2)})$, showing that our protocol is optimal in the standard setting where $\varepsilon = \Theta(1)$. Finally, we study robustness to malicious users and show that malicious users can incur large additive error with a single shuffler.

paragraphs: This paper studies private estimation of the mean of unit vectors held by different users in the shuffle model. Its central question is how communication affects achievable accuracy: can each user send just one message, or does optimal error require multiple messages?

The authors give a multi-message protocol achieving optimal error with a message count per user on the order of the smaller of the dimension and the number of users times epsilon squared. They also prove that any unbiased protocol achieving optimal error needs nearly that many messages, up to a logarithmic factor. The unbiasedness qualification applies to this communication lower bound.

For the single-message setting, the paper supplies a protocol and a lower bound applying to any such protocol. Their rates establish optimality when the privacy parameter epsilon is of constant order. The authors additionally show that malicious users can introduce large additive error when there is a single shuffler. Together, the results separate accuracy, communication, and robustness: an accurate private estimator may require substantial messaging, and its privacy setting does not itself resolve malicious-user interference.
summary.tldr: Optimal shuffle-private vector estimation needs nearly the proposed message count for unbiased protocols, while single-message protocols face stronger error limits.

title: Private Vector Mean Estimation in the Shuffle Model: Optimal Rates Require Many Messages

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are trained on massive text corpora, which are encoded with diverse personality traits. This triggers an interesting goal of eliciting a desired personality trait from the LLM, and probing its behavioral preferences. Accordingly, we formalize the persona elicitation task, aiming to customize LLM behaviors to align with a target persona. We present Persona In-Context Learning (PICLe), a novel persona elicitation framework grounded in Bayesian inference. At the core, PICLe introduces a new ICL example selection criterion based on likelihood ratio, which is designed to optimally guide the model in eliciting a specific target persona. We demonstrate the effectiveness of PICLe through extensive comparisons against baseline methods across three contemporary LLMs. Code is available at https://github.com/deeplearning-wisc/picle.

paragraphs: Language models learn from text containing many different personality traits and behavioral preferences. This paper asks how to elicit a chosen persona from that variety. It formalizes persona elicitation as a task in which the model’s behavior should align with a specified target, making behavioral customization an explicit objective.

Persona In-Context Learning, or PICLe, approaches that objective through Bayesian inference. Its central mechanism is a likelihood-ratio criterion for choosing in-context examples. Those examples provide guidance within the prompt, and the criterion is designed to select examples that optimally steer the model toward the desired persona.

The authors evaluate PICLe against baseline methods across three language models and report evidence of its effectiveness. The contribution links a formal account of persona elicitation to a concrete example-selection strategy. This matters because the prompt examples become a deliberate tool for shaping behavioral preferences, with a selection rule grounded in the target persona and an empirical evaluation across multiple models.
summary.tldr: PICLe uses a Bayesian likelihood-ratio criterion to select prompt examples that steer language models toward a target persona.

title: PICLe: Eliciting Diverse Behaviors from Large Language Models with Persona In-Context Learning

abstract: Much of the causal discovery literature prioritises guaranteeing the identifiability of causal direction in statistical models. For structures within a Markov equivalence class, this requires strong assumptions which may not hold in real-world datasets, ultimately limiting the usability of these methods. Building on previous attempts, we show how to incorporate causal assumptions within the Bayesian framework. Identifying causal direction then becomes a Bayesian model selection problem. This enables us to construct models with realistic assumptions, and consequently allows for the differentiation between Markov equivalent causal structures. We analyse why Bayesian model selection works in situations where methods based on maximum likelihood fail. To demonstrate our approach, we construct a Bayesian non-parametric model that can flexibly model the joint distribution. We then outperform previous methods on a wide range of benchmark datasets with varying data generating assumptions.

paragraphs: Determining which of two variables causes the other is difficult when competing causal structures are Markov equivalent. Much existing work seeks assumptions strong enough to guarantee that the direction can be identified. This paper argues that those assumptions can restrict applicability and instead places causal assumptions inside a Bayesian framework.

The resulting task is Bayesian model selection: compare models representing different causal directions using the assumptions built into them. The authors explain why this approach can distinguish structures in situations where maximum-likelihood methods fail. The distinction matters because fitting the observed distribution well does not, by itself, settle which causal direction should be preferred.

To demonstrate the approach, the paper constructs a Bayesian non-parametric model that flexibly represents the joint distribution of the variables. It outperforms previous methods across benchmark datasets with varied data-generating assumptions. The contribution is a way to reason about causal direction through explicit Bayesian modeling, with empirical evidence across different settings, rather than a claim that causal direction can be recovered without assumptions.
summary.tldr: Bayesian model selection incorporates causal assumptions to distinguish competing causal directions and improves results across varied benchmark datasets.

title: Bivariate Causal Discovery using Bayesian Model Selection

abstract: This paper studies the problem of stochastic bilevel optimization where the upper-level function is nonconvex with potentially unbounded smoothness and the lower-level function is strongly convex. This problem is motivated by meta-learning applied to sequential data, such as text classification using recurrent neural networks, where the smoothness constant of the upper-level loss function scales linearly with the gradient norm and can be potentially unbounded. Existing algorithm crucially relies on the nested loop design, which requires significant tuning efforts and is not practical. In this paper, we address this issue by proposing a Single Loop bIlevel oPtimizer (SLIP). The proposed algorithm first updates the lower-level variable by a few steps of stochastic gradient descent, and then simultaneously updates the upper-level variable by normalized stochastic gradient descent with momentum and the lower-level variable by stochastic gradient descent. Under standard assumptions, we show that our algorithm finds an $\epsilon$-stationary point within $\widetilde{O}(1/\epsilon^4)$[Here $\widetilde{O}(\cdot)$ compresses logarithmic factors of $1/\epsilon$ and $1/\delta$, where $\delta\in(0,1)$ denotes the failure probability.] oracle calls of stochastic gradient or Hessian-vector product, both in expectation and with high probability. This complexity result is nearly optimal up to logarithmic factors without mean-square smoothness of the stochastic gradient oracle. Our proof relies on (i) a refined characterization and control of the lower-level variable and (ii) establishing a novel connection between bilevel optimization and stochastic optimization under distributional drift. Our experiments on various tasks show that our algorithm significantly outperforms strong baselines in bilevel optimization.

paragraphs: Bilevel optimization involves an outer objective whose optimization depends on an inner problem. This paper studies a difficult stochastic setting: the outer objective is nonconvex and may have unbounded smoothness, while the inner objective is strongly convex. Sequential meta-learning motivates this setting because the outer loss's smoothness can grow with its gradient norm.

The proposed SLIP algorithm avoids repeatedly running nested optimization loops. After a few initial stochastic gradient steps on the inner variable, it updates both variables together. The outer update uses normalized stochastic gradients with momentum, while the inner update uses stochastic gradient descent. This design addresses the tuning burden associated with the existing nested approach.

Under the stated assumptions, SLIP reaches an epsilon-stationary point using roughly inverse-fourth-power dependence on epsilon in stochastic gradient or Hessian-vector calls, ignoring logarithmic factors. The result holds both in expectation and with high probability and is nearly optimal without requiring mean-square smoothness of the gradient oracle. The proof connects bilevel optimization to optimization under distributional drift, and experiments report substantial improvements over strong baselines.
summary.tldr: SLIP simplifies stochastic bilevel optimization to a single loop while retaining nearly optimal convergence guarantees under its assumptions.

title: A Nearly Optimal Single Loop Algorithm for Stochastic Bilevel Optimization under Unbounded Smoothness

abstract: In the context of proxy modeling for process systems, traditional data-driven deep learning approaches frequently encounter significant challenges, such as substantial training costs induced by large amounts of data, and limited generalization capabilities. As a promising alternative, physics-aware models incorporate partial physics knowledge to ameliorate these challenges. Although demonstrating efficacy, they fall short in terms of exploration depth and universality. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a physics-aware proxy model (PAPM) that fully incorporates partial prior physics of process systems, which includes multiple input conditions and the general form of conservation relations, resulting in better out-of-sample generalization. Additionally, PAPM contains a holistic temporal-spatial stepping module for flexible adaptation across various process systems. Through systematic comparisons with state-of-the-art pure data-driven and physics-aware models across five two-dimensional benchmarks in nine generalization tasks, PAPM notably achieves an average performance improvement of 6.7%, while requiring fewer FLOPs, and just 1% of the parameters compared to the prior leading method.

paragraphs: Proxy models approximate process systems, but purely data-driven models can require substantial training resources and generalize poorly beyond their training examples. Physics-aware models try to improve this situation by incorporating available physical knowledge. PAPM develops that approach by making partial prior knowledge central to the model's design.

The model incorporates multiple input conditions and the general form of conservation relations. These provide structure for learning how a process behaves, supporting predictions outside the training sample. PAPM also includes a unified module for stepping through space and time, designed to adapt flexibly across different process systems.

The evaluation compares PAPM with leading data-driven and physics-aware models on five two-dimensional benchmarks spanning nine generalization tasks. It reports an average performance improvement of 6.7%, fewer floating-point operations, and only 1% of the parameters of the prior leading method. These findings suggest that incorporating the available physical structure can improve generalization while reducing model size and computation in the tested settings. The contribution combines physical knowledge with an architecture intended for use across process systems.
summary.tldr: PAPM incorporates partial physical knowledge to improve process-system generalization with substantially fewer parameters.

title: PAPM: A Physics-aware Proxy Model for Process Systems

abstract: Longitudinal data are important in numerous fields, such as healthcare, sociology and seismology, but real-world datasets present notable challenges for practitioners because they can be high-dimensional, contain structured missingness patterns, and measurement time points can be governed by an unknown stochastic process. While various solutions have been suggested, the majority of them have been designed to account for only one of these challenges. In this work, we propose a flexible and efficient latent-variable model that is capable of addressing all these limitations. Our approach utilizes Gaussian processes to capture correlations between samples and their associated missingness masks as well as to model the underlying point process. We construct our model as a variational autoencoder together with deep neural network parameterised decoder and encoder models, and develop a scalable amortised variational inference approach for efficient model training. We demonstrate competitive performance using both simulated and real datasets.

paragraphs: Data collected over time can be difficult to model for several reasons at once. Each observation may contain many variables, missing measurements may follow a structured pattern, and observation times may arise from an unknown random process. This paper develops a latent-variable model that addresses these challenges together.

The approach uses Gaussian processes to represent correlations involving observations and their missingness masks, which record what was observed. It also uses them to model the point process governing measurement times. This brings observation content, missingness structure, and the timing of observations into a shared modeling framework.

The authors implement the model as a variational autoencoder with neural-network encoders and decoders. They develop scalable amortized variational inference to make training efficient, sharing the inference machinery across observations. Experiments on simulated and real datasets show competitive performance. The main contribution is the integrated treatment of difficulties that many earlier approaches address individually, providing a flexible way to analyze longitudinal data when missingness and measurement timing also need to be modeled.
summary.tldr: A Gaussian-process-based variational autoencoder jointly models high-dimensional observations, structured missingness, and random measurement times.

title: Latent variable model for high-dimensional point process with structured missingness

abstract: We design new differentially private algorithms for the problems of adversarial bandits and bandits with expert advice. For adversarial bandits, we give a simple and efficient conversion of any non-private bandit algorithm to a private bandit algorithm. Instantiating our conversion with existing non-private bandit algorithms gives a regret upper bound of $O\left(\frac{\sqrt{KT}}{\sqrt{\epsilon}}\right)$, improving upon the existing upper bound $O\left(\frac{\sqrt{KT \log(KT)}}{\epsilon}\right)$ for all $\epsilon \leq 1$. In particular, our algorithms allow for sublinear expected regret even when $\epsilon \leq \frac{1}{\sqrt{T}}$, establishing the first known separation between central and local differential privacy for this problem. For bandits with expert advice, we give the first differentially private algorithms, with expected regret $O\left(\frac{\sqrt{NT}}{\sqrt{\epsilon}}\right), O\left(\frac{\sqrt{KT\log(N)}\log(KT)}{\epsilon}\right)$, and $\tilde{O}\left(\frac{N^{1/6}K^{1/2}T^{2/3}\log(NT)}{\epsilon ^{1/3}} + \frac{N^{1/2}\log(NT)}{\epsilon}\right)$, where $K$ and $N$ are the number of actions and experts respectively. These rates allow us to get sublinear regret for different combinations of small and large $K, N$ and $\epsilon.$
