paragraphs: Bandit learning involves repeatedly choosing actions while receiving limited feedback about their outcomes. This paper studies adversarial bandits under differential privacy, asking how much privacy protection increases regret, the accumulated cost of learning compared with a reference choice. It also considers a version in which the learner receives advice from a collection of experts.

The authors give a simple, efficient conversion from any non-private bandit algorithm into a private one. With existing algorithms, the conversion yields a regret bound proportional to the square root of KT divided by the square root of epsilon, where K counts actions and T counts rounds. This improves the previous bound for epsilon at most one and permits sublinear expected regret in some regimes with epsilon at or below one over the square root of T.

That result establishes a separation between central and local differential privacy for this problem. For bandits with expert advice, the paper provides the first private algorithms and several regret bounds. Different bounds support sublinear regret for different combinations of action counts, expert counts, and privacy levels.
summary.tldr: A general conversion improves privacy-dependent regret bounds for adversarial bandits, alongside new private algorithms for bandits with expert advice.

title: Faster Rates for Private Adversarial Bandits

abstract: Principal-agent problems model scenarios where a principal aims at incentivizing an agent to take costly, unobservable actions through the provision of payments. Such interactions are ubiquitous in several real-world applications, ranging from blockchain to the delegation of machine learning tasks. In this paper, we initiate the study of hidden-action principal-agent problems under approximate best responses, in which the agent may select any action that is not too much suboptimal given the principal’s payment scheme (a.k.a. contract). Our main result is a polynomial-time algorithm to compute an optimal contract under approximate best responses. This is perhaps surprising, as computing an optimal commitment under approximate best responses is known to be computationally intractable in Stackelberg games. We also investigate the learnability of contracts under approximate best responses, by providing a no-regret learning algorithm for a natural application scenario where the principal does not know anything about the environment.

paragraphs: In a hidden-action principal-agent problem, one party offers payments to encourage another party to take costly actions that cannot be directly observed. Designing those payments requires reasoning about how the agent will respond. This paper studies contracts when the agent may choose any action whose payoff is sufficiently close to the best available payoff.

Allowing approximate best responses changes the design problem because the contract must account for several potentially acceptable actions. The main result is a polynomial-time algorithm for computing an optimal contract in this setting. The abstract contrasts this tractability with the known difficulty of computing optimal commitments under approximate responses in Stackelberg games, showing that the distinction between these settings matters computationally.

The paper also examines learning when the principal initially knows nothing about the environment. For a natural application scenario, it provides a no-regret algorithm. Together, the results address both computing contracts with approximate responders and learning to choose contracts when the relevant environment must be discovered through interaction.
summary.tldr: Optimal contracts remain efficiently computable in the studied hidden-action setting even when agents choose approximately optimal responses.

title: Contract Design Under Approximate Best Responses

abstract: Unsupervised pre-training and transfer learning are commonly used techniques to initialize training algorithms for neural networks, particularly in settings with limited labeled data. In this paper, we study the effects of unsupervised pre-training and transfer learning on the sample complexity of high-dimensional supervised learning. Specifically, we consider the problem of training a single-layer neural network via online stochastic gradient descent. We establish that pre-training and transfer learning (under concept shift) reduce sample complexity by polynomial factors (in the dimension) under very general assumptions. We also uncover some surprising settings where pre-training grants exponential improvement over random initialization in terms of sample complexity.

paragraphs: Pre-training and transfer learning are commonly used to give a neural network a useful starting point, especially when labeled data are limited. This paper studies their benefit through sample complexity: how many samples are needed for supervised learning. It focuses on high-dimensional problems, where that requirement can depend strongly on the input dimension.

The theoretical setting involves training a single-layer neural network with online stochastic gradient descent. Within this framework, the authors establish that unsupervised pre-training and transfer learning under concept shift can reduce sample complexity by factors polynomial in the dimension. They state that these reductions hold under very general assumptions in their analyzed setting.

The paper also identifies particular settings where pre-training improves sample complexity exponentially compared with random initialization. That stronger result is specific to those settings, rather than a universal promise for pre-training. Together, the findings give a mathematical account of how initialization can change data requirements. The contribution concerns provable learning efficiency in the studied model, connecting a practical training choice to the number of examples required.
summary.tldr: For the studied single-layer networks, pre-training and transfer learning provably reduce sample needs, with exponential benefits in some settings.

title: Provable Benefits of Unsupervised Pre-training and Transfer Learning via Single-Index Models

abstract: We address the problem of estimating heterogeneous treatment effects in panel data, adopting the popular Difference-in-Differences (DiD) framework under the conditional parallel trends assumption. We propose a novel doubly robust meta-learner for the Conditional Average Treatment Effect on the Treated (CATT), reducing the estimation to a convex risk minimization problem involving a set of auxiliary models. Our framework allows for the flexible estimation of the CATT, when conditioning on any subset of variables of interest using generic machine learning. Leveraging Neyman orthogonality, our proposed approach is robust to estimation errors in the auxiliary models. As a generalization to our main result, we develop a meta-learning approach for the estimation of general conditional functionals under covariate shift. We also provide an extension to the instrumented DiD setting with non-compliance. Empirical results demonstrate the superiority of our approach over existing baselines.

paragraphs: A treatment can affect different groups differently, even when its overall average effect looks modest. This paper studies those differences using panel data within the Difference-in-Differences framework. Its target is the conditional average treatment effect among people who received the treatment. The analysis assumes conditional parallel trends: after accounting for relevant variables, the treated and comparison groups would have followed parallel trends without treatment.

The proposed meta-learner turns this estimation task into a convex risk minimization problem supported by auxiliary models. It allows generic machine learning methods to estimate effects conditional on whichever subset of variables is of interest. The approach combines double robustness with Neyman orthogonality, making its estimates less sensitive to errors in the auxiliary models.

The authors also extend the framework to general conditional quantities under covariate shift and to instrumented Difference-in-Differences with non-compliance. Their empirical results outperform existing baselines. Together, these contributions offer a flexible way to investigate variation in treatment effects while explicitly addressing errors introduced by intermediate estimation steps.
summary.tldr: A doubly robust meta-learner estimates how treatment effects vary across treated groups under conditional parallel trends.

title: A Meta-learner for Heterogeneous Effects in Difference-in-Differences

abstract: Factored Markov Decision Processes (FMDPs) offer a promising framework for overcoming the curse of dimensionality in reinforcement learning (RL) by decomposing high-dimensional MDPs into smaller and independently evolving components. Despite their potential, existing studies on FMDPs face three key limitations: reliance on perfectly factorizable models, suboptimal sample complexity guarantees for model-based algorithms, and the absence of model-free algorithms. To address these challenges, we introduce approximate factorization, which extends FMDPs to handle imperfectly factored models. Moreover, we develop a model-based algorithm and a model-free algorithm (in the form of variance-reduced Q-learning), both achieving the first near-minimax sample complexity guarantees for FMDPs. A key novelty in the design of these two algorithms is the development of a graph-coloring-based optimal synchronous sampling strategy. Numerical simulations based on the wind farm storage control problem corroborate our theoretical findings.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning becomes difficult when a decision process has many interacting dimensions. Factored Markov Decision Processes address this by decomposing a large process into smaller components that evolve independently. The paper identifies a restrictive aspect of earlier work: requiring this decomposition to be perfect can exclude models that only approximately have the desired structure.

The authors introduce approximate factorization to accommodate imperfect decompositions. They develop both a model-based algorithm and a model-free algorithm based on variance-reduced Q-learning. A shared design contribution is an optimal synchronous sampling strategy based on graph coloring. Sampling is therefore a central part of how the algorithms exploit the factored structure.

Both algorithms achieve what the authors describe as the first near-minimax sample complexity guarantees for factored Markov Decision Processes. These guarantees concern how much data learning requires relative to the best possible worst-case requirement. Simulations involving wind farm storage control corroborate the theoretical findings. The contribution combines a more flexible modeling framework with strong sampling guarantees and a model-free learning method.
summary.tldr: Approximate factorization extends factored reinforcement learning to imperfect decompositions, with model-based and model-free algorithms offering near-minimax sample guarantees.

title: Overcoming the Curse of Dimensionality in Reinforcement Learning Through Approximate Factorization

abstract: Recently, numerous cross-modal hashing (CMH) methods have been proposed, yielding remarkable progress. As a static learning paradigm, existing CMH methods often implicitly assume that all modalities are prepared before processing. However, in practice applications (such as multi-modal medical diagnosis), it is very challenging to collect paired multi-modal data simultaneously. Specifically, they are collected chronologically, forming streaming-media data (SMA). To handle this, all previous CMH methods require retraining on data from all modalities, which inevitably limits the scalability and flexibility of the model. In this paper, we propose a novel CMH paradigm named Streaming-media Hashing rEtrieval (SHE) that enables parallel training of each modality. Specifically, we first propose a knowledge library mining module (KLM) that extracts a prototype knowledge library for each modality, thereby revealing the commonality distribution of the instances from each modality. Then, we propose a knowledge library transfer module (KLT) that updates and aligns the new knowledge by utilizing the historical knowledge library, ensuring semantic consistency. Finally, to enhance intra-class semantic relevance and inter-class semantic disparity, we develop a discriminative hashing learning module (DHL). Comprehensive experiments on four benchmark datasets demonstrate the superiority of our SHE compared to 14 competitors.
originalAbstract: Recently, numerous cross-modal hashing (CMH) methods have been proposed, yielding remarkable progress. As a static learning paradigm, existing CMH methods often implicitly assume that all modalities are prepared before processing. However, in practice applications (such as multi-modal medical diagnosis), it is very challenging to collect paired multi-modal data simultaneously. Specifically, they are collected chronologically, forming streaming-media data (SMA). To handle this, all previous CMH methods require retraining on data from all modalities, which inevitably limits the scalability and flexibility of the model. In this paper, we propose a novel CMH paradigm named Streaming-media Hashing rEtrieval (SHE) that enables parallel training of each modality. Specifically, we first propose a knowledge library mining module (KLM) that extracts a prototype knowledge library for each modality, thereby revealing the commonality distribution of the instances from each modality. Then, we propose a knowledge library transfer module (KLT) that updates and aligns the new knowledge by utilizing the historical knowledge library, ensuring semantic consistency. Finally, to enhance intra-class semantic relevance and inter-class semantic disparity, we develop a discriminative hashing learning module (DHL). Comprehensive experiments on four benchmark datasets demonstrate the superiority of our SHE compared to 14 competitors.

paragraphs: Cross-modal hashing methods often assume that all data modalities are available before processing begins. In applications where paired modalities arrive at different times, that assumption creates a practical problem: incorporating new information can require retraining on all modalities. SHE introduces a streaming-media retrieval approach intended to support parallel training of individual modalities.

Its first component extracts a prototype knowledge library for each modality, summarizing common patterns among its instances. A second component uses historical libraries to update and align new knowledge, maintaining semantic consistency as information arrives. A third component learns discriminative hash representations that strengthen similarities within classes and increase differences between classes.

The authors evaluate SHE on four benchmark datasets against 14 competitors and report superior performance. The method’s central contribution is the use of explicit knowledge libraries to connect separately arriving modalities. Those libraries provide a mechanism for transferring and aligning information, while the hashing component preserves distinctions useful for retrieval. This addresses the mismatch between static multimodal training assumptions and data collection processes that unfold over time.
summary.tldr: SHE uses transferable prototype knowledge libraries to align asynchronously arriving modalities and improve cross-modal hashing retrieval.

title: SHE: Streaming-media Hashing Retrieval

abstract: Decoding visual images from brain activity has significant potential for advancing brain-computer interaction and enhancing the understanding of human perception. Recent approaches align the representation spaces of images and brain activity to enable visual decoding. In this paper, we introduce the use of human-aligned image encoders to map brain signals to images. We hypothesize that these models more effectively capture perceptual attributes associated with the rapid visual stimuli presentations commonly used in visual brain data recording experiments. Our empirical results support this hypothesis, demonstrating that this simple modification improves image retrieval accuracy by up to 21% compared to state-of-the-art methods. Comprehensive experiments confirm consistent performance improvements across diverse EEG architectures, image encoders, alignment methods, participants, and brain imaging modalities.

This paper asks whether the choice of image representation can improve that connection, especially when experiments present visual stimuli rapidly.

The authors introduce human-aligned image encoders into the decoding pipeline. Their hypothesis is that these encoders capture perceptual attributes better suited to the brain responses recorded during rapid presentations. The proposed change therefore concerns the image side of the alignment: a representation more closely matched to human perception may provide a better target for mapping brain activity.

Experiments support that hypothesis, with image retrieval accuracy improving by up to 21% over state-of-the-art methods. The authors also report consistent improvements across different EEG architectures, image encoders, alignment methods, participants, and imaging modalities. This breadth suggests that the encoder choice can benefit several decoding configurations. The stated gain concerns retrieving images from brain signals, and the 21% figure is the largest reported improvement rather than a uniform gain.
summary.tldr: Human-aligned image encoders improve visual retrieval from brain activity, with gains of up to 21% in the reported experiments.

title: Human-Aligned Image Models Improve Visual Decoding from the Brain

abstract: LLMs are typically trained to answer user questions or follow instructions similarly to how human experts respond. However, in the standard alignment framework they lack the basic ability of explicit thinking before answering. Thinking is important for complex questions that require reasoning and planning – but can be applied to any task. We propose a training method for equipping existing LLMs with such thinking abilities for general instruction following without use of additional human data. We achieve this by an iterative search and optimization procedure that explores the space of possible thought generations, allowing the model to learn how to think without direct supervision. For each instruction, the thought candidates are scored using a judge model to evaluate their responses only, and then optimized via preference optimization. We show that this procedure leads to superior performance on AlpacaEval and Arena-Hard, and shows gains from thinking on non-reasoning categories such as marketing, health and general knowledge, in addition to more traditional reasoning & problem-solving tasks.

paragraphs: This paper develops a way to train existing language models to generate explicit thoughts before answering general instructions. The objective extends beyond tasks conventionally labeled as reasoning problems. The method uses no additional human data and does not require direct supervision specifying what the thought process should contain.

Training alternates between searching for candidate thought generations and optimizing the model. For each instruction, a judge model evaluates the resulting responses only. Those response evaluations score the thought candidates, which then guide preference optimization. The learning signal therefore comes from the quality of the final answer rather than direct judgments of the intermediate thought text.

The researchers report superior performance on AlpacaEval and Arena-Hard. They also find gains in marketing, health, and general knowledge, alongside reasoning and problem-solving tasks. These results support the usefulness of learned thought generation across several instruction categories in the evaluated setting. The contribution is a training procedure that searches for helpful intermediate generation and reinforces it through answer-level feedback.
summary.tldr: Iterative search and preference optimization teach language models useful thought generation using feedback on final responses without additional human data.

title: Thinking LLMs: General Instruction Following with Thought Generation

abstract: Class-incremental learning (CIL) enables models to learn new classes continually without forgetting previously acquired knowledge. Multi-label CIL (MLCIL) extends CIL to a real-world scenario where each sample may belong to multiple classes, introducing several challenges: label absence, which leads to incomplete historical information due to missing labels, and class imbalance, which results in the model bias toward majority classes. To address these challenges, we propose Label-Augmented Analytic Adaptation (L3A), an exemplar-free approach without storing past samples. L3A integrates two key modules. The pseudo-label (PL) module implements label augmentation by generating pseudo-labels for current phase samples, addressing the label absence problem. The weighted analytic classifier (WAC) derives a closed-form solution for neural networks. It introduces sample-specific weights to adaptively balance the class contribution and mitigate class imbalance. Experiments on MS-COCO and PASCAL VOC datasets demonstrate that L3A outperforms existing methods in MLCIL tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/scut-zx/L3A.

paragraphs: Multi-label class-incremental learning asks a model to learn new classes over time when each sample can belong to several classes. Missing labels leave the learner with incomplete historical information, while uneven class frequencies can bias it toward common classes. L3A addresses both problems without keeping past samples, making its approach exemplar-free.

The method combines label augmentation with a weighted analytic classifier. Its pseudo-label module generates additional labels for samples in the current learning phase to address label absence. The classifier uses a closed-form solution and introduces weights specific to individual samples. Those weights adapt the contribution of different classes, aiming to reduce the influence of class imbalance on learning.

Experiments on MS-COCO and PASCAL VOC show that L3A outperforms existing methods on the evaluated multi-label incremental tasks. The two modules address complementary sources of difficulty: incomplete supervision and unequal class representation. The results support combining these mechanisms when extending a model’s class knowledge without storing earlier examples.
summary.tldr: L3A combines pseudo-labels and a weighted closed-form classifier to improve multi-label incremental learning without storing past samples.

title: L3A: Label-Augmented Analytic Adaptation for Multi-Label Class Incremental Learning

abstract: Ensuring the safety and harmlessness of Large Language Models (LLMs) has become equally critical as their performance in applications. However, existing safety alignment methods typically suffer from safety-performance trade-offs and susceptibility to jailbreak attacks, primarily due to their reliance on direct refusals for malicious queries. In this paper, we propose STAIR, a novel framework that integrates SafeTy Alignment with Itrospective Reasoning. We enable LLMs to identify safety risks through step-by-step analysis by self-improving chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning with safety awareness. STAIR first equips the model with a structured reasoning capability and then advances safety alignment via iterative preference optimization on step-level reasoning data generated using our newly proposed Safety-Informed Monte Carlo Tree Search (SI-MCTS). Specifically, we design a theoretically grounded reward for outcome evaluation to seek balance between helpfulness and safety. We further train a process reward model on this data to guide test-time searches for improved responses. Extensive experiments show that STAIR effectively mitigates harmful outputs while better preserving helpfulness, compared to instinctive alignment strategies. With test-time scaling, STAIR achieves a safety performance comparable to Claude-3.5 against popular jailbreak attacks. We have open-sourced our code, datasets and models at https://github.com/thu-ml/STAIR.

STAIR addresses these problems by teaching models to analyze safety risks through structured, step-by-step reasoning. The framework makes safety awareness part of the reasoning process used to produce a response.

With additional test-time search, its safety performance is comparable to Claude-3.5 against popular jailbreak attacks. This comparison is specifically tied to test-time scaling and the evaluated attacks. The results support combining safety-aware training with guided reasoning during response generation.
summary.tldr: STAIR trains safety-aware reasoning and guides test-time search to reduce harmful responses while better preserving helpfulness.

title: STAIR: Improving Safety Alignment with Introspective Reasoning

abstract: We investigate learning approximate Nash equilibrium (NE) policy profiles in two-player zero-sum imperfect information extensive-form games (IIEFGs) with last-iterate convergence guarantees. Existing algorithms either rely on full-information feedback or provide only asymptotic convergence rates. In contrast, we focus on the bandit feedback setting, where players receive feedback solely from the rewards associated with the experienced information set and action pairs in each episode. Our proposed algorithm employs a negentropy regularizer weighted by a "virtual transition" over the information set-action space to facilitate an efficient approximate policy update. Through a carefully designed virtual transition and leveraging the entropy regularization technique, we demonstrate finite-time last-iterate convergence to the NE with a rate of $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(k^{-\frac{1}{8}})$ under bandit feedback in each episode $k$. Empirical evaluations across various IIEFG instances show its competitive performance compared to baseline methods.

paragraphs: This paper studies how two players can learn approximate Nash equilibrium strategies in zero-sum games with hidden information and sequential decisions. Feedback is limited to rewards for the information-set and action pairs actually experienced in each episode. The learner therefore cannot directly inspect the outcomes of all alternatives when updating its strategy.

The algorithm combines entropy regularization with a specially designed virtual transition over information-set and action pairs. That virtual transition weights a negentropy regularizer and supports efficient approximate policy updates. The construction is used to establish convergence of the latest policy profile itself, giving a guarantee about the strategies currently produced by learning.

The authors prove a finite-time last-iterate convergence rate of approximately k to the power of negative one eighth, with logarithmic factors suppressed, where k counts episodes. The guarantee applies under the stated bandit feedback setting. Experiments on several imperfect-information games show competitive performance against baselines. The main contribution is a quantitative convergence guarantee under restricted feedback, supplemented by empirical evidence of practical competitiveness.
summary.tldr: An entropy-regularized algorithm provides finite-time convergence of current strategies toward Nash equilibrium in two-player zero-sum games with bandit feedback.

title: Learning Imperfect Information Extensive-form Games with Last-iterate Convergence under Bandit Feedback

abstract: Dual-encoder vision-language models (VLMs) expose a similarity interface that enables zero-shot retrieval but fails compositional constraints: queries like “umbrella and no person” retrieve images containing both, even when concept detection is reliable. We trace this to an interface-level Bag-of-Concepts effect, where similarity scores approximate mean pooling of concept evidence regardless of operators. Although operator-dependent signals exist in text embeddings, they are too weak or misaligned to affect rankings. Fine-tuning does not reliably resolve this failure because the dominant bottleneck is how similarity aggregates evidence rather than what encoders represent. We propose factored inference, which separates evidence extraction from constraint execution, and introduce LCSE (Logic-Constrained Score Editing), a training-free method that executes constraints externally using concept scores from frozen encoders. We also introduce FACTOR-Bench, where LCSE achieves 85.5% accuracy versus 73.2% for the best fine-tuned baseline, 90.7% when applied to SigLIP 2, and improves NegBench COCO MCQ accuracy from 27.2% to 65.2% while preserving retrieval performance.

paragraphs: A vision-language model can recognize individual concepts yet mishandle a request such as finding an umbrella with no person present. This paper traces that failure to the similarity interface: scores tend to pool evidence for concepts without adequately enforcing the operators connecting them. Signals about those operators exist in text embeddings but are too weak or misaligned to reliably change rankings.

The proposed factored inference approach separates obtaining concept evidence from executing constraints. Its LCSE method uses concept scores from frozen encoders and applies the constraints externally, requiring no training. This targets the aggregation bottleneck that the authors find fine-tuning does not reliably resolve.

The results show that changing how existing concept evidence is used can substantially improve compliance with compositional queries.
summary.tldr: LCSE improves compositional image retrieval by extracting concept scores from frozen encoders and enforcing logical constraints separately.

title: Similarity Is Not Logic: Factored Inference for Dual-Encoder Vision-Language Models

abstract: We introduce test prediction variance (TPV)—the first-order sensitivity of a trained model’s outputs to parameter perturbations—as a unifying framework for analyzing post-training robustness. TPV’s trace form $\mathrm{Tr}(H_{\mathrm{eff}}C)$ separates the geometry of the trained model $H_{\mathrm{eff}}$ from the perturbation covariance $C$, placing SGD noise, label noise, quantization, and pruning under a single lens. The resulting expressions recover the wide-minima hypothesis for SGD and quantization noise, and yield a distinct Jacobian-spectral characterization for label noise connecting label-noise TPV with benign overfitting in nonlinear networks. Theoretically, we prove that training-set TPV converges to its test-set counterpart in the overparameterized limit, irrespective of generalization performance, providing the first result that prediction variance under local parameter perturbations can be inferred from training inputs alone. Empirically, this stability holds far more broadly, including at very low widths. Further, TPV correlates well with test loss, enabling practical applications: JBR, a label-free pruning criterion derived from TPV geometry matching state-of-the-art baselines; and training-set based model selection signal for in-distribution and transfer learning scenarios. https://github.com/devansharpit/TPV/tree/main

paragraphs: Test prediction variance, or TPV, measures how a trained model’s outputs respond to small parameter perturbations at first order. The paper expresses it through a trace that separates model geometry from perturbation covariance. This provides one framework for studying effects associated with SGD noise, label noise, quantization, and pruning.

The analysis recovers the wide-minima view for SGD and quantization noise, while label noise leads to a distinct characterization based on Jacobian spectra and a connection to benign overfitting. The authors also prove that training-input TPV approaches test-input TPV in the overparameterized limit, irrespective of generalization performance. Thus, estimating local prediction sensitivity from training inputs need not depend on good generalization.

The authors use it to derive JBR, a label-free pruning criterion matching state-of-the-art baselines, and a training-set model-selection signal for both in-distribution and transfer settings. These applications turn perturbation geometry into practical information for post-training decisions.
summary.tldr: TPV unifies local parameter-perturbation sensitivity and supports training-input estimates useful for pruning and model selection.

title: TPV: Parameter Perturbations Through the Lens of Test Prediction Variance

abstract: The learning rate in stochastic gradient methods is a critical hyperparameter that is notoriously costly to tune via standard grid search, especially for training modern large-scale models with billions of parameters. We identify a theoretical advantage of learning rate annealing schemes that decay the learning rate to zero at a polynomial rate, such as the widely-used cosine schedule, by demonstrating their increased robustness to initial parameter misspecification due to a coarse grid search. We present an analysis in a stochastic convex optimization setup demonstrating that the convergence rate of stochastic gradient descent with annealed schedules depends sublinearly on the multiplicative misspecification factor $\rho$ (i.e., the grid resolution), achieving a rate of $O(\rho^{1/(2p+1)}/\sqrt{T})$ where $p$ is the degree of polynomial decay and $T$ is the number of steps. This is in contrast to the $O(\rho/\sqrt{T})$ rate obtained under the inverse-square-root and fixed stepsize schedules, which depend linearly on $\rho$. Experiments confirm the increased robustness compared to tuning with a fixed stepsize, that has significant implications for the computational overhead of hyperparameter search in practical training scenarios.

paragraphs: Choosing a learning rate by grid search can require many costly training runs. A coarse search saves computation but may choose an initial rate far from the best value. This paper asks how strongly that mistake affects convergence, and identifies an advantage of schedules that decay the learning rate to zero at a polynomial rate.

In stochastic convex optimization, the authors show that annealed stochastic gradient descent has a convergence rate of O(rho^(1/(2p+1))/sqrt(T)). Here rho measures multiplicative misspecification, p is the polynomial decay degree, and T is the number of steps. The dependence on rho is sublinear, compared with the linear dependence in the O(rho/sqrt(T)) rates for fixed and inverse-square-root schedules.

This means the analyzed annealing schedules are less sensitive to coarse tuning of the initial learning rate. Experiments also confirm increased robustness compared with fixed-step tuning. The theoretical guarantee belongs to the stochastic convex setting, while the empirical results support the practical relevance of reducing the computational burden of hyperparameter search.
summary.tldr: Learning-rate schedules that decay to zero can reduce sensitivity to coarse tuning, with a sublinear misspecification penalty in the paper’s convex analysis.

title: Learning Rate Annealing Improves Tuning Robustness in Stochastic Optimization

abstract: Learning algorithms can be significantly improved by routing complex or uncertain inputs to specialized experts, balancing accuracy with computational cost. This approach, known as learning to defer, is essential in domains like natural language generation, medical diagnosis, and computer vision, where an effective deferral can reduce errors at low extra resource consumption. However, the two-stage learning to defer setting, which leverages existing predictors such as a collection of LLMs or other classifiers, often faces challenges due to an expert imbalance problem. This imbalance can lead to suboptimal performance, with deferral algorithms favoring the majority expert. We present a comprehensive study of two-stage learning to defer in expert imbalance settings. We cast the deferral loss optimization as a novel cost-sensitive learning problem over the input-expert domain. We derive new margin-based loss functions and guarantees tailored to this setting, and develop novel algorithms for cost-sensitive learning. Leveraging these results, we design principled deferral algorithms, MILD (Margin-based Imbalanced Learning to Defer), specifically suited for expert imbalance settings. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, showing clear improvements over existing baselines on both image classification and real-world Large Language Model (LLM) routing tasks.

paragraphs: Learning to defer routes inputs to specialized predictors, seeking better accuracy at an acceptable computational cost. In the two-stage setting, those predictors already exist and the main task is learning which one to use. Expert imbalance can bias this routing process toward a majority expert and lead to poorer overall decisions.

This paper recasts deferral-loss optimization as cost-sensitive learning over input–expert pairs. That formulation makes the choice of expert part of the learning domain and allows the training objective to account for differing decision costs. The authors derive margin-based losses, associated guarantees, and new cost-sensitive learning algorithms tailored to the imbalance problem.

These results lead to MILD, a family of deferral algorithms designed specifically for imbalanced expert settings. Experiments on image classification and real-world language-model routing report clear improvements over existing baselines. The contribution combines a formal reformulation with practical routing methods, showing that explicitly addressing expert imbalance can improve how existing predictors are used rather than requiring those predictors to be trained again.
summary.tldr: MILD reformulates expert routing as cost-sensitive learning to improve deferral when expert imbalance biases existing methods.

title: Optimized Deferral for Imbalanced Settings

abstract: Training deep learning models on single-cell datasets with hundreds of millions of cells requires loading data from disk, as these datasets exceed available memory. While random sampling provides the data diversity needed for effective training, it is prohibitively slow due to the random access pattern overhead, whereas sequential streaming achieves high throughput but introduces biases that degrade model performance. We present scDataset, a PyTorch data loader that enables efficient training from on-disk data with seamless integration across diverse storage formats. Our approach combines block sampling and batched fetching to achieve quasi-random sampling that balances I/O efficiency with minibatch diversity. On Tahoe-100M, a dataset of 100 million cells, scDataset achieves more than two orders of magnitude speedup compared to true random sampling while working directly with AnnData files. We provide theoretical bounds on minibatch diversity and empirically show that scDataset matches the performance of true random sampling across multiple classification tasks and model architectures.

paragraphs: Single-cell datasets can contain hundreds of millions of cells, making it necessary to load training data from disk. Fully random access provides diverse minibatches but incurs substantial storage-access overhead. Reading examples sequentially is faster, yet the resulting sampling biases can harm model performance. scDataset addresses this tension between loading efficiency and training-data diversity.

The method is a PyTorch data loader that combines block sampling with batched fetching. This produces quasi-random sampling: access is organized for efficient input/output while retaining diversity within training minibatches. The loader works across multiple storage formats, and the authors provide theoretical bounds on minibatch diversity to characterize the statistical side of this design.

On the 100-million-cell Tahoe-100M dataset, scDataset delivers more than a hundredfold speedup over true random sampling while reading AnnData files directly. Across multiple classification tasks and model architectures, it matches the predictive performance achieved with true random sampling. These results show that carefully organizing disk access can substantially accelerate data loading without losing the training benefits of diverse minibatches in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: scDataset combines block sampling and batched reads to accelerate single-cell data loading while matching random-sampling classification performance.

title: scDataset: Scalable Data Loading for Deep Learning on Large-Scale Single-Cell Omics

abstract: Task-vector–based model merging enables low-cost, training-free multi-task learning for large language models, but suffers from severe performance degradation due to task conflict. Prior mitigation strategies largely rely on validation data for costly hyperparameter tuning, limiting both interpretability and practicality. We therefore propose OPIC, an evolutionary optimization–based model merging framework. Our preliminary experiments reveal that the degradation of In-Context Learning (ICL) capabilities is a primary driver of task conflict. Motivated by this insight, we formulate model merging as an optimization problem with ICL preservation as the objective. OPIC introduces a hierarchical refinement operators and optimizes it using self-generated data, effectively eliminating the reliance on external validation sets. Experimental results demonstrate that OPIC achieves an average performance retention of 80.73%, outperforming SOTA methods and improving by up to 11.1% over recent validation-free approaches. In addition, OPIC is compatible with existing merging pipelines, offering a new alternative solution for deploying without validation dependencies. Code is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/OPIC-CFFE.

paragraphs: Task-vector merging combines specialized language models at low cost, but their capabilities can interfere and degrade the merged model. Existing mitigation often depends on expensive tuning against validation data. OPIC approaches the problem through in-context learning: the ability to use information supplied in the prompt. Preliminary experiments identify deterioration of this capability as a primary driver of task conflict.

The framework turns model merging into an evolutionary optimization problem whose objective is preserving in-context capability. It introduces hierarchical refinement operators and uses self-generated data to guide optimization. This removes dependence on external validation sets, connecting the search criterion to a capability the authors found important for successful merging.

Experiments report average performance retention of 80.73%, results above state-of-the-art methods, and improvements of up to 11.1% over recent validation-free approaches. OPIC is also compatible with existing merging pipelines. These findings support in-context preservation as a useful optimization target in the evaluated settings, with the practical advantage of performing the search without an external validation dataset.
summary.tldr: OPIC uses evolutionary optimization and self-generated data to preserve in-context learning capability during language-model merging without external validation sets.

title: OPIC: Enhancing Language Model Merging via Optimizing In-Context Capability

abstract: Large Language Models(LLMs) have revolutionized text generation and multimodal perception, but their capabilities in 3D content generation remain underexplored. Existing methods compromise by producing either low-resolution meshes or coarse structural proxies, failing to capture fine-grained geometry natively. In this paper, we propose CG-MLLM, a novel Multi-modal Large Language Model (MLLM) capable of 3D captioning and high-resolution 3D generation in a single framework. Leveraging the Mixture-of-Transformer architecture, CG-MLLM decouples disparate modeling needs, where the Token-level Autoregressive (TokenAR) Transformer handles token-level content, and the Block-level Autoregressive (BlockAR) Transformer handles block-level content. By integrating a pre-trained vision-language backbone with a specialized 3D VAE latent space, CG-MLLM facilitates long-context interactions between standard tokens and spatial blocks within a single integrated architecture. Experimental results show that CG-MLLM significantly outperforms existing MLLMs in generating high-fidelity 3D objects, effectively bringing high-resolution 3D content creation into the mainstream LLM paradigm.

The challenge is to accommodate spatial content alongside the tokens handled by language-based models.

The architecture separates these modeling responsibilities through a Mixture-of-Transformer design. A TokenAR transformer handles token-level content, while a BlockAR transformer handles content organized into blocks. The authors report that CG-MLLM significantly outperforms existing multimodal language models at generating high-fidelity 3D objects. The architectural significance is the combination of shared interaction and specialized processing: language and spatial representations can communicate, while different transformer components handle their respective forms of content. This supports both describing 3D content and generating detailed objects within the same framework.
summary.tldr: CG-MLLM combines token-level and block-level transformers to support 3D captioning and high-resolution generation in one multimodal model.

title: CG-MLLM: Captioning and Generating 3D content via Multi-modal Large Language Models

abstract: Asynchronous reinforcement learning has become increasingly central to scaling LLM post-training, delivering major throughput gains by decoupling rollout generation from policy updates. However, widely used policy-gradient objectives such as REINFORCE and GRPO suffer under high asynchrony: stale rollouts produce heavy-tailed importance weights, so a small number of trajectories dominate updates and the policy-gradient estimator becomes markedly higher variance. Through systematic analysis on math, reasoning, and tool-use benchmarks, we establish that this increasing variance is reliably predicted by collapsing effective sample size (ESS), which prior stabilization methods largely fail to address. Motivated by this diagnosis, we introduce Variance Controlled Policy Optimization (VCPO), a method that (i) dynamically scales the learning rate with ESS to dampen unreliable updates and (ii) applies a closed-form minimum-variance baseline for off-policy settings, without a critic model and adding minimal overhead. Empirically, across math and general reasoning benchmarks, this enables robustly stable asynchronous training compared to previous stabilization and algorithmic methods, even in highly off-policy regimes (128 steps off-policy). In a long-horizon, tool-use task, VCPO matches synchronous performance while delivering a 2.5$\times$ speedup in training time. Code is available at: https://github.com/mit-han-lab/vcpo

paragraphs: Asynchronous reinforcement learning increases training throughput by generating rollouts separately from policy updates. The difficulty is that a rollout may come from an older policy. Importance weights used to account for this difference can become heavy-tailed, allowing a few trajectories to dominate the update and sharply increasing policy-gradient variance.

The paper finds that collapsing effective sample size reliably predicts this problem across math, reasoning, and tool-use analyses. VCPO responds in two ways: it adjusts the learning rate according to effective sample size, damping less reliable updates, and uses a closed-form minimum-variance baseline for the off-policy setting. This adds little overhead and does not require a separate critic model.

Experiments report stable asynchronous training across math and general reasoning benchmarks, including rollouts 128 policy steps out of date. In a long-horizon tool-use task, VCPO matches synchronous training performance while reducing training time by a factor of 2.5. The results connect statistical reliability controls with the practical throughput benefits of asynchronous training.
summary.tldr: VCPO stabilizes asynchronous language-model reinforcement learning by controlling update variance using effective sample size and an off-policy baseline.

title: Stable Asynchrony: Variance-Controlled Off-Policy RL for LLMs

abstract: We study how individual training examples shape the internal computation of looped transformers, where a shared block is applied for $\tau$ recurrent iterations to enable latent reasoning. Existing training-data influence estimators such as TracIn yield a single scalar score that aggregates over all loop iterations, obscuring when during the recurrent computation a training example matters. We introduce Step-Decomposed Influence (SDI), which decomposes TracIn into a length-$\tau$ influence trajectory by unrolling the recurrent computation graph and attributing influence to specific loop iterations. To make SDI practical at transformer scale, we propose a TensorSketch implementation that never materialises per-example gradients. Experiments on looped GPT-style models and algorithmic reasoning tasks show that SDI scales excellently, matches full-gradient baselines with low error and supports a broad range of data attribution and interpretability tasks with per-step insights into the latent reasoning process.

paragraphs: Looped transformers repeatedly apply a shared block, allowing computation to unfold over several internal iterations. A training example may influence different parts of that process differently. Standard TracIn attribution combines those effects into one scalar score, hiding when the example matters during the model’s recurrent computation.

Step-Decomposed Influence separates that aggregate into an influence trajectory with one entry per loop iteration. It does so by unrolling the recurrent computation graph and assigning influence to specific iterations. The resulting trajectory retains the temporal structure of the internal computation, giving a more detailed view of how individual training examples shape latent reasoning.

To make the method practical for transformers, the authors introduce a TensorSketch implementation that avoids materializing per-example gradients. Experiments on looped GPT-style models and algorithmic reasoning tasks report strong scalability and low error relative to full-gradient baselines. The method also supports several attribution and interpretability tasks. Its contribution is therefore both analytical resolution across reasoning steps and a computational approach that makes that finer resolution feasible at transformer scale.
summary.tldr: SDI decomposes training-data influence across a looped transformer’s iterations, using TensorSketch to avoid storing per-example gradients.

title: Step-Resolved Data Attribution for Looped Transformers

abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have achieved remarkable progress, yet the object hallucination remains a critical challenge for reliable deployment. In this paper, we present an in-depth analysis of instruction token embeddings and reveal that they implicitly encode visual information while effectively filtering erroneous information introduced by misleading visual embeddings. Building on this insight, we propose the Instruction Lens Score (InsLen), which combines a Calibrated Local Score with a Context Consistency Score that measures context consistency of the object tokens. The proposed approach serves as a plug-and-play object hallucination detector without relying on auxiliary models or additional training. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks and diverse MLLM architectures demonstrate that InsLen consistently outperforms existing hallucination detection methods, highlighting its effectiveness and robustness. The code will be publicly available.

paragraphs: Multimodal language models can mention objects that are not supported by an image. This paper investigates a source of evidence for detecting those hallucinations: the model’s internal representations of instruction tokens. The authors find that these representations carry visual information while filtering erroneous information introduced by misleading visual embeddings.

They use this observation to build the Instruction Lens Score, or InsLen. The detector combines a Calibrated Local Score with a Context Consistency Score that evaluates the contextual consistency of object tokens. This gives the method a way to assess object mentions using information already present inside the multimodal model.

InsLen operates as a plug-and-play detector without additional training or auxiliary models. That design makes the analysis of instruction representations directly useful for checking generated object claims. Across multiple benchmarks and diverse multimodal model architectures, the reported experiments show consistent improvements over existing hallucination detectors. The findings support the usefulness of instruction-token information for detection across the tested settings.
summary.tldr: InsLen detects object hallucinations using instruction-token representations and contextual consistency, without extra training or auxiliary models.

title: Instruction Lens Score: Your Instruction Contributes a Powerful Object Hallucination Detector for Multimodal Large Language Models

abstract: Despite the remarkable fidelity of generative models, they frequently suffer from mode collapse. Existing strategies for enhancing diversity predominantly focus on intervening during the generation trajectory. We identify a critical oversight that the standard Gaussian initialization often causes trajectories to collapse into dominant modes because it is agnostic to the guidance potential landscape. In this work, we formulate selecting the initial noise from a guidance potential posterior, which effectively re-weights the prior towards diversity-rich regions. To sample from this distribution efficiently, we introduce Diversity-inducing Initialization (DivIn), which leverages Langevin dynamics to actively navigate the initialization landscape, steering initial noise away from collapsing regions while anchoring them to the valid data manifold. Our method serves as an inference-time diversity enhancement compatible with both diffusion and flow matching models. Extensive experiments show that DivIn exhibits a superior performance in both class-to-image and text-to-image scenarios. Furthermore, we highlight that as DivIn is orthogonal to trajectory-based methods, combining them significantly expands the diversity-quality Pareto frontier beyond what either achieves in isolation.

paragraphs: Image generators can produce high-quality outputs yet repeatedly favor a narrow set of possibilities. This paper identifies the starting noise as a source of that limited diversity: standard Gaussian initialization ignores the guidance landscape and can send generation trajectories toward dominant modes. The authors therefore make initialization itself the target of intervention.

They formulate a guidance potential posterior that reweights the noise prior toward regions associated with greater diversity. Diversity-inducing Initialization, or DivIn, samples this distribution using Langevin dynamics. It actively moves starting noise away from regions associated with collapse while keeping it anchored to the valid data manifold. The method operates at inference time and supports both diffusion and flow matching models.

Experiments in class-conditioned and text-conditioned image generation show superior performance. DivIn can also be combined with methods that intervene along the generation trajectory. The authors report that this combination substantially expands the achievable diversity-quality frontier, supporting initialization as a complementary place to improve the range of generated images.
summary.tldr: DivIn improves image diversity by selecting starting noise using the guidance landscape and complements methods that modify generation trajectories.

title: Initialization is Half the Battle: Generating Diverse Images from a Guidance Potential Posterior

abstract: Tabular foundation models, exemplified by TabPFN, perform prediction via in-context learning, inferring test labels directly from labeled training examples. They have demonstrated competitive performance, particularly on small-to-medium datasets. However, recent tabular foundation models often improve accuracy with increasingly complex architectures, incurring higher inference cost and limiting practical deployment. In this work, we revisit the original TabPFN design and show that a lightweight row-wise attention–only backbone can remain highly competitive with two simple enhancements: a gated attention stabilization mechanism and a small set of learnable register tokens that provide global context and improve pretraining quality. The resulting model, TabSwift, supports both classification and regression, and is competitive with stronger tabular foundation models (e.g., TabPFN v2 and TabICL) while being more efficient at inference. For latency-sensitive serving, we further introduce an adaptive layer-wise early-exit mechanism that dynamically adjusts inference depth per sample. Overall, TabSwift enables efficient and anytime tabular in-context learning for practical deployments.

paragraphs: Tabular foundation models predict test labels directly from labeled examples supplied in context. They can perform competitively on small-to-medium datasets, but increasingly complex architectures raise inference costs. TabSwift revisits the original TabPFN design to investigate how much performance a simpler backbone can retain with a small number of targeted enhancements.

The model uses only row-wise attention in its backbone. A gating mechanism stabilizes attention, while a small collection of learned register tokens supplies global context and improves pretraining quality. These additions support both classification and regression while keeping the central architecture lightweight. The authors report competitive performance against stronger models such as TabPFN v2 and TabICL, with more efficient inference.

For applications where response time matters, TabSwift also introduces adaptive early exit across layers. This adjusts inference depth separately for each sample, making computation responsive to the prediction being processed. Together, the compact architecture and variable-depth inference support efficient, anytime tabular prediction, with the reported results showing that architectural complexity is not required for competitive performance in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: TabSwift combines a lightweight row-attention backbone with stabilization, global-context tokens, and adaptive early exit for efficient tabular prediction.

title: TabSwift: An Efficient Tabular Foundation Model with Row-Wise Attention

abstract: Current 3D spatial reasoning methods face a fundamental trade-off: neuro-symbolic 3D (NS3D) concept learners achieve interpretable reasoning through compositional programs but are constrained to closed-set concept vocabularies and simple programs; end-to-end 3D multi-modal LLMs (3D MLLMs) could handle complex natural language and open-vocabulary concepts but suffer from black-box reasoning without explicit spatial verification. We introduce APEIRIA, a neuro-symbolic 3D MLLM to bridge two paradigms by distilling symbolic reasoning patterns into MLLMs with natural language chain-of-thought. Our three-stage curriculum progressively builds reasoning capabilities: a) 3D perception alignment grounds object visual-geometric features to the LLM, b) CoT-SFT teaches query decomposition and stepwise verification from symbolic program traces, and c) CoT-RL extends reasoning patterns to open-set concepts and deeply nested instructions. By transferring reasoning patterns rather than concept-specific knowledge, APEIRIA preserves key NS3D virtues: transparent reasoning and modular interchangeability of planning and perception components. Evaluations on grounding, question answering, and captioning show that APEIRIA surpasses prior NS3D methods and matches state-of-the-art 3D MLLMs on 3D spatial reasoning datasets, unifying symbolic methods’ systematic reasoning with MLLMs’ flexibility. Code is available at https://github.com/oceanflowlab/APEIRIA.

Neuro-symbolic systems use compositional programs that make their reasoning interpretable, but are restricted by fixed concept vocabularies and simple programs. Multimodal language models offer more flexible language handling, yet lack explicit spatial verification. APEIRIA aims to combine systematic spatial reasoning with this linguistic flexibility.

Training proceeds through three stages. First, perception alignment connects object appearance and geometry to the language model. Next, supervised training on symbolic program traces teaches it to break down queries and verify intermediate steps using natural-language reasoning. Finally, reinforcement learning extends those patterns to open-set concepts and more deeply nested instructions. The intended transfer is of reasoning procedures rather than knowledge tied to individual concepts.

The resulting system retains transparent reasoning and interchangeable planning and perception components, according to the paper. Evaluations cover grounding, question answering, and captioning. APEIRIA surpasses earlier neuro-symbolic methods and matches leading 3D multimodal language models on the evaluated spatial reasoning datasets. These results support using symbolic traces as a training resource for flexible models while preserving useful structure in how they reason.
summary.tldr: APEIRIA teaches 3D multimodal language models reusable symbolic reasoning patterns through a staged training curriculum.

title: Distilling Neuro-Symbolic Programs into 3D Multi-modal LLMs

abstract: Mean Field Variational Inference (MFVI) is widely understood to underestimate posterior variance. By analysing conjugate Bayesian linear regression, we show that this characterisation is incomplete: while MFVI underestimates the variance in parameter space, it can overestimate the predictive variance compared to the exact posterior. We show that if the MFVI posterior underestimates predictive variances in some directions, it necessarily overestimates them in others. Crucially, this overestimation occurs in directions where the training data concentrates. This leads to the surprising result that, for a test point drawn from the training distribution, MFVI’s expected predictive variance exceeds that of the exact posterior. We demonstrate a pathological case of this effect, where the MFVI posterior fails to reduce predictive variance compared to the prior on i.i.d. data. We connect these results to the Cold Posterior Effect, arguing that varying the temperature can correct this overestimation, yielding predictions closer to those of the exact posterior. We validate our theory on synthetic and real-world regression tasks.

Crucially, this overestimation occurs in directions where the training data concentrates. This leads to the surprising result that, for a test point drawn from the training distribution, MFVI’s expected predictive variance exceeds that of the exact posterior. We demonstrate a pathological case of this effect, where the MFVI posterior fails to reduce predictive variance compared to the prior on i.i.d. data. paragraphs: Mean field variational inference is commonly described as underestimating uncertainty. This paper shows that the description depends on which uncertainty is measured. In conjugate Bayesian linear regression, the approximation underestimates variance in model parameters, yet it can overestimate the variance of predictions relative to the exact posterior.

The analysis establishes a directional relationship: if predictive variance is underestimated in some directions, it must be overestimated in others. Overestimation occurs in directions where training data concentrates. Consequently, for a test point drawn from the training distribution, the approximation's expected predictive variance exceeds that of the exact posterior in the analyzed setting.

The authors also demonstrate a pathological case in which predictive variance on independent, identically distributed data does not decrease from its prior level. They connect the findings to the Cold Posterior Effect, arguing that temperature adjustment can correct overestimation and bring predictions closer to exact Bayesian results. Synthetic and real-world regression experiments validate the theory, refining how uncertainty from this approximation should be interpreted.
summary.tldr: In Bayesian linear regression, mean field inference can underestimate parameter variance while overestimating predictive variance where training data concentrates.

title: Gaussian Mean Field Variational Inference can Overestimate Predictive Variance

abstract: Existing insertion-based masked diffusion models that generate sequences by interleaving token insertion with unmasking use fixed schedules that are not dependent on the data. For structured sequences like graphs and molecules, learning data-dependent generation orders can improve generation quality by reducing uncertainty over the action space. We propose LoFlexMDM, an insertion-based masked diffusion model with learnable order dynamics that learns data-dependent insertion and unmasking rates. We generalize the discrete flow matching framework to work with variable-length sequences, propose a tractable schedule parameterization and a training objective for joint training of the generator and the target order dynamics. On De Novo and fragment-constrained molecule generation, LoFlexMDM improves sample quality over FlexMDM by up to 17.5% and 6.7%, respectively. These results show that learning the target generation order can improve insertion-based diffusion models without giving up tractable training. We open source the code at https://github.com/dhruvdcoder/LoFlexMDM.

paragraphs: Insertion-based masked diffusion generates sequences by adding positions and revealing their token contents. Existing methods use fixed schedules for these operations, regardless of the data. For structured objects such as molecules, choosing an order that reflects the developing sequence can reduce uncertainty about which action to take next.

LoFlexMDM learns data-dependent insertion and unmasking rates. To make this possible, the authors extend discrete flow matching to variable-length sequences and introduce a tractable schedule parameterization. A joint objective trains both the generator and its target order dynamics, so the sequence-building process itself becomes part of what the model learns.

On de novo molecule generation, sample quality improves over FlexMDM by up to 17.5%; on generation constrained by molecular fragments, the improvement reaches 6.7%. These are reported gains for the evaluated tasks, demonstrating that learned generation orders can help in both settings. The contribution combines that flexibility with tractable training, allowing the model to adapt when it inserts and resolves tokens.
summary.tldr: LoFlexMDM learns when to insert and unmask tokens, improving reported molecular generation quality while retaining tractable training.

title: Insertion Based Sequence Generation with Learnable Order Dynamics

abstract: Vision language models (VLMs) often generate hallucination, i.e., content that cannot be substantiated by either textual or visual inputs. Prior work primarily attributes this to over-reliance on linguistic prior knowledge rather than visual inputs. Some methods attempt to mitigate hallucination by amplifying visual token attention proportionally to their attention scores. However, these methods overlook the visual attention sink problem, where attention is frequently misallocated to task-irrelevant visual regions, and neglect cross-modal fusion balance by enhancing only visual attention without adjusting attention to the user query. This can result in amplifying incorrect areas while failing to properly interpret the user query. To address these challenges, we propose a simple yet effective method called Gaze Shift-Guided Cross-modal Fusion Enhancement (GIFT). GIFT pre-computes a holistic visual saliency map by tracking positive changes in visual attention, or "gaze shifts", during user query comprehension, and leverages this map to amplify attention to both salient visual information and the user query at each decoding step. This reduces the impact of visual attention sink, as irrelevant tokens exhibit minimal shifts, while ensuring balanced cross-modal fusion for well-integrated representation. Extensive experiments show that GIFT effectively mitigates hallucination in VLMs across both generative and classification tasks, achieving up to 20.7% improvement over greedy decoding, while maintaining general vision-language performance with low computational overhead.

However, these methods overlook the visual attention sink problem, where attention is frequently misallocated to task-irrelevant visual regions, and neglect cross-modal fusion balance by enhancing only visual attention without adjusting attention to the user query. This can result in amplifying incorrect areas while failing to properly interpret the user query. To address these challenges, we propose a simple yet effective method called Gaze Shift-Guided Cross-modal Fusion Enhancement (GIFT). This reduces the impact of visual attention sink, as irrelevant tokens exhibit minimal shifts, while ensuring balanced cross-modal fusion for well-integrated representation. Extensive experiments show that GIFT effectively mitigates hallucination in VLMs across both generative and classification tasks, achieving up to 20.7% improvement over greedy decoding, while maintaining general vision-language performance with low computational overhead.

paragraphs: A vision-language model can generate statements unsupported by its image or text inputs. Increasing attention to image tokens might seem helpful, but some image regions already attract attention despite being irrelevant. Simply amplifying existing attention can strengthen this problem. It can also leave the model paying too little attention to what the user actually asked.

GIFT instead tracks increases in visual attention while the model processes the query. These changes, described as gaze shifts, produce a visual saliency map before answer generation. During each decoding step, the method strengthens attention to both salient image information and the user query. The approach relies on the observation that irrelevant attention sinks show relatively little change during query comprehension.

Experiments cover both generative and classification tasks and report hallucination mitigation, with gains reaching 20.7% over greedy decoding. General vision-language performance is maintained with low computational overhead. The findings support using query-related changes in attention to guide visual emphasis, while treating attention to the question itself as part of the same fusion problem.
summary.tldr: GIFT uses query-driven shifts in visual attention to strengthen relevant image and text signals, reducing hallucinations with low overhead.

title: Capturing Gaze Shifts for Guidance: Cross-Modal Fusion Enhancement for VLM Hallucination Mitigation

abstract: Nash regret has recently emerged as a principled fairness-aware performance metric for stochastic multi-armed bandits, motivated by the Nash Social Welfare objective. Although this notion has been extended to linear bandits, existing results suffer from suboptimality in ambient dimension $d$, stemming from proof techniques that rely on restrictive concentration inequalities. In this work, we resolve this open problem by introducing new analytical tools that yield an order-optimal Nash regret bound in linear bandits. Beyond Nash regret, we initiate the study of $p$-means regret in linear bandits, a unifying framework that interpolates between fairness and utility objectives and strictly generalizes Nash regret. We propose a generic algorithmic framework, FairLinBandit, that works as a meta-algorithm on top of any linear bandit strategy. We instantiate this framework using two bandit algorithms: Phased Elimination and Upper Confidence Bound, and prove that both achieve sublinear $p$-means regret for the entire range of $p$. Extensive experiments on linear bandit instances generated from real-world datasets demonstrate that our methods consistently outperform the existing state-of-the-art baseline.

paragraphs: Linear bandits model repeated decisions whose expected rewards depend on action features. This paper studies fairness-aware evaluation of those decisions through Nash regret. Earlier guarantees had a suboptimal dependence on the feature dimension, which the authors attribute to restrictive concentration inequalities used in their proofs.

The authors introduce analytical tools that establish an order-optimal Nash regret bound. They also extend the objective to p-means regret, a broader family that interpolates between fairness and utility and includes Nash regret as a special case. Their FairLinBandit framework operates as a wrapper around a linear bandit strategy, separating the fairness-oriented framework from the underlying decision algorithm.

The paper instantiates this framework with Phased Elimination and Upper Confidence Bound, proving sublinear p-means regret across the entire range of p. Sublinear growth means that regret per decision decreases as the number of decisions increases. Experiments on linear bandit instances constructed from real-world datasets consistently outperform the existing state-of-the-art baseline. The contribution combines sharper theory for Nash regret with a more general way to study fairness-utility objectives.
summary.tldr: New analysis improves Nash regret guarantees, while FairLinBandit extends fairness-aware linear bandits to the broader family of p-means objectives.

title: Improved Algorithms for Nash Welfare in Linear Bandits

abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) excel at complex reasoning but suffer from inefficient reasoning, like overthinking and overshoot. These issues stem from excessive or misdirected reasoning triggered by the model’s "doubt", manifested as self-validation and exploratory extension, increasing computational cost and degrading performance. Existing efficient reasoning methods seek to regulate reasoning via internal signals or static schedules, lacking specialization in the "doubt" characteristics of LRMs. To address this, we propose a Conjunction-Guided Intervention (CGI) reasoning framework that intervenes when the model shows signs of doubt. Our key insight is that overthinking and overshoot in LRMs arise from conjunction-triggered extensions where LRMs exhibit "doubt" through transitional conjunctions, extending redundant self-validation and exploration without timely state-based correction. Building on this insight, CGI pauses reasoning at conjunction markers of doubt for external state-based feedback, adaptively extending or terminating reasoning to reduce redundancy while preserving accuracy. The feedback is generated via criteria evaluation (rationality and completeness) and comes from either human or LLM proxies. We train the target model by Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to adapt to the interactive mode. Experiments show that our framework achieves a superior balance between accuracy and reasoning length.

paragraphs: Large reasoning models can spend excessive effort checking their own answers or exploring additional directions. This paper connects such overthinking and overshoot to expressions of doubt, particularly transitional conjunctions that introduce further reasoning. The authors argue that these moments can extend redundant checking or misdirected exploration when the model receives no timely feedback about its current progress.

Conjunction-Guided Intervention pauses reasoning at these markers so an external evaluator can assess the current state. A human or another language model evaluates rationality and completeness, providing feedback that helps determine whether reasoning should continue or terminate. The target model is trained with Group Relative Policy Optimization to adapt to this interactive process. Intervention timing therefore follows observable features of the reasoning rather than a fixed schedule.

Experiments report a better balance between accuracy and reasoning length. The approach matters because it connects computation control to specific moments when the model appears inclined to extend its reasoning. External feedback can then distinguish useful continuation from unnecessary elaboration, allowing the system to reduce redundancy while seeking to preserve answer accuracy.
summary.tldr: CGI pauses reasoning at linguistic signs of doubt and uses external feedback to reduce unnecessary reasoning while preserving accuracy.

title: Intervene When It Doubts: Conjunction-Guided Interactive Reasoning

abstract: Annotating large-scale LiDAR point clouds for 3D semantic segmentation is costly and time-consuming, which motivates the use of semi-supervised learning (SemiSL). Standard LiDAR SemiSL methods typically adopt a two-step training paradigm, where pseudo-labels are separately generated from a single distillation source, either from the same or another LiDAR representation. Such supervision relies on a unique source of pseudo-labels, which can reinforce confirmation bias and propagate errors during training, ultimately limiting performance. To address this challenge, we introduce CoLLiS, a novel framework that leverages Collaborative Learning for LiDAR Semi-supervised segmentation. Unlike prior paradigms with decoupled pseudo-labeling and training phases, CoLLiS trains multiple representations collaboratively in a single step by treating them as coequal students. Each student is adaptively distilled from multiple representations, while inter-student disparities are monitored online to resolve contradictory supervision and effectively mitigate confirmation bias. Extensive experiments on three datasets demonstrate that CoLLiS consistently outperforms state-of-the-art LiDAR SemiSL methods, with particularly strong gains in low-label regimes.
