paragraphs: Labeling large LiDAR point clouds is expensive, motivating methods that learn from both labeled and unlabeled data. A common approach generates pseudo-labels from one source and then uses them for training. The problem is that errors from that source can become supervision, causing a model to reinforce its own mistaken interpretations.

CoLLiS replaces this separated process with collaborative training across multiple representations of the LiDAR data. Each representation is treated as an equal student and receives adaptive supervision from several others. The framework monitors disagreements during training and uses them to resolve contradictory guidance, reducing dependence on any single source of pseudo-labels.

This arrangement matters because collaboration affects the supervision while learning is taking place, rather than supplying a fixed set of labels beforehand. Experiments on three datasets show that CoLLiS consistently outperforms the compared state-of-the-art semi-supervised LiDAR segmentation methods. Gains are especially strong when labeled data are scarce, supporting the value of combining supervision sources in the setting where reliable human labels are most limited.
summary.tldr: CoLLiS trains multiple LiDAR representations collaboratively to reduce pseudo-label confirmation bias, with particularly strong results when labels are scarce.

title: Collaborative Learning for Semi-Supervised LiDAR Semantic Segmentation

abstract: Unified Foundation Models (UFMs), which support interleaved multimodal generation and understanding, have been proposed as a promising paradigm for reasoning about dynamic world states, yet it remains unclear whether the visual content they generate functions as grounded evidence for subsequent reasoning or merely as auxiliary output. Existing benchmarks largely evaluate generation and understanding as separate capabilities and do not test their functional dependence during reasoning. We introduce UFO, a benchmark designed to evaluate whether UFMs generate and use image and text cues as evidence for compositional multimodal reasoning. UFO spans three state-transition regimes, state determination, state reconstruction, and state augmentation, which correspond to progressively smaller transformations of the underlying world state. Our analysis reveals a significant modality gap, as models often achieve high prediction accuracy even when the generated visual cues exert limited influence on their decisions, indicating weakened evidential coupling and a reliance on textual shortcuts rather than robust cross-modal grounding.

paragraphs: A model that generates images while reasoning might appear to use those images as evidence, even if its answers mostly depend on text. This paper asks whether unified foundation models actually connect their generated visual content to later decisions. Evaluating image generation and understanding separately cannot establish that functional connection.

The authors introduce UFO, a benchmark for compositional reasoning with generated image and text cues. It covers state determination, state reconstruction, and state augmentation, ordered by progressively smaller changes to the underlying world state. These regimes provide a way to examine evidence use across different kinds of state-transition reasoning within the same evaluation framework.

The analysis reveals a substantial gap between modalities: models often predict accurately even when their generated images have little influence on the decision. The authors interpret this as weakened coupling between visual evidence and reasoning, alongside reliance on textual shortcuts. The finding makes answer accuracy alone an incomplete indicator of whether a model grounds its reasoning in both modalities.
summary.tldr: UFO finds that accurate multimodal answers can coexist with weak use of generated visual evidence.

title: Do Vision and Text Cues Exhibit Evidential Coupling? UFO: A Benchmark for Compositional Multimodal Reasoning in Unified Models

abstract: Offline black-box optimization aims to discover novel designs with high property scores using only a static dataset, a task fundamentally challenged by the out-of-distribution (OOD) extrapolation problem. Existing approaches typically bifurcate into inverse methods, which struggle with the ill-posed nature of mapping scores to designs, and forward methods, which often lack the distributional expressivity to quantify uncertainty effectively. In this work, we propose SPADE (Support-Proximity Augmented Diffusion Estimation), a novel framework that reimagines forward surrogate modeling through the lens of conditional generative modeling. SPADE models the forward likelihood $p(y|\boldsymbol{x})$ using a diffusion model, but with two critical enhancements to tailor it for optimization: (1) a Calibrated Diffusion Estimation module that enforces global consistency in statistical moments and pairwise rankings, and (2) a Support-Proximity Regularization mechanism that implicitly internalizes the data manifold constraint $p(\boldsymbol{x})$ via kNN-based density estimation. Theoretically, we prove that our regularization is first-order equivalent to maximizing a Bayesian posterior with a valid design prior. Empirically, SPADE achieves state-of-the-art performance across Design-Bench tasks and an LLM data mixture optimization benchmark. Our code is available at https://github.com/HarryYoung2018/spade.

paragraphs: Offline black-box optimization seeks high-scoring new designs using only a fixed dataset. The central difficulty is judging designs outside the observed distribution. SPADE approaches this by using a diffusion model as a forward surrogate: it models the distribution of property scores conditioned on a design, rather than directly mapping a desired score back to a design.

Two additions adapt that predictive distribution for optimization. Calibrated Diffusion Estimation enforces consistency in statistical moments and pairwise rankings. Support-Proximity Regularization uses nearest-neighbor density estimation to incorporate proximity to the observed design distribution. These mechanisms connect predicted score behavior with information about where the dataset provides support.

The theoretical analysis shows that the regularizer is first-order equivalent to maximizing a Bayesian posterior with a valid design prior. This is a local equivalence claim, rather than an unrestricted identity. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance on Design-Bench tasks and a language-model data-mixture optimization benchmark, supporting the combination of expressive forward prediction and distribution-aware regularization.
summary.tldr: SPADE combines diffusion-based score prediction with data-support regularization to improve offline design optimization.

title: Support-Proximity Augmented Diffusion Estimation for Offline Black-Box Optimization

abstract: Autonomous reasoning is among the most scientifically and economically motivating topics in AI today. Historically the purview of symbolic AI, recent advances have mainly emerged from deep probabilistic generative models. Despite immense interest and rapid progress, the generative AI community has not clearly converged on operational definitions for reasoning and often implicitly rejects the historical treatment of this topic in logic and verifiable automated reasoning. This position contends that definitional ambiguity leaves the construct validity of reasoning evaluation unverifiable, undermining quantifiable progress toward trustworthy autonomous reasoning. We also contend that this ambiguity is addressable. To that end, we provide (1) operational definitions based on a synthesis of the literature, positioning valid and sound reasoning as a learnable rule-based process; and (2) a checklist for best practices in the communication of AI reasoning research.

paragraphs: This paper argues that AI reasoning research lacks sufficiently shared operational definitions. Although recent progress has largely come from probabilistic generative models, reasoning also has a long history in logic and automated verification. The authors contend that the generative AI community often overlooks that history when deciding what counts as reasoning.

The problem affects evaluation directly. If researchers do not clearly specify the capability a test is meant to measure, they cannot verify that the test actually measures reasoning. The paper describes this as a construct-validity problem and argues that it weakens claims of measurable progress toward trustworthy autonomous reasoning. Better scores need a clear connection to the capability being claimed.

To address the ambiguity, the authors synthesize existing literature into operational definitions that frame valid and sound reasoning as a learnable process governed by rules. They also provide a checklist for communicating reasoning research. The intended contribution is a common foundation for defining capabilities, interpreting evaluations, and stating research claims with enough precision to assess them.
summary.tldr: The paper proposes rule-based operational definitions and reporting practices to make AI reasoning claims meaningfully evaluable.

abstract: We apply nonparametric hierarchical Bayesian modelling to relational learning. In a hierarchical Bayesian approach, model parameters can be “personalized”, i.e., owned by entities or relationships, and are coupled via a common prior distribution. Flexibility is added in a nonparametric hierarchical Bayesian approach, such that the learned knowledge can be truthfully represented. We apply our approach to a medical domain where we form a nonparametric hierarchical Bayesian model for relations involving hospitals, patients, procedures and diagnosis. The experiments show that the additional flexibility in a nonparametric hierarchical Bayes approach results in a more accurate model of the dependencies between procedures and diagnosis and gives significantly improved estimates of the probabilities of future procedures.

paragraphs: Relational learning models dependencies involving connected entities. This paper applies nonparametric hierarchical Bayesian modeling to that setting. Its starting point is that model parameters can belong to particular entities or relationships, giving them a personalized character, while a shared prior distribution couples those parameters. The hierarchy therefore accommodates local differences within a connected statistical model.

The nonparametric extension adds flexibility to this arrangement so that learned relationships can be represented more faithfully. The paper develops a medical application involving hospitals, patients, procedures, and diagnoses. These different kinds of entities and relationships make the setting a concrete example of why personalized parameters and shared statistical structure can both be useful.

In the reported experiments, the additional flexibility produces a more accurate model of dependencies between procedures and diagnoses. It also significantly improves estimates of the probabilities of future procedures. The findings support the value of the nonparametric hierarchical approach for this relational prediction problem: a more flexible representation of existing dependencies leads to better probability estimates in the studied application.
summary.tldr: A nonparametric hierarchical Bayesian model improves relational modeling and future-procedure probability estimates in a medical application.

abstract: In multi-task learning (MTL), multiple tasks are learnt jointly. A major assumption for this paradigm is that all those tasks are indeed related so that the joint training is appropriate and beneficial. In this paper, we study the problem of multi-task learning of shared feature representations among tasks, while simultaneously determining ``with whom'' each task should share. We formulate the problem as a mixed integer programming and provide an alternating minimization technique to solve the optimization problem of jointly identifying grouping structures and parameters. The algorithm monotonically decreases the objective function and converges to a local optimum. Compared to the standard MTL paradigm where all tasks are in a single group, our algorithm improves its performance with statistical significance for three out of the four datasets we have studied. We also demonstrate its advantage over other task grouping techniques investigated in literature.

In this paper, we study the problem of multi-task learning of shared feature representations among tasks, while simultaneously determining ``with whom'' each task should share. We formulate the problem as a mixed integer programming and provide an alternating minimization technique to solve the optimization problem of jointly identifying grouping structures and parameters. The algorithm monotonically decreases the objective function and converges to a local optimum. paragraphs: Multi-task learning trains several tasks jointly on the assumption that their relationships make sharing useful. This paper examines how to learn shared feature representations while also deciding which tasks should share them. The grouping of tasks becomes part of learning, so the method can discover a more selective sharing arrangement.

The authors formulate the joint choice of task groups and model parameters as a mixed integer programming problem. They use alternating minimization to solve it, updating the grouping structure and parameters through an iterative procedure. The objective decreases monotonically, and the algorithm converges to a local optimum, which specifies the scope of its optimization guarantee.

Compared with placing all tasks in one shared group, the method produces statistically significant improvements on three of the four studied datasets. The authors also report advantages over other task-grouping techniques. These findings support learning the sharing structure alongside the representation, while the three-of-four result keeps the empirical claim specific to where significant improvements were observed.
summary.tldr: Jointly learning task groups and shared features improves over sharing across all tasks on three of four studied datasets.

title: Learning with Whom to Share in Multi-task Feature Learning

abstract: Probabilistic principal component analysis (PPCA) seeks a low dimensional representation of a data set in the presence of independent spherical Gaussian noise, Σ = σ^2 I . The maximum likelihood solution for the model is an eigenvalue problem on the sample covariance matrix. In this paper we consider the situation where the data variance is already partially explained by other factors, e.g. conditional dependencies between the covariates, or temporal correlations leaving some residual variance. We decompose the residual variance into its components through a generalised eigenvalue problem, which we call residual component analysis (RCA). We explore a range of new algorithms that arise from the framework, including one that factorises the covariance of a Gaussian density into a low-rank and a sparse-inverse component. We illustrate the ideas on the recovery of a protein-signaling network, a gene expression time-series data set and the recovery of the human skeleton from motion capture 3-D cloud data.

paragraphs: Probabilistic principal component analysis finds a low-dimensional representation while assuming independent Gaussian noise with equal variance in every direction. This paper considers a different situation: some variation has already been explained by known structure, such as dependencies among variables or correlations over time. The remaining task is to identify components in the residual variation.

The authors formulate residual component analysis, or RCA, as a generalized eigenvalue problem. This extends the eigenvalue-based solution associated with probabilistic PCA to a setting that accounts for previously explained variance. The method gives a structured way to ask what additional low-dimensional organization remains after those other factors have been considered.

The framework produces several algorithms, including one that decomposes a Gaussian covariance into a low-rank component and a component with a sparse inverse. The paper illustrates the ideas through protein-signaling network recovery, gene-expression time series, and recovering a human skeleton from three-dimensional motion-capture point clouds. These examples show the range of structures to which residual-variance analysis can be applied.
summary.tldr: Residual component analysis extracts low-dimensional structure from variation left unexplained by existing dependency or temporal models.

title: Residual Components Analysis
